RCT

LTE Radio Conformance Tests — What You Run Daily

TS 36.141 · PUSCH/PUCCH/PRACH waveforms · B3 (1747.5/1842.5 MHz) · PropSim channel emulation · ETM 1.1

Test cadence hierarchy (from your config)
P0 — CI
Continuous Integration gate
Runs on every commit. Fastest possible validation. TS_DL_CI + TS_UL_CI only.
DL: ACLR only — fm frequency, ETM 1.1, 1 BW per band
UL: Reference Sensitivity Level only — fm, ETM 1.1
Bands: b0103=10MHz · b0307=20MHz · b41=10MHz · b082028=10MHz
P1 — Nightly
Nightly regression build
Broader coverage, all three frequency points (fb/fm/ft), no ETM on DL.
DL: PA Protection + modulation analysis + ACLR + dynamic range
UL: Sensitivity + RSSI + PRACH · ETM 1.1
P2 — Regression
Full regression — all BWs
All bandwidth variants: b0103=[5,10,15,20], b0307=[5,20], b41=[5,10,15,20]
DL: Output Power + Freq Error + EVM + time offset + ACLR
UL: Sensitivity + RSSI + PRACH · all 3 frequency points
P3 — Sanity
Quick sanity check
Single BW per band, fm only, ETM 1.1. Fast go/no-go check after config changes.
P4 — Smoke
Smoke test — pre-checks only
test_PreChecks only. Verifies hardware is alive, firmware loads, ports are responsive.
P5 — RSSI Accuracy
RSSI accuracy — fb (band edge)
TS_UL_RSSI_ACC. Runs at fb (band-edge frequency) — the hardest frequency for RSSI accuracy. ETM 1.1.
Tx test deep-dive — downlink (base station transmit)
test_Tx_BS_Output_Power
BS output power accuracy
Verifies RU transmits at declared output power within ±1.5 dB tolerance (normal conditions) or ±3.2 dB (extreme). Measured using EXM channel power measurement at fm.
Normal band 0–3 GHz: pass ±1.5 dB · extreme: ±3.2 dB
Normal band 3–4.2 GHz: pass ±1.5 dB · extreme: ±3.5 dB
Tolerance from your RRH-Thresholds config: channelPower normal band_0_3000: min -1.5 max +1.5
test_Tx_EVM
Error vector magnitude
Modulation quality. 3GPP TS 36.141 limits per ETM: ETM 1.1 tests 64QAM EVM. Measured at fm. Also run OTA (test_Tx_EVM_OTA) for ETM 3.1a.
QPSK: ≤ 17.5% EVM
16QAM: ≤ 12.5% EVM
64QAM: ≤ 8% EVM
test_Tx_ACLR
Adjacent channel leakage ratio
How much TX power leaks into adjacent LTE/UTRA channels. Most frequently run test (CI, Nightly, Regression, Sanity). ETM 1.1, fm.
E-UTRA ACLR ≥ 45 dBc (±1 carrier offset)
UTRA ACLR ≥ 50 dBc (±5/10 MHz offset)
Also runs OTA (test_Tx_ACLR_OTA) at ETM 3.1a. OTA ACLR accounts for beam pattern effects.
test_Tx_FrequencyError
Carrier frequency error
How accurately the RU hits the target center frequency. 3GPP limit: ±0.05 ppm (Wide Area BS). At B3 (1800 MHz) that's ±90 Hz. Caused by oscillator drift, temperature, aging.
Wide Area BS: ±0.05 ppm
Local Area BS: ±0.1 ppm
test_Tx_time_offset
Transmit time offset
Timing accuracy of the transmitted frame vs. expected timing reference. Runs at ETM 1.1, 2a, and 3.1a — broadest ETM coverage of any single test. fm only.
test_lte_Tx_Mask
Spectrum emission mask (SEM)
Checks TX spectrum against 3GPP emission mask out to ±30 MHz and beyond the carrier. ETM 1.1 and 1.2. Broader than ACLR — covers all out-of-band emissions.
SEM failures can cause regulatory non-compliance — blocks deployment approval.
test_lte_Tx_Spurious
Transmitter spurious emissions
Measures harmonic and intermodulation products appearing outside the operating band. TS 36.141 clause checked by spectrum sweep across 30 MHz–12.75 GHz range.
test_Tx_dynamic_range
Output power dynamic range
Tests the RU can accurately produce power from maximum down to minimum (−6 dB, −10 dB, etc.). ETM 2a, 3.1a, 2.0, 3.1. Nightly and Sanity only. Verifies PA linearity across its range.
test_Tx_DLRS
Downlink reference signal quality
Checks the Cell Reference Signal (CRS) EVM and power accuracy. ETM 1.1 only. CRS must be accurate for UE channel estimation — degraded CRS = UE cannot decode DL data.
test_Tx_TimeAlignment
Time alignment error (TAE)
For multi-antenna MIMO: maximum timing difference between antenna branches. 3GPP limit: ≤ 65 ns (intra-band) for release 8+. Critical for MIMO spatial multiplexing quality.
test_Tx_modulation_analysis
Modulation analysis bundle
Compound test = [Output Power + EVM + Freq Error + DLRS + time offset] in one run. Used in Nightly and Sanity. Efficient: 5 measurements from one captured waveform.
Rx test deep-dive — uplink (base station receive)
test_Rx_Reference_Sensitivity_Level
Reference sensitivity (REFSENS)
The minimum signal level the RU can correctly receive. 3GPP defines this as the power level at which PUSCH throughput ≥ 95% of max for a fixed reference channel (FRC).
Wide Area BS: −69 dBm (1.4/3/5/10/15/20 MHz) — from your rx_limits_validation_conditions
Test signal: PUSCH QPSK, 1 layer, specific FRC
Channel: AWGN (baseline), EPA5, EVA70 for fading
Most critical UL test. If REFSENS fails, coverage shrinks — cell edge users cannot connect.
test_Rx_RSSI
Received signal strength indicator
Verifies the RU accurately reports RSSI — the total received power across the channel bandwidth including signal, interference, and noise.
Measured at fm (mid-band frequency)
Compared against expected value with ±2 dB typical tolerance
test_Rx_RSSI_Accuracy
RSSI accuracy at band edge
Tests RSSI accuracy specifically at fb (band-edge frequency) — where filter roll-off causes the most measurement error. P5 cadence only. ETM 1.1.
Band-edge is hardest: filter response is not flat, RU must still accurately report RSSI within spec. Most RUs show highest RSSI error here.
test_lte_Rx_ACS
Adjacent channel selectivity (ACS)
RU's ability to receive a wanted signal in the presence of a strong adjacent channel interferer. Tests all 3 frequency points (fb/fm/ft). Signal is on wanted channel, interferer is ±1 channel offset.
Wanted signal at REFSENS + 3 dB
Interferer: +16 dB above wanted signal (adjacent channel)
Pass: throughput ≥ 95% of max
test_lte_Rx_ICS
In-channel selectivity (ICS)
Ability to receive a weak wanted resource block allocation in the presence of a strong interferer within the same channel bandwidth. Tests all 3 freq points.
test_lte_Rx_NB_blocking
Narrowband blocking
RU must correctly receive wanted signal when a strong CW (narrowband) interferer is present just outside the operating band. Tests fb/fm/ft. Models real-world out-of-band interference.
test_lte_Rx_blocking
In-band blocking
Blocking by a strong signal anywhere within the operating band but on a different channel. fm only. Tests AGC and front-end linearity when a nearby strong signal is present.
test_lte_Rx_intermodulation
Receiver intermodulation
Two interfering signals create an intermodulation product that falls on the wanted signal's frequency. Tests the RU receiver's third-order intercept point (IIP3) — a measure of linearity.
Two interferers: f1 and f2, spaced so 2f1−f2 or 2f2−f1 falls on wanted channel
Tests fb/fm/ft

What each field means in your PUCCH test vectors
FieldValue (example)Meaning

Channel profiles: EPA5 = Extended Pedestrian A at 5 km/h (low mobility, 3 taps). EVA70 = Extended Vehicular A at 70 km/h (medium mobility, 9 taps). ETU300 = Extended Typical Urban at 300 km/h (high speed, 9 taps). These model real-world propagation for receiver sensitivity testing under fading.
OTA

NR OTA Tests — TS 38.141-2 (Radiated Conformance)

Massive MIMO / AAS base stations · EIRP · TRP · EIS · CATR anechoic chamber · FR1 (sub-6 GHz)

OTA testing fundamentals — before any test
WHY OTA?
Why radiated testing exists
Modern 5G NR massive MIMO (AAS — Active Antenna Systems) has the antenna array integrated inside the RU with no external RF connectors. You cannot plug in a cable to the antenna port. The only way to measure the RU's radiated performance is over the air.
Your RU (Metro AAU) is exactly this type — the 3GPP calls it BS Type 1-O (FR1 OTA only) or BS Type 1-H (hybrid — some conducted TAB connectors + OTA at RIB).
EIRP
Effective isotropic radiated power
The power that a hypothetical isotropic (radiating equally in all directions) antenna would need to emit to match the power the DUT radiates in its peak beam direction. EIRP = TX Power + Antenna Gain.
Measured in the far field in the beam peak direction
Units: dBm (absolute) or dBi relative to isotropic
Used for TX conformance: output power, ACLR, EVM
TRP
Total radiated power
Integral of radiated power over the entire sphere (all angles). TRP is lower than peak EIRP — it captures the efficiency of the whole antenna pattern. Requires 3D sphere scan.
TRP = sum of EIRP in all measured directions, weighted by solid angle
Radiated transmit power test (TS 38.141-2 §6.2)
EIS
Effective isotropic sensitivity
Minimum signal power density (W/m²) from a far-field source that the receiver can successfully decode. EIS is the OTA analogue of conducted REFSENS. Lower EIS = more sensitive receiver.
Used for RX conformance: sensitivity, ACS, blocking
Measured in beam peak direction
CATR
Compact antenna test range
The anechoic chamber method used for OTA testing. A parabolic reflector converts the near-field spherical wave from a feed antenna into a plane wave (far-field equivalent) in a much shorter distance. The quiet zone (QZ) is where the DUT sits.
Far-field distance = 2D²/λ. At 2 GHz a 30 cm array needs 60m — CATR reduces this to 2-3m
3GPP-approved method per TR 38.810
BS TYPES
3GPP base station type taxonomy
3GPP defines which test standard applies based on BS type. Your Metro AAU is most likely Type 1-H or 1-O.
Type 1-C: conducted only (traditional macro BTS with external antenna) → TS 38.141-1
Type 1-H: hybrid — has TAB connectors AND OTA RIB → both TS 38.141-1 and 38.141-2
Type 1-O: FR1, OTA only, no connectors → TS 38.141-2 only
Type 2-O: FR2 (mmWave), OTA only → TS 38.141-2 only
OTA transmitter tests — TS 38.141-2 Chapter 6
§6.2 — Radiated TX Power
OTA base station output power (TRP)
Measures total radiated power across the full sphere. Compares measured TRP against the manufacturer's declared TRP value within the specified accuracy window. Requires full 3D sphere measurement.
Declared EIRP per beam identity and beam direction pair
Rated beam EIRP = max power at beam peak direction
Accuracy window specified per operating band in TS 38.104
§6.3 — OTA Output Power
OTA base station output power (EIRP)
Measured at the beam peak direction using EIRP. Verifies the RU hits its declared EIRP within the specified tolerance. Single direction measurement — faster than TRP but less complete.
Test at declared beam peak direction
EIRP tolerance: typically ±3 dB for normal conditions
§6.4 — Output Power Dynamics
OTA output power dynamics
Tests accurate power control across the full dynamic range. RU must hit target power at all levels from maximum down to minimum (−6/−10/−30 dB below max). Tests PA linearity and power control accuracy.
On/off power ratio: ratio of TX-ON to TX-OFF power level
Transient period: time for power to ramp up/down within spec
§6.5.1 — OTA Frequency Error
OTA carrier frequency accuracy
Same concept as conducted freq error but measured OTA. The radiated carrier must be within ±0.05 ppm of the declared frequency. Measured by demodulating the received OFDM signal and comparing subcarrier positions to nominal.
Wide Area BS: ±0.05 ppm (same as conducted)
At 3.5 GHz: ±0.05 ppm = ±175 Hz
§6.5.2 — OTA EVM
OTA error vector magnitude
Modulation quality measured OTA in the beam peak direction. Uses a probe antenna in the CATR quiet zone connected to the signal analyzer. Same EVM limits as conducted, but now includes antenna array effects.
QPSK: ≤ 17.5% · 16QAM: ≤ 12.5% · 64QAM: ≤ 8%
256QAM: ≤ 3.5% (where supported)
Uses NR test models (NR-TM 1.1, 2, 3.1 etc.)
§6.5.3 — OTA TAE
OTA time alignment error
Maximum timing difference between antenna branches, measured OTA. For AAS systems the timing of all antenna elements must be coordinated for correct beamforming. TAE error degrades MIMO and beamforming gain.
Intra-band: ≤ 65 ns (Rel-15/16)
Measured between beam pairs at known angular positions
§6.6.2 — OTA OBW
OTA occupied bandwidth
Bandwidth containing 99% of total radiated power. Must remain within the allocated channel bandwidth. For a 100 MHz NR channel: OBW ≤ 99 MHz (leaving 0.5 MHz guard each side).
§6.6.3 — OTA ACLR
OTA adjacent channel leakage ratio
Measured OTA in beam peak direction. Power leaking into adjacent NR/LTE channels. Adds beamforming pattern effects on top of conducted PA nonlinearity.
NR ACLR: ≥ 45 dBc (sub-6 GHz)
UTRA ACLR: ≥ 45 dBc
§6.6.4 — OTA OBUE
OTA operating band unwanted emissions
Spectrum emission mask measured OTA — checks unwanted emissions across the operating band from the carrier edge out to the channel edge. Tests the overall spectral cleanliness of the radiated signal.
§6.6.5 — OTA Spurious
OTA transmitter spurious emissions
Harmonic and intermodulation products measured OTA across the full spurious domain (9 kHz–12.75 GHz). These can interfere with completely different services (GPS, aviation, emergency services). Strict absolute power limits.
§6.7 — OTA Tx Intermod
OTA transmitter intermodulation
A second signal is injected into the RU transmitter path. The resulting intermodulation products (2f1−f2, etc.) are measured OTA. Tests PA linearity when the antenna port faces a strong reflected signal (antenna mismatch or nearby transmitter).
Requires a second signal generator injecting into the antenna port — different test setup from all other TX tests.
OTA receiver tests — TS 38.141-2 Chapter 7
§7.2 — OTA Sensitivity
OTA reference sensitivity (EIS)
OTA equivalent of conducted REFSENS. The signal generator illuminates the RU via a probe antenna in the CATR. Level is swept down until PUSCH throughput falls below 95%. The level at which this happens (expressed as EIS in dBm/m²) is the sensitivity.
EIS = EIRP of source − path gain + DUT sensitivity angle correction
Measured in beam peak direction
Equivalent to conducted: −69 dBm for Wide Area BS
This is the single hardest OTA test to pass — any beamforming loss, PA noise leakage, or antenna inefficiency shows up directly as degraded EIS.
§7.3 — OTA Dynamic Range
OTA receiver dynamic range
Tests the RU can receive correctly when a strong in-band signal is present simultaneously. AGC must handle the level difference. Measured OTA with wanted signal and interferer both transmitted from the CATR.
§7.4/7.5 — OTA ACS/IB Blocking
OTA in-band selectivity and blocking
ACS: wanted signal + adjacent channel interferer transmitted simultaneously from different angles (DFF chamber) or same angle (CATR). RU must correctly receive the wanted signal at 95% throughput.
Wanted: fm at REFSENS + 3 dB
Interferer: +16 dBm above wanted, ±1 channel offset
§7.6 — OTA OOB Blocking
OTA out-of-band blocking
Strong CW interferer well outside the operating band. Tests the RU receiver front-end filter rejection. If the filter is inadequate, the interferer desensitizes the LNA or saturates the ADC.
§7.7 — OTA Rx Spurious
OTA receiver spurious emissions
The RU receiver can itself radiate spurious signals via the antenna (LO leakage, oscillator harmonics). These must be below specified absolute limits. Unique to OTA — the antenna is radiating these spurious signals into free space.
§7.8 — OTA Rx Intermod
OTA receiver intermodulation
Two strong interferers at f1 and f2 create an intermodulation product at 2f1−f2 that falls on the wanted channel. Tests RU receiver front-end IIP3. Critical for deployments near existing base stations on adjacent bands.

Test Config — JSON Reference Decoder

Test-IDs · Group-IDs · Cadence-IDs · Thresholds · rx_limits — what every field means

Frequency point meanings (fm / fb / ft)
fm — mid-band
Channel center frequency
The nominal center of the operating band. For B3: 1800 MHz DL. This is the most representative operating frequency. All CI and smoke tests use fm only — fewest variables, fastest result.
fb — band-bottom
Lower band edge frequency
First channel in the operating band. Most affected by the high-pass response of the band-select filter. RSSI accuracy and blocking tests at fb reveal filter roll-off effects on receiver performance.
ft — band-top
Upper band edge frequency
Last channel in the operating band. Affected by the low-pass response of the band-select filter. Together fb/fm/ft give full coverage of performance variation across the band.
ETM — E-UTRA Test Model meanings
ETM 1.1
Full allocation 64QAM
All resource blocks allocated, 64QAM modulation, full power. Used for ACLR, EVM, output power — represents peak stress on the PA and spectral performance.
ETM 2a
Partial allocation
Sub-set of RBs allocated. Used for dynamic range tests where partial loading is required. Also used for time offset testing to see offset behavior under partial load.
ETM 3.1a
Multi-antenna reference signal
Includes cell-specific reference signals across multiple antenna ports. Used for EVM and ACLR OTA tests — the reference signal structure is needed for beam coherence measurements.

A01 RF fundamentals — signals, power, frequency, wavelength Beginner click to expand▾
1.1 What is RF?
RF stands for Radio Frequency — electromagnetic waves that carry energy and information through space without any physical conductor. The RF spectrum spans from roughly 3 Hz to 300 GHz. Below 20 kHz is audio; above 300 GHz is infrared/optical. Everything in between is RF.
An electromagnetic wave has two components oscillating perpendicular to each other and perpendicular to the direction of travel: the electric field (E) and the magnetic field (H). These cannot exist independently — changing E creates H and vice versa (Maxwell's equations). The wave travels at the speed of light c = 3×10⁸ m/s in free space.
Key bands you work with:
BandFrequencyWavelength (λ)Use case
B28700 MHz42.9 cmRural coverage — penetrates buildings, long range
B8900 MHz33.3 cmWide area coverage, voice fallback
B31800 MHz16.7 cmUrban capacity + coverage balance
B12100 MHz14.3 cmUMTS/LTE urban capacity
B412500 MHz12.0 cmTDD, high capacity in dense areas
Why B28 gives better range than B1: Lower frequency → longer wavelength → lower path loss exponent in the Friis equation. At 700 MHz, a signal travels ~10 dB further for the same power compared to 2100 MHz. That's why B28 is used for rural/coverage layers and B1/B3/B41 for urban capacity.
1.2 dB — The most important unit in RF
Almost everything in RF is expressed in decibels (dB). The reason: RF engineers deal with power ranges spanning 12 orders of magnitude — from 100 W transmitters to −120 dBm received signals. Logarithmic scale makes this manageable.
Power ratio in dB: dB = 10 · log₁₀(P₂/P₁)
Voltage ratio in dB: dB = 20 · log₁₀(V₂/V₁)
Power ratiodB valueMemory trick
2×+3 dB"Double = 3 dB"
10×+10 dB"10× = 10 dB"
100×+20 dB10 dB + 10 dB
1000×+30 dB1 W when P₁ = 1 mW
0.5×−3 dB"Half power = −3 dB"
0.1×−10 dBOne tenth
dBm = power in dB relative to 1 milliwatt. Absolute power unit. 0 dBm = 1 mW.
dBmActual powerContext
+43 dBm20 WTypical macro base station TX (per port)
+30 dBm1 WSmall cell TX
+23 dBm200 mWMobile phone max TX
0 dBm1 mWVNA source output level
−10 dBm100 µWTypical signal into EXA
−69 dBm126 pW3GPP LTE REFSENS limit (Wide Area BS)
−107 dBm0.2 fWThermal noise in 10 MHz BW at 290 K
Rules for dB arithmetic:
Multiply power ratios → ADD their dB values. A 3 dB attenuator followed by a 10 dB amplifier = net +7 dB gain.
dBm + dB = dBm. Input power 0 dBm + 20 dB gain amp = +20 dBm output. ✓
dBm + dBm is MEANINGLESS. You cannot add absolute power levels in dB. (Two 0 dBm sources combined = +3 dBm, not 0 dBm.)
dBm − dBm = dB. Output (−10 dBm) − input (−30 dBm) = gain of 20 dB. ✓
1.3 Impedance — why everything is 50 Ω
All RF equipment uses 50 Ω impedance as the standard interface. This is a compromise: 30 Ω gives minimum loss in a coaxial cable, 77 Ω gives maximum power handling. 50 Ω is the geometric mean — chosen by military in the 1940s and it stuck. Every connector, cable, port on your EXA, EXM, and VNA is 50 Ω.
When the impedance of connected devices doesn't match (source impedance ≠ load impedance), some power is reflected back rather than transmitted. This is the cause of return loss, VSWR, and all the reflections you see in VNA measurements.
Reflection coefficient: Γ = (ZL − Z0) / (ZL + Z0). If ZL = Z0 = 50 Ω: Γ = 0 (no reflection). If ZL = open (∞): Γ = +1 (all reflected). If ZL = short (0): Γ = −1 (all reflected, 180° phase shift).
Return loss: RL = −20·log₁₀|Γ| dB. Higher return loss = better match. Target: >10 dB for antennas, >20 dB for connectors and cables.
A02 Noise, noise figure, sensitivity, dynamic range Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾
2.1 Thermal noise — the fundamental floor
Every resistor at temperature T generates random voltage fluctuations due to thermal agitation of electrons. This is Johnson-Nyquist noise. The available noise power is:
P_noise = k · T · B
Where k = Boltzmann's constant = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, T = temperature in Kelvin (290 K = 17°C = room temp), B = bandwidth in Hz.
At 290 K: P_noise = kTB = −174 dBm/Hz (the "kTB" number every RF engineer memorizes).
Channel BWNoise powerCalculation
1 MHz−114 dBm−174 + 60 (10·log10(10⁶))
10 MHz−104 dBm−174 + 70
20 MHz−101 dBm−174 + 73
100 MHz (NR)−94 dBm−174 + 80
This is why your EXA's noise floor changes when you change RBW. RBW 100 kHz → noise floor ≈ −114 dBm. RBW 1 MHz → noise floor rises to −104 dBm. Same physics.
2.2 Noise figure (NF)
A real amplifier or receiver adds noise on top of the input thermal noise. Noise Figure (NF) quantifies how much worse the SNR gets as the signal passes through a component.
NF = SNR_in (dB) − SNR_out (dB)
NF = 0 dB would be a perfect, noiseless component. Real LNAs: NF = 1–3 dB. Mixers: 5–8 dB. Long cables at high frequency: significant NF contribution.
Effective noise figure (Friis formula for cascaded stages):
NF_total = NF₁ + (NF₂−1)/G₁ + (NF₃−1)/(G₁·G₂) + ...
Where NF values are linear (not dB) and G is gain (linear). The first stage (LNA) dominates. This is why the LNA quality matters most for receiver sensitivity — everything after it is "noise that follows the first gain stage."
Practical example for your RU receiver (B3, 10 MHz):
Thermal noise floor: −174 + 70 = −104 dBm
LNA NF = 3 dB → receiver noise floor = −104 + 3 = −101 dBm
Required SNR for LTE QPSK (1 RB): ~−1 dB
Implementation margin (filter losses, ADC, etc.): ~3 dB
REFSENS ≈ −101 − 1 + 3 = −99 dBm → 3GPP specifies −69 dBm (30 dB margin for real deployments)
2.3 Dynamic range
Dynamic range is the ratio between the strongest signal a receiver can handle and the weakest it can detect. It is limited at the bottom by the noise floor and at the top by non-linearity (compression or clipping).
For a spectrum analyzer (your EXA):
Bottom limit: Noise floor = kTB + NF of analyzer front end. Set by thermal noise and RBW.
Top limit: Mixer 1 dB compression point (P1dB). Above this, gain compresses, measurements are invalid.
Spurious-free dynamic range (SFDR): Range where the fundamental signal is visible above noise AND no third-order intermodulation products exceed the noise floor. SFDR = (2/3) · (IIP3 − kTBF).
For your RU receiver: Must handle UL signals from −120 dBm (cell edge UE) to −30 dBm (nearby UE at full power) — a 90 dB range. The AGC system adjusts LNA gain and attenuators to keep the ADC input within its linear range across this entire range.
When you do ACS/blocking tests, you're deliberately testing the edge of this dynamic range. A strong blocking signal in the adjacent channel partially saturates the front end, raising the effective noise floor and reducing the wanted signal's SNR below the required level.
A03 Filters, S-parameters, VNA measurements in depth Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾
3.1 S-parameters — the language of VNA measurements
S-parameters (Scattering parameters) describe how RF signals are transmitted and reflected at the ports of a device. For a 2-port device (like a filter or cable), there are 4 S-parameters organized in a 2×2 matrix:
ParameterMeaningWhat you measureGood value
S11Input reflection (Port 1)Return loss / input match< −10 dB (VSWR < 2:1)
S21Forward transmission (Port 1→2)Insertion loss / gainNear 0 dB for cable; depends on filter
S12Reverse transmission (Port 2→1)Reverse isolation= S21 for passive, <−40 dB for amplifier
S22Output reflection (Port 2)Output match< −10 dB
S-parameters are complex numbers — they have both magnitude AND phase. Your E5071C measures both simultaneously. Log Magnitude format shows just the magnitude in dB. Phase format shows the angle. Smith chart shows both on one plot.
3.2 What the E5071C screen is showing (your filter)
Your E5071C screen throughout the videos shows S21 of what appears to be a bandpass filter or duplexer. Let's decode what you're looking at:
The passband (left side, wiggly trace): The frequency range where the filter lets signals through. The ripple you see is intentional — it's the equiripple characteristic of a Chebyshev filter design. The amplitude varies between the ripple peaks and dips (typically 0.1 to 1 dB ripple). Insertion loss at the center of the passband tells you how much signal you lose just from passing through the filter (typically 0.5–2 dB for a good diplexer).
The rolloff (middle, sharp drop): The filter transition band — where it goes from passing to blocking. A steep rolloff means better selectivity — the filter can separate closely-spaced signals. Chebyshev designs sacrifice passband flatness for steeper rolloff. Elliptic (Cauer) filters add transmission zeros in the stopband for even sharper rolloff.
The stopband (right side, flat floor): How much the filter blocks unwanted signals. Your trace shows ~50–60 dB rejection. This is how much isolation the duplexer provides between TX and RX bands — absolutely critical. If the TX signal at +43 dBm gets −50 dB isolation → only −7 dBm reaches the RX input — still easily detectable but the duplexer filter would reject it further. A real duplexer needs >50 dB between TX and RX port.
3.3 Filter types — your practical guide
Filter typePassbandRolloffBest for
ButterworthMaximally flat (no ripple)Gentle (−20 dB/decade per pole)Wideband systems where flatness matters
ChebyshevEquiripple (your E5071C trace!)Steeper than ButterworthMost bandpass/duplexer filters in cellular
Elliptic (Cauer)Equiripple in pass AND stopSteepest possible for given orderDuplexers needing extreme TX/RX isolation
BesselFlat, linear phaseGentlePulse/wideband signals where group delay flatness matters
3.4 VNA calibration in detail — why and how
A VNA works by sweeping a source signal across a frequency range, injecting it into the DUT, and measuring what comes back (S11) and what comes out (S21). The problem: the cables, connectors, and adapters between the VNA port and your DUT have their own S-parameters (loss, reflections). These systematic errors contaminate your measurement.
The three systematic errors the SOLT cal corrects:
Directivity error: The VNA's directional coupler isn't perfect — some of the incident signal leaks into the reflected wave measurement even with a perfect match at the DUT.
Source match error: The VNA source isn't perfectly matched to 50 Ω — some reflected signal from the DUT bounces back off the source and re-enters the DUT.
Frequency response error: The test cables, connectors, and adapters have their own insertion loss and phase shift which varies with frequency.
SOLT procedure step by step:
Short: Connect a short circuit (0 Ω) to Port 1 at the calibration reference plane. The VNA measures: all power should reflect back with 180° phase shift (Γ = −1). Any deviation = directivity and source match errors at that frequency.
Open: Connect an open circuit (no connection). All power reflects, 0° phase shift (Γ = +1). The known parasitic capacitance of the open is stored in the cal kit — the VNA uses it to distinguish directivity from source match.
Load: Connect a precision 50 Ω termination. Should produce Γ = 0 (perfect match, no reflection). Any measured signal = raw directivity error of the coupler. This establishes the error floor.
Thru (2-port cal only): Connect Port 1 directly to Port 2. Now the VNA can measure transmission errors — cable loss, adapter insertion loss, phase delay.
After these four measurements the VNA solves 12 error terms (for full 2-port cal) and removes them from subsequent DUT measurements. Your calibration reference plane is now at the tip of the cable/connector where you connected the Short/Open/Load — everything between VNA port and that tip is removed from the measurement.
If you move or flex the cable after calibration, the cal is invalidated. The cable's S-parameters change with flex. Always recalibrate if the setup changes. Check the cal status indicator — 'C' = active, 'Cc' = interpolated (acceptable but not ideal), no 'C' = no cal, results are uncorrected and unreliable.
3.5 Time domain analysis on the E5071C
One of the most powerful E5071C features is converting the frequency sweep into a time-domain response. The math is an inverse FFT (IFFT) of the swept S-parameter data. The result shows when reflections arrive at the measurement port — which tells you where they come from.
A signal travels at roughly 2×10⁸ m/s in typical coaxial cable (velocity factor ~0.67). So a reflection arriving at t = 5 ns came from a point 5 ns × 2×10⁸ m/s / 2 = 50 cm away from the calibration plane (divide by 2 because signal makes a round trip).
Spike at t=0: Reflection at the calibration plane itself — connector interface, impedance step at the DUT port.
Spike at t=2 ns: Reflection 20 cm down the cable — could be a kinked cable, damaged connector, or moisture ingress.
Spike at t=10 ns: Reflection 1 m from the port — cable end, unterminated stub, or mismatch at the antenna.
For your RU antenna port verification: do a 1-port S11 measurement in time domain. You should see a small reflection at t=0 (connector), then ideally nothing else. Any additional spike between the connector and the antenna location = impedance discontinuity in the feed path that's causing reflections and reducing radiated power.
A04 LTE/NR air interface — OFDM, resource blocks, FDD/TDD, physical channels Intermediate click to expand▾
4.1 Why OFDM?
A wideband channel (20 MHz of LTE) has frequency-selective fading — some frequencies fade more than others depending on the multipath environment. In a single-carrier system, a deep fade at one frequency wipes out a chunk of your data. OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing) slices the wideband channel into N narrow subcarriers, each so narrow (15 kHz in LTE) that it experiences flat fading. A fade at one subcarrier only kills data on that one subcarrier — easy to correct with FEC coding.
OFDM mechanics: N subcarriers spaced Δf = 15 kHz apart. Each subcarrier carries one OFDM symbol over duration T_symbol = 1/Δf = 66.7 µs (plus cyclic prefix). All subcarriers transmitted simultaneously — their orthogonality ensures zero ICI (inter-carrier interference) at the exact sampling points.
LTE OFDM structure:
Subcarrier spacing: 15 kHz (also 7.5 kHz for MBSFN)
Symbol duration: 66.7 µs + cyclic prefix (4.69 µs normal, 16.67 µs extended)
Resource element (RE): 1 subcarrier × 1 symbol slot = smallest unit
Resource block (RB): 12 subcarriers × 7 symbols (0.5 ms slot) = 84 REs
Frame: 10 ms → 10 subframes → 20 slots
Channel BWNumber of RBsSubcarriers (used)
1.4 MHz672
5 MHz25300
10 MHz50600
15 MHz75900
20 MHz1001200
This is why the EXM shows 50 RBs when testing B3 at 10 MHz and 100 RBs at 20 MHz. Each colored cell in the RB map = one resource block. Red = fully allocated and transmitting, blue/dark = idle or lower power.
4.2 FDD vs TDD — how your bands differ
FDD (Frequency Division Duplex): Uplink and downlink use separate, paired frequency bands simultaneously. The gap between UL and DL is the duplex gap.
BandUL frequency (base station RX)DL frequency (base station TX)Duplex gap
B11920–1980 MHz2110–2170 MHz130 MHz
B31710–1785 MHz1805–1880 MHz95 MHz
B8880–915 MHz925–960 MHz45 MHz
B28703–748 MHz758–803 MHz55 MHz
Your PUCCH test vectors for B3 use DL_Freq 1842.5 MHz (mid of 1805–1880 DL band) and UL_Freq 1747.5 MHz (mid of 1710–1785 UL band). The duplexer in the RU separates these — the TX filter passes 1805–1880 and the RX filter passes 1710–1785, with >50 dB isolation between them.
TDD (Time Division Duplex): UL and DL share the same frequency, alternating in time according to a configurable UL/DL ratio. B41 (2496–2690 MHz) is TDD. The base station transmits in DL subframes and receives in UL subframes. There is a Guard Period (GP) between DL and UL to allow propagation delay from far UEs to clear.
This is why B41 requires frame trigger on the EXA/EXM. Without it, you capture a mix of DL + UL time slots in the same measurement window. EVM calculated over mixed DL+UL data is meaningless — the reference signals (CRS/DMRS) are only in DL subframes.
4.3 Physical channels — DL and UL
Downlink (base station TX, what you measure with EXM Channel Power / EVM):
PDSCH: Physical Downlink Shared Channel — actual user data. The bulk of DL bandwidth. Carries IP packets to users. Uses QPSK/16QAM/64QAM/256QAM depending on channel quality.
PDCCH: Physical Downlink Control Channel — scheduling grants. Tells UEs which RBs they are allocated, what MCS to use. 1–3 OFDM symbols at the start of each subframe.
PBCH: Physical Broadcast Channel — system information (cell ID, bandwidth, frame structure). Transmitted every 40 ms. The first signal a UE decodes when searching for a cell.
CRS: Cell-specific Reference Signals — pilot tones used by UE for channel estimation and signal quality measurement (RSRP, RSRQ). Always present on specific RE positions regardless of traffic. This is what test_Tx_DLRS (downlink reference signal test) checks.
Uplink (base station RX, what you test with PUCCH waveforms):
PUSCH: Physical Uplink Shared Channel — UE data. Your sensitivity tests inject a known PUSCH waveform and measure whether the RU can decode it at the required signal level.
PUCCH: Physical Uplink Control Channel — control info only: ACK/NACK feedback (did the UE receive the downlink data?), Scheduling Request (UE asking for UL allocation), Channel Quality Indicator (CQI). Occupies the edges of the UL bandwidth (first and last 6 RBs) and frequency-hops between the two edges each slot to exploit frequency diversity.
PRACH: Physical Random Access Channel — initial access. UE sends a Zadoff-Chu preamble sequence to establish uplink timing synchronization. The base station measures the arrival time to compute Timing Advance (TA) — how early the UE must transmit to arrive at the right time.
4.4 PUCCH formats — decoding your JSON config
FormatContentBitsModulationYour waveforms
Format 1Scheduling Request (SR) only0 bits (on/off keying)OOKPUCCH_format_1_*MHz_rnti_0.wfm
Format 1a1-bit ACK/NACK1BPSKPUCCH_format_1a_*MHz_rnti_0.wfm
Format 1b2-bit ACK/NACK2QPSKPUCCH_format_1b_*MHz_rnti_0.wfm
Format 1b_csACK/NACK + channel selection2QPSKPUCCH_format_1bcs_*MHz.wfm
Format 1a_SRSR + ACK/NACK combined1+SRBPSK+OOKPUCCH_format_1a_SR_delta_*_10MHz.wfm
delta_shift (ΔS): Controls the cyclic shift spacing between PUCCH users sharing the same resource block. ΔS=1 allows up to 36 simultaneous users per RB. ΔS=2 allows 18 users. Your config tests both: some vectors use delta_shfit=1 (for 36-user capacity tests, num_resource 20_of_36) and delta_shfit=2 (for 18-user capacity, num_resource 10_of_18). This directly tests the RU's PUCCH receiver's multi-user separability.
A05 TX chain — PA, linearity, EVM, ACLR, DPD in full depth Intermediate click to expand▾
5.1 Power amplifier (PA) — the heart of the TX chain
The PA takes the modulated signal from the DAC and amplifies it to the required output power (+43 dBm for a macro RU). The PA is the most power-hungry and performance-critical component in the RU.
PA operating regions:
Linear region: Output power increases proportionally with input. Gain is constant. EVM and ACLR are excellent here. The PA runs cool and efficient but doesn't deliver maximum power.
Compression region: Input drive is high enough that the PA begins to saturate. Gain decreases (gain compression). For every 1 dB increase in input, output increases less than 1 dB. EVM and ACLR degrade significantly.
P1dB (1 dB compression point): The output power at which the gain has dropped by 1 dB from its small-signal value. Typically the maximum usable output power for linear operation. OFDM signals must be backed off from P1dB due to their high PAPR.
Saturation: Maximum output power. Gain = 0. Signal is severely clipped. Never operate here for communications — catastrophic EVM and ACLR.
5.2 PAPR — why OFDM is hard on PAs
PAPR (Peak-to-Average Power Ratio) is the ratio between the peak instantaneous power and the average power of a signal. An unmodulated CW signal has PAPR = 0 dB (peak = average). An OFDM signal with N subcarriers can have peaks up to N times the average when all subcarriers align in phase simultaneously — in theory PAPR = 10·log10(N) dB.
For a 20 MHz LTE signal (100 RBs × 12 subcarriers = 1200 subcarriers), theoretical max PAPR ≈ 31 dB. Practical PAPR (with random data, 0.01% exceedance probability) ≈ 10–12 dB.
This means: if you want average output power of +43 dBm, the PA must handle peaks of +43 + 12 = +55 dBm without clipping. This forces the PA to have a much higher P1dB than the average output power, making it less efficient. PA efficiency at back-off is terrible — a PA might be 50% efficient at P1dB but only 20% efficient at 10 dB back-off.
This is why modern RUs use DPD (digital pre-distortion) — it lets the PA operate closer to P1dB while maintaining acceptable EVM/ACLR, significantly improving efficiency and reducing heat generation.
5.3 Nonlinearity — where EVM and ACLR come from
A real PA's output is not perfectly proportional to its input. The transfer function can be modeled as a polynomial:
y(t) = a₁·x(t) + a₂·x²(t) + a₃·x³(t) + ...
The linear term (a₁) is the desired gain. Higher-order terms create distortion:
Even-order terms (a₂): Create harmonics at 2f, 3f and DC offset. Filtered out easily by the band-select filter. Less of a problem in practice.
Odd-order terms (a₃, a₅): Create intermodulation products that fall INSIDE the signal band and adjacent channels. Cannot be filtered without removing wanted signal. This is the source of EVM degradation and ACLR.
How ACLR happens physically: Consider two tones at f1 and f2 within your LTE channel. The a₃ term produces products at 2f1−f2 and 2f2−f1 — these land in the adjacent channel, appearing as spectral regrowth extending outside your carrier. With 1200 subcarriers, there are billions of such mixing products, creating the characteristic "skirt" shape seen on the spectrum analyzer when a PA is driven into compression.
How EVM happens: AM-AM distortion (gain changes with power level) and AM-PM distortion (phase shift changes with power level) both cause each subcarrier's constellation point to move away from its ideal position. The distance from ideal position = EVM. High PAPR signals constantly sweep through the PA's nonlinear region, creating EVM that varies per symbol.
5.4 IP3 — the linearity figure of merit
The Third-order Intercept Point (IP3) is the theoretical power level where the fundamental output and the third-order intermodulation product would be equal (they never actually reach this point because the PA saturates first). Higher IP3 = more linear device.
IIP3 (Input-referred IP3): The input power at which this theoretical crossing would occur. For an LNA: IIP3 typically −10 to +10 dBm. For a PA: IIP3 typically well above P1dB.
OIP3 (Output-referred IP3): OIP3 = IIP3 + Gain. Relationship between IIP3, OIP3, and P1dB: OIP3 ≈ P1dB + 9 to 11 dB (rule of thumb for class AB PAs).
Cascaded IIP3 (Friis for nonlinearity):
1/IIP3_total = 1/IIP3₁ + G₁/IIP3₂ + G₁G₂/IIP3₃ + ...
Unlike noise (where first stage dominates), for IIP3 the LAST high-gain stage often dominates. The PA is typically the worst nonlinear element in the entire chain and the one DPD must correct.
5.5 DPD — Digital Pre-Distortion
DPD pre-distorts the input signal with the mathematical inverse of the PA's nonlinearity, so the PA's output is linear even when the PA itself isn't. Think of it as teaching the PA to lie about its input so that the actual output is correct.
How DPD works in your RU:
1. Observation path: A small coupler takes a sample of the PA output and routes it back to a dedicated ADC (the "DPD observation receiver").
2. Error calculation: The baseband processor compares the PA output (observed) with the desired output (reference). The difference = distortion introduced by the PA.
3. Model update: An adaptive algorithm (LMS, RLS, or more complex) updates the DPD model coefficients to reduce this error.
4. Pre-distortion: The updated model pre-distorts the TX signal so the PA output is linearized.
DPD can improve ACLR by 10–20 dB and EVM by 5–10 dB while allowing the PA to operate at higher average power (better efficiency). The limitation: DPD must be retrained when the PA characteristics change due to temperature, aging, or power level changes. This is why you see DPD adaptation time in your test setup — the RU must "settle" after a power change before measurements are valid.
If DPD fails or is miscalibrated (wrong observation path calibration, coefficient overflow, wrong center frequency), you'll see sudden ACLR degradation of 10–20 dB. This is distinct from a PA hardware failure. Always check whether DPD is enabled and converged before declaring an ACLR failure as a hardware fault.
A06 RX chain — LNA, mixer, ADC, AGC, sensitivity in depth Intermediate click to expand▾
6.1 Receiver chain architecture
The RU receiver takes the UE's uplink signal from the antenna, downconverts it to baseband, and hands off to the digital baseband processor for decoding. The chain is:
Antenna → Duplexer/Filter → LNA → Band-pass filter → Mixer → IF filter → ADC → Digital baseband
Each stage's role and what can go wrong:
Duplexer RX filter: Passes the UL band (e.g. 1710–1785 MHz for B3), blocks the DL band (1805–1880 MHz) and everything else. This is the first and most important rejection of out-of-band blockers. Your E5071C S21 measurement of the filter is this stage.
LNA (Low Noise Amplifier): First active component. Sets the system NF (Friis formula — first stage dominates). Must balance NF, IIP3, and gain. Low NF = better REFSENS. High IIP3 = better blocking performance. Usually the gain is 15–25 dB. Temperature and aging affect NF by 0.1–0.5 dB over life.
Band-pass filter (post-LNA): Additional image reject filtering and further blocker suppression after the first gain stage. Prevents large off-frequency blockers from hitting the mixer with high power.
Downconversion mixer: Multiplies the RF signal with a local oscillator (LO) signal to shift frequency to baseband (direct conversion) or IF. The LO is generated by the RU's frequency synthesizer (PLL). LO phase noise here degrades the downconverted signal's SNR — you see this as EVM on the received signal.
ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter): Samples the analog baseband at Nyquist rate. Quantization noise = 6.02·N_bits + 1.76 dB SQNR (signal-to-quantization-noise ratio). A 14-bit ADC: ~86 dB SQNR. This sets the ADC dynamic range ceiling. You must keep the signal level well within this range using AGC.
6.2 REFSENS derivation from first principles
Let's derive the −69 dBm REFSENS spec for a Wide Area BS from the physics, then understand why the actual implementation can do better.
Step 1 — Thermal noise floor at 10 MHz BW:
P_noise = kTB = −174 dBm/Hz + 10·log10(10×10⁶ Hz) = −174 + 70 = −104 dBm
Step 2 — Add typical receiver NF (LNA + rest of chain):
Noise floor at RX input = −104 + NF_total. Assume NF = 5 dB → −99 dBm
Step 3 — Required SNR for the test signal: The REFSENS test uses a Fixed Reference Channel (FRC) with QPSK modulation, 1/3 coding rate, in 1 RB. Required SNR for 95% throughput: approximately −1 to +1 dB depending on exact conditions.
Step 4 — Sensitivity:
REFSENS = noise floor + required SNR = −99 + (−1) = −100 dBm
3GPP specifies −69 dBm as the required minimum REFSENS. This gives ~31 dB of margin over the theoretical limit. Why so much margin? In practice:
  • The test measures with 1 RB allocated — not optimal usage of the full channel bandwidth
  • Real implementations have ADC quantization noise, IQ imbalance, LO phase noise all adding to the noise floor
  • The spec must accommodate low-cost/small-cell base stations with worse NF than premium macros
  • A modern macro RU with a good LNA can achieve REFSENS of −100 dBm or better — well beyond the −69 dBm spec
6.3 ACS — Adjacent Channel Selectivity in depth
ACS tests whether the RU can correctly receive a wanted signal on channel fm when a strong interferer is present on an adjacent channel (fm ± channel bandwidth). The interferer level is +16 dBm above the wanted signal.
What happens physically:
At the LNA input: Both wanted (at −69 dBm) and interferer (at −53 dBm) enter simultaneously. The LNA amplifies both. If the interferer is strong enough, it partially compresses the LNA, raising the effective NF seen by the wanted signal. This is called desensitization or blocking gain compression.
At the mixer: If the IF filter's rejection at ±BW is insufficient, the interferer leaks into the wanted channel's IF bandwidth, adding noise. The mixer's IIP3 also generates intermodulation products between the interferer and any other signal that can land in the wanted band.
At the ADC: If the interferer level causes the ADC to clip or use too many quantization levels for the interferer, there are fewer bits available for the wanted signal — degraded effective resolution on the wanted signal.
A good ACS result requires high IIP3 in the LNA, steep IF filter rolloff, and sufficient ADC headroom. The duplexer RX filter's rejection of out-of-band signals is the first line of defense — if the filter is good, the LNA never sees the full interferer power.
6.4 AGC — Automatic Gain Control
The received UL signal level can vary from −120 dBm (distant cell-edge UE at minimum power) to −30 dBm (nearby UE at full power) — a 90 dB range. The ADC has maybe 70–86 dB of useful dynamic range. AGC maps the received signal into the ADC's optimal input range.
AGC control loop:
Measurement: The digital baseband measures the received signal power every subframe (1 ms).
Decision: If signal is too strong → increase attenuation (reduce LNA gain or add a digital attenuator). If too weak → decrease attenuation.
Settling time: AGC takes 1–3 subframes to settle after a large level change. During this time, the SNR may be suboptimal. This is why throughput-based tests use long averaging (many subframes) and ignore initial transient.
The RSSI measurement in your tests (test_Rx_RSSI) verifies that after AGC settles, the reported RSSI value accurately reflects the actual received power. The RSSI accuracy test at band edge (test_Rx_RSSI_Accuracy at fb) is harder because the filter roll-off means the AGC must account for the non-flat band edge response.
A07 Massive MIMO, beamforming, OTA physics in full depth Advanced click to expand▾
7.1 Antenna fundamentals
Antenna gain: An antenna doesn't amplify — it redistributes power. Gain G (in dBi) describes how much more power is radiated in the peak direction compared to an isotropic antenna that radiates equally in all directions. A 17 dBi antenna radiates 50× more power in its peak direction than an isotropic antenna — by concentrating energy spatially rather than amplifying.
EIRP = TX power (dBm) + Antenna gain (dBi)
Example: Your RU TX = +43 dBm (20 W) per port. Antenna array gain = 18 dBi (64 elements). EIRP = 43 + 18 = +61 dBm (1.26 kW equivalent isotropic). This is the number that 3GPP tests under TS 38.141-2 §6.3.
Beamwidth: The angular range over which the antenna gain is within 3 dB of peak. Narrower beamwidth = higher gain but less spatial coverage. A 64-element massive MIMO array: horizontal beamwidth ~5°, vertical beamwidth ~8°. The beam must be steered electronically to serve different users.
7.2 Massive MIMO — from theory to your Metro AAU
Traditional macro base stations use 2–8 antennas. Massive MIMO uses 32, 64, 128, or 192 antenna elements. The advantages are profound:
Array gain: N antenna elements coherently combined → N× power (in linear terms) = 10·log10(N) dB gain. 64 elements: +18 dB. This 18 dB extra gain vs. a single antenna can be traded for coverage, capacity, or reduced TX power (for energy efficiency).
Spatial multiplexing: Use the many degrees of freedom to serve multiple users simultaneously in the same time-frequency resource. With 64 antennas, the base station can create 8–16 independent spatial beams, each carrying data for a different user — multiplying spectral efficiency by 8–16×.
Interference rejection: Steer nulls toward interfering sources. The many antennas allow precise spatial filtering — useful in dense deployments where neighboring cells cause significant interference.
Your Metro AAU has this full 2D array architecture. The antenna elements are arranged in rows and columns on a flat panel. Horizontal steering controls azimuth (left-right). Vertical steering controls elevation (tilt — crucial for controlling which floors of a building or which cells receive the beam).
7.3 Beamforming — the physics
Beamforming works by adjusting the phase (and optionally amplitude) of the signal fed to each antenna element so that the radiated waves from all elements add constructively in the desired direction and destructively in other directions.
Simple 2-element example: Two antennas separated by λ/2. If both antennas transmit at the same phase (0° difference), the waves add constructively broadside (perpendicular to the array) and cancel end-fire (along the array axis). To steer the beam to angle θ, introduce a phase difference Δφ = π·sin(θ) between the elements. For a 64-element array, this creates very fine angular resolution.
Analog beamforming: Phase shifters in the RF path (before or after the PA). Fast switching, simple, but can only form one beam at a time. Used in FR2 (mmWave) due to the large number of elements and cost of having a full radio chain per element.
Digital beamforming: Each element has its own full radio chain (DAC, PA, LNA, ADC). Phase and amplitude weights applied in the digital baseband. Can form multiple simultaneous beams. Used in FR1 massive MIMO. More expensive but full flexibility.
Hybrid beamforming (your Metro AAU): Combination of analog sub-arrays and digital chains. Fewer digital chains than elements — cost/performance tradeoff. Typical: 8 digital chains driving 64 antenna elements via analog phase shifters (8 elements per chain).
7.4 Why OTA testing is unavoidable for AAS
In a traditional macro base station, you can unplug the antenna and connect a cable to a specific TRX port. You measure one PA at a time. The antenna gain is known separately. The conducted power is the reference.
In your Metro AAU, the antennas are permanently integrated. There is no connector where you can isolate "the antenna" from "the PA." The antenna elements couple to each other (mutual coupling) — the radiation pattern of element N depends on what all other elements N−1, N+1, etc. are doing. You cannot characterize the antenna pattern from element measurements alone.
The only correct way to characterize the full system — antenna + PA + beamforming weights all working together — is to measure the radiated power in the far field. This is exactly what OTA testing does. The CATR creates a far-field equivalent plane wave in a compact space, and the probe antenna measures what the RU actually radiates at each beam angle.
7.5 The CATR — compact antenna test range explained
The far-field distance for an antenna of physical size D at wavelength λ is:
Far field distance = 2D²/λ (Fraunhofer distance)
For a 30 cm massive MIMO panel at 2 GHz (λ = 15 cm): far field distance = 2 × 0.3² / 0.15 = 1.2 m. That's manageable. But at 3.5 GHz for a 50 cm panel: 2 × 0.5² / 0.086 = 5.8 m. And at 28 GHz for a 10 cm mmWave module: 2 × 0.1² / 0.011 = 1.8 m. So for FR2 the chamber can be compact; for FR1 massive MIMO panels, 5–10m far-field distances would require a very large chamber.
The CATR solves this by using a parabolic reflector to convert the spherical wave from a feed antenna into a plane wave over a short distance. The feed antenna sits at the focal point of the reflector. The plane wave exists in the "quiet zone" — the region where the wave is sufficiently flat and uniform for measurement. The DUT sits in the quiet zone, and a probe antenna measures the received signal level at various DUT orientations controlled by a precision turntable.
What happens during TRP measurement:
Step 1: Position DUT at reference orientation (beam peak pointing toward probe). Measure EIRP = reference power.
Step 2: Rotate DUT through N_θ × N_φ grid of angles (typically 5° or 10° steps). Measure EIRP at each angle.
Step 3: TRP = discrete integral of EIRP × sin(θ) over all measured angles (the sin(θ) is the solid angle weighting factor for spherical integration).
Step 4: Compare measured TRP against declared TRP. Pass if within ±specification window.
A08 Propagation channel models — AWGN, EPA, EVA, ETU, PropSim Intermediate click to expand▾
8.1 Why channel models exist
In the real world, a UE's signal travels to the base station via many different physical paths: direct line-of-sight, reflections off buildings, diffraction over rooftops, ground reflection, etc. Each path has different delay (due to different path length) and different amplitude (due to different path loss and reflection coefficient). The received signal is the sum of all these copies.
These paths change as the UE moves, causing the channel to fade — sometimes coherently constructive (signal peaks), sometimes destructive (signal dips). At a UE speed of 70 km/h on a 1.8 GHz channel, a complete fade cycle (UE moves λ/2 = 8.3 cm) takes 8.3 cm / (70/3.6 m/s) = 4.3 ms — very fast.
3GPP defined standardized channel models so that every manufacturer tests under the same conditions. A channel emulator (PropSim in your setup) implements these models as real-time digital filters with random phase evolution at the Doppler rate. This makes lab testing reproducible — anyone, anywhere, with the same PropSim model gets the same fading statistics.
8.2 AWGN — the baseline
Additive White Gaussian Noise — no multipath, no fading. Just thermal noise added to a clean signal. This represents the absolute best-case propagation — as if the UE were in line-of-sight with no reflectors.
AWGN sensitivity is always the best (lowest input power at which throughput passes). If the RU fails AWGN sensitivity, it has a fundamental receiver problem (NF too high, hardware fault). Fading models always give worse sensitivity than AWGN because multipath adds ICI and ISI.
All your PUCCH format 1 vectors test AWGN first (along with EPA5 and EVA70). AWGN is the reference — it's the point where you first verify the receiver is working at all before stressing it with fading.
8.3 3GPP channel profiles — technical detail
ProfileTapsRMS delay spreadDoppler (typical)ModelsIn your config
EPA5743 ns4.6 Hz (5 km/h)Indoor/pedestrianPUCCH format 1/1a/1b all BWs
EVA59357 ns4.6 Hz (5 km/h)Suburban low speedPUCCH format 1a/1b at 5 MHz
EVA709357 ns64.7 Hz (70 km/h)Suburban vehicularPUCCH format 1/1a/1b all BWs
ETU3009991 ns277.6 Hz (300 km/h)High-speed train urbanPUCCH format 1a/1b — harder formats only
What "taps" means: Each tap represents one multipath component. A 7-tap EPA profile means there are 7 distinct propagation paths, each with its own delay (relative to the first arriving path) and power level (relative to the strongest path). The PropSim hardware applies these 7 delays and power levels, each with independently fading envelopes following a Rayleigh distribution.
RMS delay spread: The standard deviation of the delays of all multipath components, weighted by their power. Large delay spread → severe ISI (inter-symbol interference) → harder for the receiver's equalizer. ETU300 has 991 ns delay spread — at 15 kHz subcarrier spacing (66.7 µs symbol), the delay spread is 991/66700 ≈ 1.5% of the symbol duration. With CP = 4.69 µs, ETU300 is within the CP for LTE. But the time-varying nature at 300 km/h Doppler makes equalization hard.
Why ETU300 is only used for format 1a/1b in your config: Format 1 (scheduling request only, 0 information bits) can be detected even under severe fading with simple energy detection. Formats 1a and 1b carry actual bits (1-2 bit ACK/NACK) and need coherent detection — more sensitive to channel estimation errors under ETU300 high Doppler. Testing format 1 under ETU300 would be overkill for what the format is used for.
8.4 PropSim — what the channel emulator actually does
PropSim is a hardware channel emulator. It takes the UL digital waveform from a signal generator (or from the waveform file loaded into the tester), applies the mathematical multipath channel model in real time, and outputs the faded signal to the RU's antenna port through the attenuated test cable (cable_loss = −77 dB in your config).
How it works internally:
Input: Baseband IQ samples (or RF signal). PropSim upconverts if needed.
Channel filter: For each tap (delay), applies a fractional delay filter and multiplies by a complex fading coefficient. The fading coefficient evolves according to the Doppler spectrum corresponding to the velocity setting (Jakes model for isotropic scattering).
Summation: All tap outputs are summed to create the faded received signal.
Noise addition: AWGN is added at a level corresponding to the desired SNR/received power.
Output: The faded, noisy signal is transmitted to the RU via the calibrated cable (cable_loss compensated by PropSim output power).
The ext_delay = 0.009997485 seconds in your config (≈10 ms) is the additional timing offset applied to compensate for the round-trip delay of the test cables and PropSim internal processing. This keeps the UL frame timing aligned with what the RU expects based on the DL reference it receives from the tester.
A09 Test automation, cadence design, ETM, measurement architecture Advanced click to expand▾
9.1 Why test hierarchies exist — the CI vs regression tradeoff
Every test you run costs time and resources. A single REFSENS test at one BW, one channel model, one frequency point: ~2–5 minutes. Your full test matrix for one band has: 4 BWs × 3 freq points × 3 channel models × 3 tests = 108 individual measurements per band. Across 5 bands: 540 measurements × 5 min each = 45 hours. Nobody runs this on every commit.
The solution is a test pyramid: fast smoke tests on every commit, comprehensive regression on a schedule, and full conformance testing only at major milestones.
CadenceWhenDuration targetCoverage goalGate for?
P0 CIEvery commit< 10 minBasic go/no-go per bandMerge approval
P1 NightlyEvery night1–3 hoursWider per-band coverage, all freq pointsRelease readiness
P2 RegressionWeekly or on-demand8–12 hoursAll BWs, all freq pointsFeature release
P3 SanityAfter firmware change30–60 minSingle BW per band, fm onlyManual QA sign-off
P5 RSSI AccPeriodic30 minBand-edge RSSI accuracyCalibration validation
9.2 ETM — E-UTRA Test Models decoded
3GPP defines standardized downlink signal configurations called E-UTRA Test Models (ETMs). Different tests need different ETMs because they stress different aspects of the system. The ETM specifies: which resource blocks are allocated, what modulation is used, how much power boosting on reference signals, and how many antenna ports are active.
ETMRB allocationModulationRS boostingPrimary use
1.1Full (all RBs)64QAM on PDSCHYes (+6 dB CRS)ACLR, output power, EVM — maximum spectral stress
1.2Full64QAMNoSpectrum emission mask — uniform power distribution
2aPartial (spread)QPSKNoDynamic range — partial load stress
2.0Full, periodic gapsQPSKNoDynamic range with on/off patterns
3.1Full multiport64QAMYesMulti-antenna EVM, time alignment
3.1aFull multiport64QAMYesOTA tests — reference signal needed for beamforming coherence measurement
Why ETM 3.1a is needed for OTA EVM (test_Tx_EVM_OTA) and not ETM 1.1: The OTA EVM measurement requires the reference signals (CRS) on all antenna ports to be active so the probe can estimate the channel from each antenna element. ETM 1.1 only has single-port CRS. ETM 3.1a includes multi-port reference signal structures needed to demodulate signals from a multi-antenna system in the OTA chamber.
9.3 Cable loss calibration — the −77 dB in your config
The cable_loss field (−77 in your PUCCH vectors) represents the total path loss between the PropSim/tester output and the RU's antenna connector. This includes:
RF cable insertion loss: typically 0.5–2 dB per meter at 1.8 GHz
SMA connector loss: 0.1–0.3 dB per connector
External attenuators or couplers: deliberate attenuation pads
Switch/combiner losses: if using a test switch matrix
Why use −77 dB total? This gives you a calibrated, controlled signal level at the RU input. To deliver −69 dBm (REFSENS) at the RU antenna port, the PropSim must output: −69 − (−77) = +8 dBm. This is a comfortable, accurate output level for the PropSim. If the cable loss were only −10 dB, the PropSim would need to output −59 dBm — much harder to maintain accurate power levels at such low output power.
If this calibration is wrong by even 1 dB, your REFSENS measurement will be wrong by 1 dB. The RU might appear to pass when it actually fails, or fail when it actually passes. Cable loss must be measured with the VNA (S21 measurement) and updated in the config whenever cables are changed or reconnected.
9.4 ci_summary_table — why this matters
Every Group-ID in your config has "ci_summary_table": true. This flag tells the test framework to record results in a structured summary table that is stored persistently across builds. This enables:
Trend tracking: Plot output power, EVM, ACLR over time across firmware builds. See if a metric is slowly degrading (NF creep, DPD model drift) before it crosses the spec limit.
Regression detection: Any sudden change between build N and build N+1 triggers an alert. This is how you caught the B28 power change between 2025.4.X and 2026.2.1 — the summary table showed a step change in channel power for the B28 entry.
Go/no-go gating: CI systems can block a merge if the summary table shows a FAIL on any P0 test. This prevents known regressions from entering the main branch.
A10 Expert: troubleshooting, root cause analysis, RF pathology patterns Expert click to expand▾
10.1 EVM failure diagnosis — systematic approach
EVM fail is one of the most common test failures and often the hardest to root cause because multiple independent faults can cause similar EVM degradation. Use this systematic approach:
Step 1 — Characterize the failure pattern:
Uniform across all RBs? → LO phase noise, DAC clock jitter, IQ imbalance (gain or phase mismatch between I and Q paths), or PA compression (check if EVM improves when you reduce TX power by 3 dB).
Worse at band edges (high/low RB index)? → Filter group delay distortion. The band-select filter's group delay is typically highest at the passband edges. This introduces frequency-dependent phase error across the channel bandwidth — different subcarriers arrive with different delays, distorting the constellation.
Worse at specific RBs in the middle? → Filter notch (narrow-band amplitude dip), stuck DAC bit (creates a spurious tone at a specific frequency), or digital clipping if a specific frequency resource hits a processing path with lower precision.
Only fails on one antenna port? → Hardware fault in that specific TX chain (DAC, up-converter, PA, or connector). Compare EVM across all antenna ports simultaneously using multi-port ETM 3.1.
Fails only after warm-up? → Thermal drift in oscillator reference, PA thermal compression, or temperature-dependent IQ imbalance. Let the unit thermally stabilize for 30+ minutes before measurement.
Step 2 — Reduce TX power: Reduce TX power 3 dB, measure EVM again. If EVM improves significantly (2+ dB), PA compression was the dominant cause. If EVM doesn't improve, PA compression is not the cause — look at signal generation (DAC, IQ modulator, LO).
Step 3 — Check DPD: If the RU has DPD, disable it (if test mode allows). If EVM gets dramatically better with DPD off, the DPD model is miscalibrated and creating pre-distortion that doesn't match the PA. If EVM gets dramatically worse, DPD was working and the underlying PA is very nonlinear.
10.2 ACLR failure — diagnosis tree
Is ACLR bad on BOTH sides (±1 channel) equally?
→ PA nonlinearity or DPD failure. PA-generated IMD products are symmetric around the carrier.
→ Test: reduce power 1 dB at a time. PA-caused ACLR improves at ~2–3 dB per 1 dB power reduction (third-order slope). DPD failure: ACLR typically steps by a large amount (10+ dB) when DPD is toggled.
Is ACLR bad on only ONE side?
→ Asymmetric clipping or filter phase asymmetry. Check the digital baseband filter coefficients are symmetric. Also check if there is a frequency offset (carrier frequency error) that causes asymmetric ACLR presentation.
→ Could also be a spur (spurious emission) landing in the adjacent channel — use the EXA with narrow RBW to inspect the adjacent channel spectrum for discrete tones vs. continuous spectral regrowth.
Difference between ACLR failure and SEM failure:
ACLR measures power in a defined adjacent channel bandwidth (e.g. 5 MHz wide). A single strong spurious tone would cause ACLR fail.
SEM checks the full spectrum shape against the mask. Broadband spectral regrowth (PA IMD) causes SEM fail across a wide frequency range. A single spur causes a localized SEM spike.
10.3 REFSENS failure — diagnostic flowchart
Check 1 — Cable loss calibration: Measure S21 of the full path from tester output to RU antenna port with the VNA. If cable_loss entry in your config doesn't match measured S21, the wrong signal level is being delivered. Correct the config value and retest.
Check 2 — Duplexer RX filter: Measure S21 of the duplexer RX port. If the passband insertion loss has increased (aging, moisture, thermal shock), you're losing extra dB before the LNA. Even 1 dB extra IL = 1 dB worse REFSENS.
Check 3 — LNA noise figure: Measure NF directly with a noise figure meter or cold-source method. If LNA NF has degraded (ESD damage, electromigration), REFSENS will be directly affected. NF increases 1 dB → REFSENS degrades 1 dB.
Check 4 — LO phase noise: Connect spectrum analyzer to the LO test point (if accessible). Increased phase noise degrades SNR of the received signal even at optimum input level. Phase noise close to the carrier (within the channel BW) directly adds to the noise floor.
Check 5 — AGC calibration: Verify the AGC sets the ADC input level correctly at the REFSENS signal level. If AGC sets too much attenuation, the ADC is underdriven and quantization noise becomes significant. If AGC sets too little, a small blocker that the ACS test introduces can partially clip the ADC.
10.4 RSSI accuracy at band edge — why it's the hardest
RSSI is defined as the total received power across the declared channel bandwidth. The problem at band edge (fb and ft): the RX filter doesn't have a perfectly flat response — it has rolloff at the band edges. This means the effective integration bandwidth for RSSI is slightly narrower than the declared channel bandwidth.
If the filter's −3 dB point is at the channel edge, roughly half the power in the edge subcarriers is attenuated. The RU's RSSI algorithm doesn't know the filter is cutting off — it integrates over what the ADC sees, which is the filtered version. Result: RSSI reads low by 0.5–1 dB at band edge vs. the true signal level.
The fix: Calibration tables that correct RSSI based on frequency. The RU stores a calibration offset per band edge, derived during factory calibration. If this calibration table is wrong (wrong duplexer type fitted, calibration not run, EEPROM corruption), RSSI_Accuracy_fb fails. Check: compare RSSI at fm (mid-band, should be accurate) vs fb (band edge, may be offset). If the error is constant across temperatures → calibration table error. If error varies with temperature → temperature compensation table fault.
10.5 B28 power anomaly between firmware builds — your specific case
The B28 TX power difference observed between 2025.4.X and 2026.2.1 firmware builds follows a recognizable pattern in multi-band RU development. When a new firmware build changes PA bias, DAC full-scale register values, or DPD model initialization, band-specific power offsets can appear.
Root cause categories — ordered by likelihood:
DAC full-scale setting change: If the firmware changed the DAC's full-scale register (VREF or digital gain coefficient) for the B28 PA chain, output power changes proportionally. A 1-LSB change in a 12-bit DAC VREF register = ~0.024 dB. But register writes in groups of 4 = ~0.1 dB steps. Check: read DAC configuration registers via I2C/SPI debug interface and compare 2025.4.X vs 2026.2.1 register dumps.
PA bias voltage change: If firmware changed the PA drain voltage or gate bias for B28 (often stored as EEPROM cal values), quiescent current changes → output power changes. More bias → more gain → more output power. This is exactly what PWK is investigating with their "DAC setting changes impacting B28 power."
DPD model initialization difference: If the new firmware initializes DPD with different coefficients (or a different iteration count before declaring convergence), the pre-distortion depth differs. DPD reduces the effective PA gain → changes output power. Check: compare output power with DPD disabled across both firmware builds. If power difference disappears → DPD initialization is the cause.
Band switching/gain table update: Modern multi-band RUs have frequency-specific gain tables that set the target output power per band. If this table was updated for B28 specifically (either intentionally or as a bug), B28 power changes while other bands don't. Check: compare output power across B1, B3, B8, B28, B41. Only B28 affected → band-specific config. All bands affected proportionally → common path (LO, reference clock, ADC/DAC VREF).
Never accept "it's within tolerance" without understanding the root cause. A B28 power change that stays within ±1.5 dB today might be a symptom of a temperature-dependent change that exceeds tolerance at extreme temperatures. Insist on root cause identification before closing the GRDEV ticket.

M11 — Link Budget: The Engineer's Core Skill

Every real-world RF decision starts with a link budget. If you can do this in your head, you're ahead of 80% of engineers.

A11 Link budget — from TX power to receiver sensitivity with every loss accounted for Intermediate click to expand▾
11.1 What a link budget is and why you need it
A link budget is a complete accounting of every gain and every loss a signal experiences from the moment it leaves the transmitter to the moment it arrives at the receiver. It answers one fundamental question: does the received signal power exceed the receiver sensitivity by enough margin to give reliable communication?
As an RF test engineer, you use link budgets constantly even if you don't call them that. Every time you calculate how much attenuation to put between your RU TX port and the EXA, you're doing a link budget. Every time you set the PropSim output level to hit −69 dBm at the RU antenna port, you're doing a link budget. Getting this wrong by even 2–3 dB changes whether a test passes or fails.
11.2 The universal link budget equation
P_rx = P_tx + G_tx − L_cable_tx − L_path + G_rx − L_cable_rx − L_connector − L_misc
Where every term is in dB or dBm:
TermWhat it isSignYour lab example
P_txTransmitter output power+RU TX = +43 dBm
G_txTX antenna gain+Conducted test: 0 dBi (cable, no antenna)
L_cable_txTX-side cable loss−SMA cable 1m at 2 GHz ≈ 0.5 dB
L_pathFree-space path loss OR attenuator−External 30 dB attenuator = 30 dB
G_rxRX antenna gain+Conducted test: 0 dBi
L_cable_rxRX-side cable loss−Cable from attenuator to EXA: 0.3 dB
L_connectorConnector losses−4 SMA connectors × 0.1 dB = 0.4 dB
P_rxReceived power at EXA input=43 − 30 − 0.5 − 0.3 − 0.4 = +11.8 dBm
This is why you enter Ext Gain = −31.2 dB on the EXA (total of all losses in the measurement path). The EXA then adds this offset to every displayed reading, correcting back to the true RU output power of +43 dBm.
11.3 Free-space path loss (FSPL)
In an OTA test (or any wireless link), the dominant loss is free-space path loss — the signal spreading out as it travels. FSPL follows the inverse-square law: power density drops as 1/r².
FSPL (dB) = 20·log₁₀(d) + 20·log₁₀(f) + 20·log₁₀(4π/c)
FSPL (dB) ≈ 20·log₁₀(d_m) + 20·log₁₀(f_MHz) − 27.55
Distance700 MHz (B28)1800 MHz (B3)2500 MHz (B41)
1 m37.4 dB45.6 dB48.4 dB
10 m57.4 dB65.6 dB68.4 dB
100 m77.4 dB85.6 dB88.4 dB
1 km97.4 dB105.6 dB108.4 dB
5 km111.4 dB119.6 dB122.4 dB
This tells you immediately why B28 has better coverage than B41: at 5 km, B28 has 11 dB less path loss. With the same TX power, B28 arrives at the UE 11 dB stronger — enough to support a much larger cell radius.
