M12 — Phase Noise: The Hidden EVM Killer

Phase noise is the #1 source of EVM degradation that isn't the PA. Most engineers can't measure or diagnose it. You will.

A12 Phase noise — what it is, why it matters, how to measure and fix it Advanced click to expand▾
12.1 What phase noise actually is
An ideal oscillator produces a perfect sine wave at exactly frequency f₀. Real oscillators produce a signal whose frequency wanders slightly from moment to moment, and whose phase drifts randomly. This random phase jitter is phase noise. On a spectrum analyzer, instead of a perfect single spike at f₀, you see a skirt of energy spreading out from the carrier on both sides — the "noise floor" rises as you approach the carrier frequency.
Phase noise is measured as L(f) — the single-sideband phase noise density at offset f from the carrier, expressed in dBc/Hz (dB below carrier per Hz of bandwidth). A good oscillator might have L(1 kHz) = −80 dBc/Hz and L(1 MHz) = −140 dBc/Hz. The phase noise decreases (improves) as you move further from the carrier.
12.2 Why phase noise destroys OFDM EVM
OFDM subcarriers are spaced 15 kHz apart in LTE. They rely on perfect orthogonality — each subcarrier is sampled at a point where all other subcarriers have zero contribution (by design). Phase noise breaks this orthogonality in two ways:
Common Phase Error (CPE): Low-frequency phase noise (offsets much less than subcarrier spacing) causes the entire OFDM symbol to rotate by the same angle — all subcarriers get the same phase error. This is detectable and correctable using pilot subcarriers. LTE uses CRS for this correction.
Inter-Carrier Interference (ICI): Phase noise at offsets comparable to and greater than the subcarrier spacing causes each subcarrier to be contaminated by energy from neighboring subcarriers. This ICI cannot be corrected — it looks like additive noise on every subcarrier and directly degrades EVM.
The ICI power from phase noise that falls within the measurement BW is approximately:
ICI_power ≈ ∫ L(f) · df over the subcarrier BW
For LTE 15 kHz subcarrier spacing: phase noise at offsets 7.5–22.5 kHz from the LO directly becomes ICI noise in the adjacent subcarriers. A phase noise of −80 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset contributes roughly −80 + 10·log10(15000) = −80 + 41.8 = −38 dBc of ICI — potentially limiting EVM to ~1.3% even with a perfect PA.
12.3 How to diagnose phase noise as the EVM cause
If EVM fails and the following symptoms are present, phase noise is likely the cause:
EVM is uniformly bad across ALL subcarriers and ALL resource blocks (not just edges or specific RBs)
Reducing TX power 6 dB does NOT improve EVM (PA compression is not the cause)
EVM is worse at higher modulation orders (256QAM fails while 64QAM marginal) — because higher-order constellations are more sensitive to phase errors
EVM is temperature-dependent — PLL VCO phase noise typically worsens by 0.1–0.3 dB/°C above 40°C
EVM is worse at higher carrier frequencies — phase noise from the LO gets multiplied up: if your reference oscillator has phase noise L(f), and it's multiplied by N to reach the carrier frequency, the phase noise becomes L(f) + 20·log10(N) dB worse
Measurement method: Use the EXA's Phase Noise measurement application (Mode → Phase Noise). Sweep offset from 100 Hz to 40 MHz. Compare against the spec limits for your LO. If phase noise at 10–100 kHz offsets is worse than −85 dBc/Hz, it will impact LTE EVM.
BM

M13 — CSI, Beam Management & 5G NR Reference Signals

The piece most RF test engineers skip — but it's what separates a 5G expert from an LTE engineer.

A13 5G NR CSI-RS, SSB, SRS, beam management — how the gNB knows where to point Advanced click to expand▾
13.1 Why 5G NR needs explicit beam management
In LTE, beamforming was relatively simple — the gNB would use feedback from the UE (PMI — Precoding Matrix Indicator) to choose a downlink precoding vector. In 5G NR with 64 or 192 antenna elements and 3D beamforming, the beam space is enormous. You need a systematic procedure to find the best beam pair between gNB and UE, track it as the UE moves, and recover when the beam fails. This is the beam management framework.
13.2 Key 5G NR reference signals (what you need to know for testing)
SignalDirectionPurposeTest relevance
SSB (Synchronization Signal Block)DLCell discovery, initial beam sweep, timing syncgNB broadcasts SSBs in multiple beam directions; UE picks strongest
CSI-RS (Channel State Info RS)DLChannel measurement for precoder selection, beam refinement, RRMgNB sends from each beam; UE reports RSRP per beam → gNB selects best
DMRS (Demodulation RS)DL+ULChannel estimation for data demodulationMust be present for EVM measurement — the EXM/EXA uses DMRS to estimate channel and compute EVM
PT-RS (Phase Tracking RS)DL+ULCPE correction from phase noiseOnly configured at high frequencies where phase noise is critical
SRS (Sounding RS)ULgNB estimates UL channel → used for TDD DL beamforming (reciprocity)In TDD B41: gNB uses SRS measurements to set DL beam weights — channel reciprocity
13.3 Beam management P1/P2/P3 procedures
3GPP defines beam management as three procedures:
P1 — Initial beam sweep (SSB-based): The gNB transmits SSBs in multiple directions (up to 64 SSB beams in FR1). The UE measures RSRP for each SSB beam and reports the best beam index. This establishes the initial beam pair link (BPL). In your OTA chamber, this is the procedure that defines which gNB beam direction the EIRP is measured in.
P2 — Beam refinement (CSI-RS-based): After initial beam is established, gNB sends CSI-RS in a narrower set of directions around the best SSB beam for finer angular resolution. UE reports best CSI-RS beam → gNB refines its TX beam to maximize EIRP toward the UE.
P3 — UE-side beam sweeping: UE sweeps its own RX beams while the gNB holds a fixed beam. Measures which UE RX beam gives best SINR. Both endpoints are now optimized. This complete beam pair is the one used for data transmission.
13.4 TDD channel reciprocity — why B41 is fundamentally different
In TDD systems (B41), the UL and DL use exactly the same frequency. This means the wireless channel experienced by a DL signal is the same as the channel experienced by a UL signal (they're at the same frequency and travel the same path in both directions within the channel coherence time).
The gNB exploits this: it measures the UL channel (using SRS from UE) and uses that channel knowledge directly for DL beamforming without waiting for UE feedback. This is called reciprocity-based beamforming. It requires the gNB's TX and RX hardware paths to be calibrated so that the RF chain itself doesn't introduce phase and amplitude differences between TX and RX — otherwise the "reciprocity" assumption breaks down.
This calibration is done with dedicated RF calibration signals measured internally or via over-the-air calibration between antenna elements. If this calibration drifts (temperature change, component aging), the DL beamforming quality degrades — EVM and EIRP in the intended direction drop, and interference in other directions increases. This is why your B41 validation pays particular attention to EVM and ACLR across temperature, and why firmware builds that change calibration procedures can affect B41 performance without affecting FDD bands.
CON

M14 — Connectors, Cables & RF Plumbing Mastery

This is the most practical skill gap. Most failures in the lab are connector problems. Know every type, know when to use it, know when it's failing.

A14 RF connectors, cables, torque specs, inspection — zero mistakes in the lab Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾
14.1 Connector types you encounter in your lab
ConnectorFrequency rangeImpedanceWhere you see itKey characteristic
SMA (SubMiniature A)DC–18 GHz50 ΩTest cables, VNA ports, EXA input, attenuatorsMost common lab connector. Torque to 0.9 N·m (8 in-lb). Never overtighten — strips threads.
N-typeDC–11 GHz50 ΩPower meters, high-power connections, outdoor equipmentLarger, robust, weatherproof. Torque to 1.4 N·m (12 in-lb). Better for high-power connections.
3.5 mmDC–26.5 GHz50 ΩVNA cal kits, precision measurementsMechanically compatible with SMA but wider bandwidth. Your E5071C (8.5 GHz) uses SMA but higher-freq VNAs use 3.5 mm.
2.92 mm (K)DC–40 GHz50 ΩmmWave test cablesFor 5G FR2 mmWave. Mates with 3.5 mm and SMA but fragile — never force.
BNCDC–4 GHz50 Ω or 75 ΩTrigger signals, 10 MHz reference, GPIBBayonet lock — quarter-turn. Good for frequent connect/disconnect. Not for precision RF.
SMP / SMPMDC–65 GHz50 ΩInternal RU connections, small form factorPush-on (no thread). Used on PCB-to-PCB connections inside your RU. Fragile.
14.2 Cable types — loss matters
Cable typeOuter diameterLoss at 1 GHzLoss at 3 GHzBest use
RG316 (thin, flexible)2.5 mm0.55 dB/m1.0 dB/mShort internal jumpers. Never for precision measurements >1 GHz.
RG585 mm0.33 dB/m0.65 dB/mShort bench connections. Avoid for critical measurement paths.
Semi-rigid (0.141")3.6 mm0.18 dB/m0.35 dB/mInstrument-to-DUT, stable — doesn't flex but doesn't move either.

Never use cheap cables for precision measurements. A low-quality cable changes its S-parameters when you flex it, bend it, or change temperature. After VNA calibration, if you move the cable, your calibration is invalid. Buy phase-stable test cables (Gore Phaseflex, Huber+Suhner Sucoflex) for any VNA or sensitivity measurement work.
14.3 Torque, inspection, and failure modes
Torque matters: Under-torqued SMA → intermittent contact → measurement jumps around, return loss suddenly changes, REFSENS test fails intermittently. Over-torqued SMA → stripped threads, deformed center conductor, permanently damaged connector. Always use a torque wrench set to 0.9 N·m for SMA, 1.4 N·m for N-type.
Visual inspection (use a connector scope, 30×–200× magnification):
Center conductor: Should be clean, shiny, perfectly centred. Scratches along the axis: normal wear. Deep gouges or bent center pin: replace immediately. Contamination (grease, metal particles): clean with IPA and lint-free swab.
Dielectric: Should be white/ivory, clean. Cracks or chips: connector is condemned, replace it. Contamination: clean carefully.
Outer conductor mating surface: Should be flat and smooth. Raised burrs or nicks: deburr carefully or condemn. A damaged female SMA will damage every male connector mated to it.
The #1 lab habit that separates good RF engineers from bad ones: Always put dust caps back on every port when not in use. A single particle of metal dust falling into a connector can cause +2 dB variation in insertion loss and make every measurement that day suspect. Caps on when not connected. Always.
14.4 Adapter rules
Every adapter in the RF path adds loss (typically 0.1–0.3 dB), return loss degradation (each adapter is a small impedance discontinuity), and a potential failure point. The rules:
Minimize adapter count in any measurement path — ideally zero adapters between the calibration plane and DUT
If you need an adapter, include it in the VNA calibration at the DUT reference plane — then it's de-embedded and its loss is removed
Never mate SMA to 3.5 mm without checking compatibility — they look the same but 3.5 mm center conductor is slightly different; forcing can damage both
Gender changers (barrel adapters) are the worst — each barrel adds ~0.3 dB and two impedance discontinuities. Replace with a cable segment if at all possible
ORAN

M15 — Open RAN, O-RU Testing & What's Next

Parallel Wireless is an Open RAN company. Understanding what that means technically sets you apart from traditional RU test engineers.

A15 Open RAN architecture, O-RU/O-DU/O-CU split, fronthaul, your RU in context Advanced click to expand▾
15.1 Traditional RAN vs Open RAN
Traditional (monolithic) RAN: The baseband unit (BBU) and radio unit (RU) are tightly coupled, often from the same vendor. The interface between them is proprietary — you can't mix Nokia BBU with Ericsson RU. This worked but locked operators into single-vendor ecosystems.
Open RAN (O-RAN): The network functions are disaggregated into standardized logical units with open, interoperable interfaces. The O-RAN Alliance defines these interfaces so that any O-RU (your Metro AAU) can connect to any O-DU (Distributed Unit) regardless of vendor.
ComponentWhat it doesInterfaceParallel Wireless context
O-RU (Open Radio Unit)RF front end — PA, LNA, ADC, DAC, antennasOpen Fronthaul (7.2x split)Your Metro AAU — this is what you test
O-DU (Open Distributed Unit)Low-PHY: iFFT/FFT, OFDM, PRACH detection, L1 processingF1 interface to O-CUParallel Wireless DU software
O-CU (Open Central Unit)RRC, PDCP, SDAP — high layer protocolsE1/F1 interfacesCloud-native, runs on COTS hardware
RIC (RAN Intelligent Controller)Near-RT and non-RT control for optimizationA1/E2 interfacesAI/ML-driven optimization of beamforming, scheduling
15.2 The 7.2x functional split — why it matters for your testing
The functional split defines where the boundary between O-RU and O-DU is drawn — which functions run in the radio and which run in the baseband software. The O-RAN Alliance standardized split 7.2x for most deployments:
O-RU side (split 7.2x lower): RF analog front-end (PA, filters, LNA), ADC/DAC, IQ sample compression/decompression, some DL/UL beam weights application, PRACH filtering
O-DU side (split 7.2x upper): FFT/iFFT, OFDM modulation, FEC encoding/decoding, HARQ, scheduling, beamforming weight calculation, CSI processing
This split means your O-RU (Metro AAU) is relatively "dumb" in processing terms — it executes beamforming weights calculated by the O-DU, converts between IQ samples and RF, and handles the analog RF chain. The intelligence is in the software stack. This is why firmware bugs in the O-DU can affect RF performance measurements at the O-RU: a wrong DPD initialization in the O-DU software causes the O-RU PA to be driven with wrong pre-distortion → ACLR fails.
15.3 Open Fronthaul — what flows between O-DU and O-RU
The Open Fronthaul (eCPRI or O-RAN Fronthaul) carries IQ samples between the O-DU and O-RU over an Ethernet/IP network (10G or 25G fiber). This is fundamentally different from traditional CPRI which carried raw IQ at high, constant bandwidth.
Key fronthaul parameters that affect RF testing:
IQ compression: To reduce fronthaul bandwidth, IQ samples are compressed (BFP — Block Floating Point compression, typically 14-bit → 9-bit). Compression artifacts add quantization noise to the TX signal — this shows up as a small EVM degradation even with a perfect PA. Your EVM spec must account for this compression noise budget.
Timing: The O-RU must transmit each subframe at the correct time. Fronthaul latency and timing jitter can cause frame timing errors. This directly affects test_Tx_time_offset results — if fronthaul latency varies, the subframe timing varies, and time offset measurements will show variation.
Beamforming control: The O-DU sends beamforming weights (antenna port weights) to the O-RU for each beam. Errors in weight delivery cause beam pointing errors → OTA EIRP in the wrong direction → OTA tests fail even though the conducted RF chain is fine.
15.4 What 6G looks like from an RF perspective
You'll be testing 6G hardware before many engineers even understand what 5G NR conformance means. Here's what's coming:
Upper mid-band (7–24 GHz): New spectrum between sub-6 GHz and mmWave. Better propagation than mmWave, wider bandwidth than sub-6. Will require new OTA test methodologies — CATR at 15 GHz needs a different chamber than at 3.5 GHz.
Extreme massive MIMO (>256 elements): More antenna elements → higher beamforming gain → more complex beam management → more beam states to test in conformance.
AI/ML-native air interface: Beam prediction using AI, channel estimation using neural networks, adaptive modulation driven by ML. New KPIs and new test methods required — you'll need to test the AI model's beam prediction accuracy, not just the RF parameters.
Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC): The gNB simultaneously communicates with UEs and senses the environment (radar mode). New RF tests: radar range resolution, velocity resolution, interference between comm and sensing waveforms.

16a RF path components — duplexer, BPF, LNA, VGA, mixer (every stage) Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾
Duplexer / T-R Switch — first after antenna
In FDD (B1/B3/B8/B28): the duplexer simultaneously passes UL and DL on separate ports with >50 dB TX→RX isolation. It stops the PA's +43 dBm TX power from flooding the LNA input and desensitising the receiver. In TDD (B41): a T/R switch replaces the duplexer — faster switching, but cannot transmit and receive simultaneously on the same antenna.
BPF — Band-pass filter
Placed after the duplexer (and sometimes again after the LNA) to provide additional out-of-band rejection. Blockers passing through the duplexer with only 50 dB suppression are further attenuated, protecting the LNA from strong interferers that would cause compression and desensitisation. Also suppresses the image frequency before downconversion.
LNA — the most critical component
David: "you have here the LNA, right? Low noise amplifier... if we receive the signal in low power, we amplify it. This is why we have the LNA here."
The LNA amplifies the weak incoming signal (maybe −80 dBm from a distant UE) while adding minimal noise. By Friis formula: the first stage dominates system NF. A 3 dB NF LNA before a 10 dB NF mixer gives system NF ≈ 3.3 dB. Swap them, and system NF ≈ 10 dB — 6.7 dB worse sensitivity.
ParameterTypical valueWhat it means for your tests
Noise Figure (NF)1–3 dBDirect hit on REFSENS. +1 dB NF = −1 dBm sensitivity (worse). If REFSENS fails, check LNA NF first.
Gain15–25 dBAmplifies signal so ADC and mixer see it clearly above their own noise floors.
IIP3−5 to +10 dBm inputLinearity. Determines blocking performance (ACS test). Higher IIP3 = better ACS.
P1dB−10 to 0 dBm inputIf a strong interferer exceeds P1dB, the LNA compresses → receiver goes blind → desensitisation.
NEVER put any lossy component (attenuator, switch, long cable) before the LNA. A 2 dB attenuator before the LNA adds exactly 2 dB to system NF — halving effective coverage range. This is why your test cable connects directly to the RU antenna port for sensitivity tests.
VGA — Variable Gain Amplifier (AGC engine)
After the LNA, the VGA provides adjustable gain (typically −20 dB to +20 dB range). The AGC loop reads RSSI and adjusts VGA gain to keep the signal level at the ADC input within the optimal range — not too strong (clipping) and not too weak (buried in quantisation noise). David: "we calibrate the RF chain to make sure we are not compressing the ADC and we are not transmitting in too much low power."
Mixer + Local Oscillator (LO) — frequency downconversion
The mixer multiplies the RF signal (e.g. 1747.5 MHz for B3 UL) by the LO signal at the same frequency → output is the difference frequency = baseband (0 Hz for direct conversion / zero-IF architecture). Modern RUs use zero-IF: I and Q channels come out at baseband, 90° apart. Together they fully represent the complex baseband signal including both amplitude and phase.
LO phase noise directly limits EVM. Phase noise at 10 kHz offset from the LO causes ICI between adjacent LTE subcarriers (spaced 15 kHz apart). This is why EVM tests fail when the reference oscillator ages or runs too hot.
16b ADC — 11-12 bit resolution, dynamic range, dBFS, clipping Intermediate click to expand▾
What the ADC does
The ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) is the boundary between the analog RF world and digital processing. It samples the baseband IQ signal at the Nyquist rate and converts each sample to a binary number. David: "we are working with 12 bits. Sorry, 11 bits. It means 2 by 11 steps of resolution."
Resolution: N bits → 2^N amplitude levels 11-bit ADC: 2^11 = 2048 levels 12-bit ADC: 2^12 = 4096 levels SQNR = 6.02 × N + 1.76 dB 11-bit: SQNR = 68 dB dynamic range 12-bit: SQNR = 74 dB dynamic range
Dynamic range — exactly what David drew on the whiteboard
The ADC has a fixed input voltage range from minimum (noise floor) to maximum (full scale). David's explanation: "the dynamic range is the minimum value that the ADC is starting to see some power from the noise itself — to separate the signal from the noise. And the maximum value. This is called dynamic range."
ADC pointdBFS valueWhat happens
Full scale (clipping)0 dBFSADC output saturates. All values above this are clipped. Waveform peaks go flat. Severe EVM and ACLR degradation.
Operating target−6 to −10 dBFSSignal is well within range with headroom for PAPR peaks.
AGC target (typical)−20 to −30 dBFSComfortable operating point with large PAPR headroom.
Noise floor−68 to −74 dBFSQuantisation noise. Signals below this cannot be distinguished from noise.
Sensitivity point~−60 to −68 dBFSWhere signal just emerges from quantisation noise — the "blur" point David described.
dBFS — decibels relative to Full Scale
David: "DBFS is DB to full scale related to the maximum dynamic range of the ADC." All dBFS values are ≤ 0 dBFS. 0 dBFS = at the clipping threshold. −20 dBFS = 10% of full-scale voltage. −74 dBFS = at the ADC noise floor for a 12-bit converter.
The get_rssi CLI command returns RSSI in both dBm AND dBFS. The dBFS reading tells you where the signal sits inside the ADC's operating range. If dBFS is close to 0 → near clipping, reduce VGA gain. If very negative (−60 dBFS or below) → signal is weak, near noise floor.
David's clipping explanation: "you're cutting the information if you're transmitting too high. You got the information — if this is the time domain and this is the amplitude domain — you're cutting the information." The ADC chops the sine wave peaks flat → massive harmonic distortion → EVM and ACLR both fail catastrophically.
16c RSSI: two methods (CLI dBFS vs DU dBm), sensitivity point, your task Intermediate click to expand▾
Two RSSI measurement methods
David described two independent ways the system measures RSSI:
Method 1 — DU RSSI (dBm): After FFT processing, IQ samples flow to the DU via eCPRI fronthaul. The DU sums power across all subcarriers and computes RSSI in dBm. This is what your test automation reads from the OAM portal or DU CLI. Also: the DU calculates the "blur" (sensitivity point) from these same samples.
Method 2 — CLI RSSI at ADC (dBFS + dBm): The FHGW firmware measures power directly at the ADC output, before FFT or compression. Command: get_rssi. Returns 8 readings (ADC channels 0–7) in both dBm (gain-corrected) and dBFS (raw ADC reference). One reading per antenna element/RX chain.
The gap — and how it was closed
David: "We had a gap between the readings from the DU and the readings from the CLI. So we managed to close this gap by adding new features from the software side to the DU." The gap existed because the two methods have different reference planes, different gain compensation tables, and different averaging windows. The DU software update added calibration offsets to align them.
Your task from David
"Start first with basic uplink test to measure the sensitivity point, measure the RSSI point manually, and then provide the automation. We need to do it for each flavor, we need to do it for each band."

16d FHGW internals — FFT, BFP compression, eCPRI fronthaul timing Advanced click to expand▾
FHGW digital processing blocks
BlockUL functionDL functionWhy it matters
FFT / iFFTTime→frequency (OFDM demod)Frequency→time (OFDM mod)Converts between IQ samples and resource elements. FFT size = N subcarriers.
CP removal / insertionRemoves cyclic prefixAdds cyclic prefixCP absorbs multipath delay. LTE normal CP = 4.69 µs.
BFP compression14→9 bit IQ samples9→14 bit decompressionReduces fronthaul BW. Small EVM floor from quantisation.
eCPRI framingWraps IQ in Ethernet+timestampUnwraps, extracts timingTiming accuracy <260 ns. Errors cause time_offset test failures.
RSSI at ADCPower measured before FFT—get_rssi CLI reads this raw ADC power in dBFS.
BFP compression — why it matters for your tests
Block Floating Point (BFP) encodes a block of 12 IQ samples (one resource block) with a shared 4-bit exponent and individual mantissas. Going from 14-bit raw to 9-bit BFP adds quantisation noise equivalent to ~5 bits of resolution loss. This contributes a small but real EVM floor (~0.1–0.3% EVM) even with a perfect PA. Your EVM spec limits must account for this irreducible floor.
The IQ compression ratio directly affects fronthaul bandwidth. A 20 MHz LTE channel (100 RBs × 12 subcarriers) at 30.72 Msps, 14-bit IQ, 2 antennas = ~3.7 Gbps raw. With 9-bit BFP: ~2.4 Gbps. eCPRI over 10GbE handles this comfortably. This is why the fronthaul is specified at 10G/25G in O-RAN deployments.

M01 The Decibel & RF Power — dB, dBm, dBc, dBFS, link budget Beginner click to expand▾
Why RF lives in logarithms
A base station may transmit 40 W; the signal it receives from a phone at the cell edge can be around 10⁻¹³ W — a ratio of ~100,000,000,000,000 to 1. You cannot reason about that range in linear watts. RF uses a logarithmic scale, the decibel, which compresses that range and turns multiplication into addition.
dB — the decibel is a RATIO
dB = 10 × log₁₀(P_out / P_in)
Memorise the toolkit: +3 dB = ×2 · −3 dB = ÷2 · +10 dB = ×10 · −10 dB = ÷10 · 0 dB = ×1
Build everything else by combining: +6 dB = ×4 · +13 dB = ×20 · +20 dB = ×100 · +30 dB = ×1000
dBm — absolute power (referenced to 1 mW)
dBm = 10 × log₁₀(Power_mW / 1 mW)
dBmActual powerContext
+43 dBm20 WYour RU TX output per port
+30 dBm1 W+30 (1W) is the anchor
0 dBm1 mWVNA source output, reference point
−69 dBm126 pW3GPP REFSENS limit Wide Area BS
−104 dBm0.04 fWThermal noise in 10 MHz at room temp
Rules: dBm + dB = dBm ✓ | dBm − dBm = dB (gain) ✓ | dBm + dBm = WRONG ✗ | Never add two absolute powers in dB.
Flavoured dB units you use daily
UnitReferenceDaily use
dBm1 mWAbsolute power — your daily unit. RSSI, output power, noise floor.
dBcThe carrierACLR, spurs, harmonics — how far below the main signal.
dBFSADC/DAC full scaleDigital domain. 0 dBFS = clipping. power_monitor reads this.
dBiIsotropic radiatorAntenna gain. EIRP = Tx(dBm) + Gain(dBi) − losses.
dBFS and power_monitor — critical for your work
The power_monitor tool on the FHGW reads power in dBFS (digital domain, before the DAC/PA). It is NOT dBm. You cannot convert without knowing the full gain chain.
DL dBFS readingMeaning
−30 to −25Very low load
−25 to −18Normal traffic — healthy reading
−18 to −10High traffic, near saturation
> −8Risk of clipping → distortion → bad EVM/ACLR
Cable-loss de-embedding: if you read −4.5 dBm at the analyzer after a 30 dB attenuator + 2.5 dB cable, the true RU output = −4.5 + 30 + 2.5 = +28 dBm. Always add the path losses back. #1 rookie error: forgetting to de-embed.
M02 The 50-Ohm World — impedance, reflection, VSWR, return loss Beginner click to expand▾
Why 50 ohms?
At RF, a cable is a transmission line with characteristic impedance Z₀ set by its geometry, not its length. The industry standardised on 50Ω: coax handles maximum power near 30Ω and minimum loss near 77Ω — 50Ω is the compromise. Rule: keep the entire path 50Ω end to end.
Reflection coefficient (Gamma)
Γ = (ZL − Z0) / (ZL + Z0) Matched (ZL=50Ω): Γ = 0 Open (ZL=∞): Γ = +1 Short (ZL=0): Γ = −1
Return loss and VSWR — the two numbers you live by
Return Loss (dB) = −20 × log₁₀|Γ| ← bigger is better VSWR = (1 + |Γ|) / (1 − |Γ|) ← near 1 is better
VSWRReturn Loss% reflectedVerdict
1.0:1∞0%Perfect
1.5:114 dB4%Good — typical spec
2.0:19.5 dB11%Marginal
3.0:16 dB25%Bad
∞0 dB100%Open or short
Keying a PA into an open port (Γ = +1, 100% reflected) returns all power into the PA — can permanently damage it. This is why VSWR-trip protection exists and why you NEVER connect a PA to an unterminated port.
VNA calibration standards: Load = perfect 50Ω (Γ=0), Open/Short = perfect reflectors (Γ=±1). The SOLT cal removes systematic errors so what you measure is the DUT, not your cables.
M03 The RF Chain — TX/RX flow, gain cascade, noise figure, sensitivity Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾
The transmit chain (left to right)
StageWhat it does
Digital IQWaveform as numbers (baseband), measured in dBFS. IQ playback injects here.
DACDigital → analog: turns IQ samples into analog baseband voltage.
Mixer + LOUp-conversion: f_RF = f_LO + f_baseband. Puts signal on carrier frequency.
FilterRemoves mixer images and out-of-band products. Leaves clean band.
PAPower amplifier: lifts milliwatt signal to tens of watts. Hottest, most non-linear block — reason DPD exists.
Duplexer / T/R switchRoutes TX to the shared antenna. FDD: frequency-split duplexer. TDD: time switch.
The receive chain (right to left)
StageWhat it does
LNAFIRST thing the weak (~−100 dBm) signal hits. High gain, very low noise — sets the whole receiver noise figure.
FilterSelects the wanted channel, rejects blockers and adjacent channels.
Mixer + LODown-conversion to baseband: f_baseband = f_RF − f_LO.
ADCAnalog → digital: samples the IQ signal for the modem.
Gain cascades — just addition
Total chain gain = sum of every stage gain and loss Example: DAC drive +5 dB + filter loss −2 dB + PA gain +40 dB = net +43 dBm output
Noise figure cascade — Friis formula
NF_total = NF₁ + (NF₂−1)/G₁ + (NF₃−1)/(G₁×G₂) + ... The FIRST stage dominates. High-gain, low-NF LNA first swamps everything downstream.
Noise floor = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) + NF Sensitivity = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) + NF + required_SNR
A bad LNA → worse NF → higher noise floor → worse sensitivity → FAILED test 7.2. When a radio hears down to −100.8 dBm, Friis decided that number. Nothing abstract — it decides whether the unit ships.
M04 Key Radio Metrics — RSSI, sensitivity, dynamic range, EIRP, TRP Intermediate click to expand▾
RSSI
Total power in the receive band at the radio input, in dBm. Wideband: it sums wanted signal + noise + interference. High RSSI alone does NOT mean good signal — it could be mostly interference. Used for coverage monitoring and AGC control.
Sensitivity
Sensitivity = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) + NF + required_SNR Example: BW=10 MHz → −174+70+NF4+SNR1 = −99 dBm
Minimum input power still meeting BLER ≤ 5% (RCT test 7.2). Set by the chain's noise figure. 3GPP Wide Area BS REFSENS limit: −69 dBm (you should easily achieve −97 to −100 dBm).
Dynamic range and receiver test family
TestWhat it proves3GPP clause
Reference sensitivityMin input power meeting BLER ≤ 5%7.2
Dynamic rangeDecode wanted signal with in-band AWGN present7.3
Adjacent channel selectivity (ACS)Reject interferer just outside the channel7.5
In-channel selectivity (ICS)Decode beside a stronger in-band signal7.4
Narrowband blockingReject 1-RB interferer near band edge7.5
Wideband / out-of-band blockingReject strong in-band LTE / OOB CW interferers7.6
Receiver intermodulationReject IM products of two interferers7.8
RSSI readback calibrationRadio's reported RSSI matches true input powerRuAuto
EIRP and TRP
EIRP = TX power (dBm) + Antenna gain (dBi) − Losses TRP = EIRP integrated over the full sphere
Your AAU beamforming gain: ~+12 dB for B1/B3/B41 (12-element arrays) · ~+6 dB for B8/B28 (6-element arrays). So per-PA output 38.4 dBm → TRP 44.4 dBm → with beamforming 50.4 dBm. Three different power numbers — don't confuse them.
M05 Modulation & IQ — constellations, OFDM, EVM, IQ playback Intermediate click to expand▾
IQ — why two numbers?
A signal has both amplitude and phase. The clean way to carry both is two numbers: I (in-phase) and Q (quadrature, 90° offset). Any modulated signal is I + jQ — a point on a 2D plane. The DAC, ADC, and all digital processing work in IQ.
Constellations and modulation orders
ModulationBits/symbolPointsEVM limit (3GPP)
QPSK24≤ 17.5%
16QAM416≤ 12.5%
64QAM664≤ 8%
256QAM8256≤ 3.5%
Higher order = more data per symbol, but points sit closer together, demanding a cleaner signal. 256QAM needs EVM ≤ 3.5% — four times tighter than QPSK. This is why DPD and CFR matter so much.
OFDM and the resource grid
LTE/5G split the channel into many narrow 15 kHz subcarriers, each a low-rate QAM symbol. One subcarrier × one symbol = one Resource Element (RE). 12 subcarriers × 7 symbols = one Resource Block (RB). The test "prb: 273" means 273 RBs are allocated (= 100 MHz 5G NR channel).
EVM — test 6.5.2
Error Vector Magnitude = distance from where a symbol SHOULD be to where it LANDED, as % of ideal magnitude. A PA driven too hard (Module 6) raises EVM. The EXM measures this via the modulation analysis mode (sa_set_modulation_analysis_mode).
IQ playback — how Rx tests work
Receiver tests need a known, repeatable uplink signal. A waveform is pre-computed as an IQ file (.bin / .wfm) and a signal generator plays it into the radio. In RuAuto: PRACH_idx158_100MHZ.wfm for PRACH tests, PUCCH format waveforms for PUCCH tests. The EXM does double duty — generator for Rx tests, analyzer for Tx tests.
M06 DL TX Chain — Power scaling, CFR, DPD, DAC scale Intermediate click to expand▾
The real FHGW DL chain order
Digital 2CC → DL Power Scaling → Gain → CFR → Gain → DPD → Per-channel Gain → DAC
The power_monitor reads dBFS at taps along the way. DPD is ONE link in this chain — not a standalone box.
PA compression and P1dB
Amplifiers are linear only up to a point. P1dB marks where gain has dropped 1 dB from linear. Past P1dB: compression, distortion, spectral regrowth (= ACLR fails), constellation smearing (= EVM fails).
PAPR — why OFDM is hard on PAs
OFDM sums hundreds of subcarriers. When they momentarily align in phase, the instantaneous power peaks ~10 dB above average (PAPR ≈ 10 dB). To prevent clipping, the average must run far below P1dB — hurting efficiency. This is why power_monitor shows DL around −21 dBFS, leaving headroom for peaks.
CFR — Crest Factor Reduction
CFR deliberately clips signal peaks (then applies a filter so it doesn't splatter) to reduce PAPR before the PA. On your FHGW: register 0xb0290000, filter_length 511, threshold 8.3. Two working points: 0xD7 (occupancy > 50%) and 0x128 (occupancy ≤ 50%). Less PAPR = PA can run with less back-off = more efficient.
DPD — Digital Pre-Distortion
DPD pre-warps the signal with the mathematical inverse of the PA's nonlinearity. The PA then "undoes" the pre-distortion → the cascade behaves linearly even though the PA itself is nonlinear. A feedback (observation) path adapts the model. CFR + DPD together let you run the PA hot (efficient) while still passing ACLR/EVM conformance tests.
If DPD fails or is miscalibrated: sudden ACLR degradation of 10–20 dB. PreCheck: DPD Gain Register and DPD Input Power + PAPR must both pass before any RF test begins.
RuAuto PreChecks for the DL chain
PreCheckWhat it confirms
Power Monitor DLDL digital power (dBFS) is in range (not clipping, not too low)
CFR Input PowerCFR input level is correct for its working point
DPD Gain RegisterDPD is configured with correct register values
DPD Input Power + PAPRDPD is being fed the right level and seeing expected PAPR
M07 ACLR & Spectrum Analysis — RBW, cable loss, TDD gating, SEM Intermediate click to expand▾
ACLR — test 6.6.2
Adjacent Channel Leakage Ratio = wanted-channel power / adjacent-channel leakage power, in dBc. The direct measure of spectral regrowth from PA nonlinearity and DPD performance. In RuAuto: sa_set_ACP_mode. Higher dBc = better (less leakage).
VerdictCondition
Passmeasured_ACLR ≥ aclr_kpi (e.g. 54 dBc)
Pass(Tolerance)aclr_kpi − tolerance ≤ measured < aclr_kpi
Failmeasured < aclr_kpi − tolerance
3GPP minimum ACLR for Wide Area BS: Offset A (±1 BW) ≥ 45 dBc, Offset B (±2 BW) ≥ 50 dBc. RuAuto typically applies tighter limits (54–55 dBc).
Spectrum emission mask (SEM) — test 6.6.3
The whole transmitted spectrum must sit under a stepped emission ceiling. ACLR checks ±1 and ±2 channel offsets. SEM checks the full spectrum out to ±30 MHz and beyond. Spurious (6.6.4) checks at specific far-field frequencies.
Cable-loss de-embedding — critical
Every cable and connector steals power. RuAuto stores per-frequency losses in cable_loss.json and applies them: extract_cable_loss() / :CORR:BTS:GAIN command to the EXM. Without de-embedding every power reading is wrong by the path loss amount.
TDD gating — mandatory for B41
On B41, the radio transmits only in downlink slots. The analyzer MUST be gated to measure only the TX slot. Without gating you average in the silent UL slots and read too low.
RuAuto TDD gate settings: standard preset config 3, special-subframe config 8 (SSFR 8), gate delay ~3.1 ms, gate length ~2.8 ms. EXM commands: sa_set_gate_view_state('ON'), sa_set_trigger_gate_length(0.001).
Rookie-error checklist: (1) Forgot cable-loss correction. (2) Wrong RBW. (3) No TDD gating on B41. (4) Reference level too low → analyzer compresses → false low reading. (5) Too little averaging. All five produce wrong results that look real.
M08 PRACH — Zadoff-Chu, Ncs/ZCZ/K, detector, timing advance Advanced click to expand▾
What PRACH is for
PRACH (Physical Random Access Channel) is how a UE first reaches the network with no uplink timing. At power-on, or to re-sync, the UE sends a random-access preamble (a "signature"). The base station detects it and replies with a timing-advance (TA) command — telling the UE how early to transmit so data arrives at exactly the right time.
Preamble structure
Preamble = Cyclic Prefix (CP) + Zadoff-Chu (ZC) sequence + Guard interval
Preamble formats 0–3 differ in CP/sequence/guard lengths — for different cell radii. Format 4 is TDD-only (rides in the UpPTS field of the special subframe). FHGW limitation: only PRACH config index 4, Frame Config 2 / SSF 6.
Zadoff-Chu sequences
ZC sequences have constant amplitude (important — not all amplitude variation means signal content), a single sharp autocorrelation peak, and low cross-correlation. 64 preamble signatures are made from one root by choosing a cyclic shift. The shift granularity is set by Ncs (defines the Zero-Correlation Zone).
Ncs / ZCZ / K trade-off
SettingEffect
ZCZ=1 → K=64, 1 rootSmall allowable delay, no inter-root noise
ZCZ=12 → K=6–7, ~10 rootsLarger allowable delay, higher inter-root noise
Allowable delay per UE = Ncs × FFT_size / 839. Bigger cells need larger allowable delay → more roots → more inter-root noise. This is a fundamental cell-size vs. capacity trade-off.
The PRACH detector (FlexRAN-style)
1. Remove CP → FFT → extract PRACH subcarriers 2. Multiply by conjugate of root ZC (correlation) 3. IFFT → power-delay profile 4. Noise estimator: Noise_est = mean(noise vector from correlation) 5. Peak multiplier: detected if peak / Noise_est exceeds threshold 6. Peak position → timing advance
In RuAuto — test_Rx_PRACH
EXM plays a PRACH IQ waveform (e.g. PRACH_idx158_100MHZ.wfm) into the RU UL port. The test sweeps input power down using binary search or sensitivity (stepped coarse→fine) to find the detection threshold against PRACH_KPI. Output: miss-detection %, false-alarm %, timing advance avg/std, SNR. FHGW KPI: base_dbm (e.g. −87 dBm) + DSA per-band offset.
M09 AAU Architecture — board split, single DPD observation loop, beamforming Advanced click to expand▾
The board split
BoardRole
FHGW (Xilinx ZU67 RFSoC)Digital: DUC/DDC, power scaling, CFR, DPD, DAC/ADC — the brains. 8 TX + 8 RX.
Mid-boardFiltering, splitting/combining, calibration coupling between FHGW and RFFE.
RFFE (RF Front End)The high-power analog: PAs, LNAs, switches, circulators, antenna feed.
Antenna arrays and beamforming gain
B1/B3/B41: 4-2-2-4 element arrangement (12 elements, 4 columns) → beamforming gain ~+12 dB. B8/B20/B28: 3-3 (6 elements, 2 columns) → beamforming gain ~+6 dB. This is why TRP is 6–12 dB higher than per-PA output power.
Single shared DPD — the calibration observation loop
One shared DPD cannot watch every PA simultaneously. The solution: directional couplers tap each branch, and a switch matrix (SW1…SW25) routes ONE branch at a time to a shared observation receiver (OBS). That OBS feeds the DPD/calibration engine. The same loop runs TX CAL, RX CAL, and OB CAL.
The calibration switches must be absorptive (50Ω at all ports) with isolation >40 dB at 2.7 GHz. If they're not — unused paths leak into the observation path, corrupting the DPD model → ACLR degrades.
Front-end components (from schematics)
ComponentFunction
Doherty PA (carrier + peaking)High-efficiency: main amp + peaking amp that engages on peaks. RENESAS F8410/F84012.
Phase shifter (PE44820DS)0–360° phase control per element — the beamforming knob.
PIN-diode switches (SP4T)Route paths. Must be absorptive, >40 dB isolation.
Directional couplers (10/20/25 dB)Tap power sample for DPD observation and power monitoring.
SAW / BPF filtersBand selection. Your E5071C S21 traces show these.
LT5581 RF power detectorPower monitoring at RF level for levelling/protection.

Source: RFFE1_TX_A block diagram — 1.6m 6-band AAU · B1B3 single DPD architecture · one TX_A antenna port shared by all three bands
What the diagram is showing — the big picture
This is the RFFE1_TX_A block diagram — the transmit signal path inside one RFFE (RF Front End) module of your 6-band AAU. The image shows THREE parallel TX chains — one for B7 (blue, top), one for B1 (red, middle), and one for B3 (orange/pink, bottom) — that all combine into a SINGLE antenna port called TX_A. This is multi-band operation on one shared antenna: B7, B1, and B3 TX signals all go out through the same physical antenna connector.
Stage-by-stage explanation — every block in the diagram
StageSymbol in diagramWhat it doesWhy it matters to your testing
TX_B7_A / TX_B1_A / TX_B3_ABlue circle (input)Digital IQ signal from FHGW DAC output, upconverted to RF. This is the starting point — the signal coming FROM the Xilinx RFSoC DAC at the correct carrier frequency.The rated power at the BOB SMA connector is measured HERE (before the RFFE). This is the P_rated in your 4G test plan (e.g. B1 = −16.7 dBm, B3 = −15.7 dBm).
Phase shifter ⊘Circle with diagonal line (⊘)A digitally-controlled phase shifter (e.g. PE44820DS) that sets the transmit phase of this antenna element relative to the others. This is THE beamforming control. By setting different phases across all RFFE elements, the array steers the beam in a chosen direction.When phase is equal across all elements → beam goes straight ahead. When phase is swept across elements → beam tilts. Phase calibration is what the OB_CAL (observation calibration) measures. If phase is wrong → no beamforming gain → TRP fails.
BPF 5×BW ≋Wavy box labeled 5×BWBandpass filter with bandwidth = 5 times the channel bandwidth. For 10 MHz LTE: BPF BW ≈ 50 MHz. This removes DAC images (mirror signals at harmonics of the sampling rate), out-of-band noise, and LO harmonics BEFORE they are amplified by the PA. Much cheaper to filter here at low power than after the PA.If this filter is degraded (insertion loss too high → output power drops). VNA S21 measurement of this filter should show <1 dB IL in passband, >30 dB rejection at image frequency. This is what your E5071C S21 traces show for these filters.
V ATT (Variable Attenuator) ∿Box with waveform symbolA voltage-controlled (PIN diode or GaAs) attenuator that provides adjustable gain/loss BEFORE the driver amplifier. This is the fine power control: sets the exact output power level by controlling how much signal reaches the PA. Also used for dynamic Vdd power optimization — at low load, reduce drive level AND reduce Vdd.The V ATT is what the DL power_monitor sees changes when you modify DAC current or gain registers. If V ATT is stuck at maximum attenuation → no TX output. At minimum attenuation → risk of PA overdrive → ACLR fails.
Pre-driver ▷Triangle (amplifier symbol)A driver amplifier (small-signal linear amp, Class A) that boosts the signal from the V ATT to the input level required by the main PA. Provides ~15–20 dB gain. Must be very linear — any distortion here is further amplified by the PA and corrupts EVM/ACLR.Pre-driver NF is not critical (signal is already strong). Pre-driver linearity IS critical — its IIP3 must be high enough that it stays linear even at peak PAPR moments. If pre-driver compresses → EVM fails even with perfect DPD on the PA.
PA (Power Amplifier) ▷▷Large double triangle (green border)The GaN Doherty PA (RENESAS F8410/F84012). Carrier amp + peaking amp. Amplifies the signal from pre-driver output (~+5 dBm) to the final output power (+40+ dBm). This is where 95% of the DC power is consumed. DPD corrects its nonlinearity.This is the most tested block. Your PA efficiency test plan (PPT2) measures drain efficiency here. ACLR test (6.6.2) verifies DPD is correcting its nonlinearity. Temperature sensor monitors its junction temperature. Dynamic Vdd (40→32→25V) is applied to this block.
Directional coupler □Rectangular box after PAA 4-port device that taps a small fraction (e.g. −20 dB) of the PA output power into the observation path, while passing the main signal through with minimal loss (~0.1–0.3 dB). The tapped signal goes to the DPD observation receiver (OBS) to update the DPD model.If the coupler is lossy → DPD observation power is wrong → DPD model diverges → ACLR suddenly degrades. If the observation switch matrix (SW1–SW25) selects the wrong coupler → DPD is modeling the wrong PA → all ACLR measurements degrade on that branch.
Circulator ◎Circle with arrowA 3-port passive ferrite device that routes RF power in ONE direction only: PA output → antenna (forward), antenna → load/RX path (reverse). It provides ~20 dB of TX-to-RX isolation AND protects the PA from reflected power. If the antenna has poor VSWR (cable disconnect, damaged connector), the reflected power goes to the circulator dump port, NOT back into the PA.CRITICAL for PA protection. If the circulator fails or is removed → any cable disconnect sends 100% reflected power back into the PA → PA damage. The VSWR trip protection works WITH the circulator. When you see PA protection events during testing → check circulators first.
Band-specific TX filter ≋ (B7/B1/B3)Wavy box after circulatorEach band has its own post-PA bandpass filter. B7 filter passes 2500–2570 MHz, rejects everything else. B1 filter passes 2110–2170 MHz, rejects everything. B3 filter passes 1805–1880 MHz, rejects everything. These suppress PA harmonics and intermodulation products that would otherwise appear in the SEM measurement.SEM test (6.6.3) directly measures what comes through here. If a TX filter is degraded → spurious emissions appear in the SEM → test fails. Your VNA E5071C S21 measurements characterise these filters. The S21 passband loss is what you de-embed in your cable_loss.json corrections.
Diplexer / Triplexer ┤├Double vertical bars (purple border)Combines the three filtered TX signals (B7 + B1 + B3) from separate paths into a SINGLE wideband output. A diplexer combines 2 bands; a triplexer combines 3. Uses reactive (LC/ceramic) filtering to pass each band on its path while blocking the other bands.Insertion loss here is in the TX path — affects output power. Cross-band isolation determines whether B7 TX power leaks into the B1 or B3 path (and vice versa). If isolation is poor → inter-band intermodulation → new spurious emissions at f_B7 ± f_B1 frequencies → fails spurious test.
Final filter + TX_A outputFilter box → green circleA final cleanup filter and the physical antenna port TX_A. This is the antenna connector where all three band signals emerge combined. The TX_A label corresponds to Antenna A — your RFFE has multiple antenna ports (A, B, C, D) for the full beamforming array.THIS is where your VNA measures cable loss (S11 return loss at this port). And where the EXM or EXA connects via attenuator pad for ACLR and power measurements. All power readings must be de-embedded back to this port.
The dashed vertical lines in the diagram — what they mark
The green and red dashed vertical lines mark functional boundaries within the RFFE board. The green dashed line separates the low-power section (phase shifter, BPF, V ATT, pre-driver) from the high-power section (PA, coupler, circulator). The red dashed line marks where the DPD observation tap exits. These boundaries matter for troubleshooting — a fault on the left of green = digital/control issue, fault between green and red = PA drive level issue, fault on the right of red = filtering/combining issue.
Single DPD architecture — one observer for three PAs
Notice the diagram shows THREE separate PAs (one per band) but the coupler taps all three. The single DPD block on the FHGW cannot observe all three simultaneously — the switch matrix (SW1–SW25) routes one band at a time to the shared observation receiver. DPD adapts the model for B7 PA, then switches to B1 PA, then B3 PA, cycling through them. This is the "single DPD" architecture referenced in the original AAU block diagram document (1.6m 6 AAU Block Diagram_B1B3 single DPD V0.2.vsdx).
What a power measurement failure tells you about which stage is faulty
Measurement failureLikely faulty stageHow to confirm
Output power low on all 3 bands on this antennaDiplexer/triplexer or final filter — common to all three pathsCheck each band individually. If all three are equally low → common path fault.
Output power low on B1 only, B7 and B3 OKB1 TX chain specific: V ATT, pre-driver, PA, circulator, or B1 band filterCheck power_monitor DL for B1 specifically. If digital power OK → analog fault between DAC output and antenna.
ACLR fails on B3 onlyB3 DPD model diverged, or B3 PA compression, or B3 coupler not routing to observationCheck DPD Gain Register PreCheck for B3. Force DPD re-adaptation. Check switch matrix routing.
All bands fail ACLR suddenlyObservation path fault — DPD cannot adapt any PACheck coupler observation output. Check switch matrix for stuck position. Check OBS receiver path in FHGW.
SEM fails — spur at B1+B3 frequencyDiplexer cross-isolation degraded → inter-band IM productCheck diplexer isolation with VNA. Replace if isolation <40 dB.
PA protection trips on B1High VSWR on B1 path — circulator seeing reflected powerCheck antenna connector and cable. Measure S11 at TX_A port with VNA. Should be <−10 dB.
Connection to your real test work
When you run test_Tx_BS_Output_Power on the B1 port — you are measuring the signal at TX_A after it has passed through ALL the stages above: Phase shifter → BPF → V ATT → Pre-driver → PA → Coupler → Circulator → B1 filter → Diplexer → Final filter → TX_A. Any one of those stages can cause the test to fail. The block diagram is your fault-isolation roadmap.
The power budget through the RFFE: enter at ~−16.7 dBm (FHGW BOB) → phase shifter ~0 dB → BPF ~−0.5 dB → V ATT ~−3 dB (variable) → pre-driver ~+18 dB → PA ~+40 dB → coupler ~−0.2 dB → circulator ~−0.3 dB → TX filter ~−0.5 dB → diplexer ~−0.5 dB → TX_A ≈ +37 to +42 dBm. That is your TRP/EIRP starting point before beamforming gain.

What this diagram shows — the complete FHGW DL signal path
This is the most important internal diagram of your FHGW. It shows the complete digital downlink chain from the DU IQ input all the way to the DAC output, with REAL power level readings at every measurement tap and REAL register values for every gain/CFR stage. This is what David Bekker uses to explain where power goes and why ACLR passes or fails.
The two sections — LowPHY and DFE
SectionWhat it containsWho controls it
LowPHY (yellow/cream background)DUC mixer CC0 + CC1 → DL Power Scaling → Adder. This is the layer-1 physical layer processing — upsampling, digital upconversion, carrier combining.DL Chain CTRL Registers — set by DU via NETCONF/YANG. 10MHz → 0x11cc = +25 dB. Different per BW.
DFE (blue background)Gain → CFR → Gain → DPD → Gain Per Channel → DAC. This is the Digital Front End — linearisation and scaling before the analog domain.FHGW firmware registers. Controlled via SSH CLI or NETCONF. Your PreChecks verify these.
Every block decoded — with real numbers from the diagram
BlockRegister / ValueWhat it doesYour test impact
DUC Mixer
CC0 / CC1		DL Chain CTRL
10MHz: 0x11cc → +25 dB		Digital UpConverter: upsamples the baseband IQ from the DU to the FHGW sample rate, then frequency-shifts (mixes) it to the correct intermediate frequency. CC0 = Component Carrier 0, CC1 = Component Carrier 1. Two carriers can coexist (2CC = 2 component carriers).Wrong CTRL register → wrong sample rate → signal at wrong IF → no RF output. Different BW requires different register: 5/10/15/20 MHz each have their own scaling value.
DL Power ScalingPer-CC scaling
from CTRL register		Scales the digital IQ amplitude of each CC before combining. Used to set the relative power between CC0 and CC1, and to implement the overall DL power target. This is the "digital gain knob" for each carrier component.Too high → ADC/DAC clips downstream. Too low → output power below P_rated. The power_monitor (red box) reads directly after this stage. PreCheck 2 (Power Monitor DL) verifies this is in range.
Adder (0 dB)No gain (0 dB)
coherent combine		Combines CC0 and CC1 carrier IQ streams into a single 2CC combined waveform. At 0 dB — the adder itself does not add gain. But combining two equal-power carriers at the same time can increase instantaneous peak power by up to +3 dB (coherent addition at peak moments).After the Adder: power_monitor reads the combined power. The diagram shows −13.7 dBFs here. This is your primary power_monitor reading that PreCheck 2 verifies.
Power Monitor
(red block)		Expected: −16.7 dBFs
Actual shown: −13.7 dBFs		A firmware measurement tap that reports the RMS digital power at the Adder output in dBFS. This is NOT the RF output power — it is purely digital. The reading changes with: traffic load (more RBs = more power), number of active CCs, and scaling register values.This is PreCheck 2. Normal range: −25 to −16 dBFs. The diagram shows −13.7 dBFs (shown in red parentheses) which is HIGHER than the expected −16.7 dBFs — indicating heavier than expected DL load at the time of measurement. If power_monitor reads > −8 dBFs → imminent clipping risk.
Gain 1Register: 0xb0290000
Value: 0xd7
Gain: −1.5 dB		First DFE gain stage before CFR. Sets the input level into the CFR block. Reducing by 1.5 dB creates headroom so CFR clipping threshold does not trigger immediately on every peak. This is a deliberate backoff to let CFR operate at its designed operating point.PreCheck 3 (CFR Input Power) verifies the level after this stage. If 0xd7 is wrong (e.g. inadvertently changed to a higher value) → CFR input too high → CFR clips everything → massive EVM degradation. The diagram shows −15.2 dBFs at this tap.
CFRfilter_length = 511
threshold = 8.3
wcfr_threshold = 8.5		Crest Factor Reduction clips OFDM signal peaks above the threshold (8.3 linear amplitude units, where full scale = 1.0). A 511-tap FIR filter then smooths the clipped peaks so the spectral splatter from clipping stays within the channel bandwidth. Result: PAPR drops from ~11 dB to ~8.3 dB (shown in diagram). This lets the PA run closer to saturation = better efficiency.After CFR: power RISES to −8.8 dBFs (up from −15.2 dBFs) — the clipping folded peak energy back into the average. PAPR = 8.3 dB is shown. If PAPR is too low → CFR is clipping too aggressively → EVM degrades. Too high → PA sees full PAPR → ACLR fails. PreCheck 3 (CFR Input Power) and threshold registers control this.
Gain 2Register: 0xb0290008
Value: 0x20b
Gain: +6.2 dB		Second gain stage AFTER CFR, BEFORE DPD. This raises the signal level back up after the CFR has reduced average power (CFR reduces PAPR but also reduces average power). The +6.2 dB gain compensates and sets the correct input drive level for the DPD block.After Gain 2: power = −14.8 dBFs (from −8.8 dBFs). Wait — that is −6 dB, but the register says +6.2 dB. The discrepancy is because the power AFTER CFR is the clipped version; Gain 2 value in the diagram says Gain = −6 dB near the DPD block → this is the NET gain of Gain2+DPD combined. The DPD input level is critical — DPD PreChecks (4 and 5) verify this exactly.
DPDRegister: 0xb02900XX
Value: 0x161		Digital Pre-Distortion applies the inverse of the PA nonlinearity. The model is a look-up table (LUT) or polynomial indexed by instantaneous IQ amplitude. At each sample: distorted_output = DPD_model(input). The PA then "un-distorts" it back to linear. DPD is adaptive — it continuously updates its model via the observation (coupler → OBS receiver) path.After DPD: power = −12 dBFs. DPD adds some power (the pre-distortion peaks are larger than the original peaks). If DPD diverges → ACLR suddenly degrades 10–20 dB. PreCheck 4 (DPD Gain Register) verifies 0x161 is correct. PreCheck 5 (DPD Input + PAPR) verifies the drive level into DPD is right.
Gain Per Channel+2.8 dBPer-antenna-port gain stage after DPD. Each of the 8 TX channels (for 8 antenna elements) can have an independent gain offset here. Used for per-element calibration: if one PA branch has slightly different gain than others (component tolerance), this corrects it so all 8 elements radiate at the same level for accurate beamforming.If Gain Per Channel is wrong for one element → that element has wrong power → beamforming pattern is distorted → TRP measurement fails (power not coherently combined correctly). Antenna calibration (TX_CAL via OB_CAL) sets these values.
DAC Output ScaleDAC Current [28318]
= −2.87 dB		The final digital-to-analog converter output scaling register. Sets the full-scale output current of the DAC, which directly controls the analog output voltage amplitude going to the RF upconverter chain. This is the LAST digital knob before the analog world. DAC current = 28318 → −2.87 dB relative to maximum DAC output.THIS is the register involved in your B28 power deficit investigation. PWK found a DAC setting change between firmware builds caused a ~3 dB drop in output power. Changing DAC current by 1 unit changes output power by a calculable dB amount. HOW TO change: wiki page "HOW TO change DAC Current" — ssh to FHGW → write register 0xb02900XX with new value.
Reading the power taps — full power budget through the chain
Measurement pointPower (dBFs)Delta from previousWhat caused the change
After Adder (power_monitor)−13.7 dBFs— (reference)DL Power Scaling + 2CC combination. Higher than expected −16.7 dBFs = heavier traffic load.
After Gain 1−15.2 dBFs−1.5 dBGain 1 register 0xd7 = −1.5 dB deliberately applied before CFR.
After CFR−8.8 dBFs, PAPR=8.3 dB+6.4 dB average powerCFR clips peaks → peak energy folds into average → average power RISES even though peaks are now lower. PAPR reduced from ~11 dB to 8.3 dB.
After Gain 2−14.8 dBFs−6 dBGain 2 is labelled +6.2 dB but the net DFE gain here is −6 dB per the diagram label near DPD — this sets the DPD input operating point.
After DPD / Gain Per Channel−12 dBFs+2.8 dBGain Per Channel +2.8 dB raises to final level. DPD itself adds distortion pre-emphasis which slightly raises peak power.
DAC Output Scale−12 dBFs − 2.87 dB−2.87 dBDAC current [28318] scales the final analog output. Net at DAC output ≈ −14.87 dBFs equivalent. This drives the RF mixer → PA chain → eventually TX_A at +38 to +42 dBm.
CFR and PAPR — the most misunderstood part of this diagram
People expect power to DROP through every stage (gain < 0). But notice: power RISES from −15.2 dBFs to −8.8 dBFs across the CFR block (+6.4 dB). This seems impossible — the CFR is supposed to clip peaks, not add power. Here is what actually happens:
An OFDM signal has high PAPR. The average power is low but the peaks are high. When you clip the peaks, you remove the energy in those peaks — but the average power calculation is dominated by how often each amplitude occurs. CFR clips just the rare high peaks, but their removal means the waveform can now run at a higher average power without clipping the ADC/DAC. In practice: after CFR, the entire waveform is scaled UP so the clipped peaks sit at the DAC full-scale limit. The average power rises because the distribution is now less peak-heavy. The PAPR goes from ~11 dB to 8.3 dB — meaning the signal is now 8.3 dB more "compact" — and this compactness is the gain.
The CFR threshold = 8.3 means clip everything above 8.3/10 = 83% of full scale. wcfr_threshold = 8.5 is the wide-CFR threshold — a second pass that clips wider peaks. filter_length = 511 is the FIR smoother length — longer = better spectral containment but more latency. These values are tuned so EVM stays within 3GPP limits (clipping adds EVM) while ACLR also passes (too little clipping = PA runs too backed-off = inefficient, too much = spectral splatter).

The B28 power deficit — exactly what happened
Your open investigation: B28 shows ~3 dB output power deficit between firmware builds. Looking at this diagram: the most likely cause is a change to the DAC Output Scale register (DAC Current value). The diagram shows DAC Current [28318] = −2.87 dB. If a firmware update accidentally changed [28318] to a lower value (e.g. 20000 → different dB offset), the output power drops by exactly that difference. PWK confirmed it was a DAC setting change between builds. The fix: restore the correct DAC current register value for B28 on the affected firmware build.
Never change DAC current registers without first noting the current value and verifying output power against P_rated. A 1-register change here affects every test: Tx power, ACLR, EVM, SEM — all measured relative to the expected output power level.

Constellation diagram — what you are seeing
The top-left quadrant shows the OFDM constellation (Layer 0, CC0). You can see 4 clusters corresponding to QPSK (4 constellation points). But the clusters are very large and spread — EVM ~9.7%. Ideal QPSK at this power should have tight clusters (EVM <2%). The spread is caused by the ADC overrange in the EXM. The blue dots in the centre are pilot/reference signal symbols that have different power from data symbols. The red scattered dots are data symbols smeared by the measurement fault.
Error Vector Spectrum — what you are seeing
Top-right quadrant shows EVM per subcarrier (−300 to +300 carriers, 601 total for 10 MHz LTE). The white line is the average EVM per subcarrier. You can see EVM is roughly uniform across all subcarriers at ~10% with spikes reaching 32% on individual subcarriers. Uniform EVM across frequency = NOT a filter notch or cable multipath (those cause frequency-selective EVM). Uniform = noise source or ADC clipping — consistent with the overrange fault.
🔧 How to fix this for next time
Problem: Channel Power = 48.333 dBm, Ext Gain = −56 dB → signal at EXM input = −7.667 dBm. EXM Range = 55 dBm is the reference level but the internal attenuator setting (10 dB shown in Screenshot 1) was not correctly applied here. The EXM ADC is overranging.

Fix option 1: Increase external attenuation (add 10–20 dB pad between PA output and EXM). This is the safest — never let the EXM input exceed its rated maximum.
Fix option 2: In EXM → AMPTD → RF Range → increase to 65 or 70 dBm to tell the instrument to expect a stronger signal.
Fix option 3: EXM → AMPTD → Atten → increase internal attenuation from 10 dB to 30 dB.
Quick check: Always verify STATUS bar shows no red errors before accepting EVM results. "ADC over range" = measurement is invalid.

ACLR margin analysis — is 46.45 dBc comfortable?
The 3GPP E-UTRA ACLR limit is 45 dBc. Your measurement is 46.45 dBc — only 1.45 dB of margin. PW internal gate is typically 54 dBc (tighter). So this full-power reading is borderline for the PW gate even though it passes 3GPP. Possible causes of marginal ACLR at B28:
B28 (700 MHz band) has wider DPD bandwidth requirements — the PA nonlinearity at 780 MHz may have different memory characteristics than B1/B3 at 2 GHz
The ~3 dB B28 power deficit (your open investigation) suggests the PA may be operating at a different point than intended — if DAC current was changed, DPD model may not match current operating point
Check: was DPD re-adapted after any power or firmware change? DPD model is valid only for the operating point it was trained on
B28 PA (RENESAS or equivalent at 700 MHz) has higher memory effects due to lower frequency — longer DPD filter taps may be needed
When ACLR is borderline: reduce TX power by 1 dB and re-measure. If ACLR improves significantly (3+ dB) → PA compression. If ACLR barely changes → DPD model mismatch or memory effects. The response shape tells you the root cause.

The pitfalls that catch every new engineer
1. Forgetting cable-loss / de-embedding — every power number is wrong without it.
2. Overloading the analyzer — reference level too low → compression → false low reading.
3. Wrong RBW, or no TDD gating on B41.
4. Loose/dirty connectors — torque to spec, inspect with magnifier, keep caps on.
5. Keying a PA into an open/short port — VSWR trip → PA damage.
6. Not waiting for DPD to converge after power change before taking measurements.
M11 PA Efficiency & Power Optimization — Dynamic Vdd, gate bias, sequencing Advanced click to expand▾
The efficiency problem
A macro PA can burn hundreds of watts. Drain efficiency = RF power out / DC power in. A PA is MOST efficient near saturation and LEAST efficient when backed off. But OFDM PAPR forces back-off. So at low traffic the PA sits deep in back-off, wasting power.
Dynamic Vdd — the core solution
Instead of one fixed drain voltage (Vdd) for all conditions, lower Vdd as traffic (RB occupancy) falls. Less Vdd at low load = efficiency peak moves to the backed-off operating point = less wasted power.
Load (occupancy)B1/B3 VddB8/B28 VddB41 Vdd
100% (full load)40 V~48 V~45 V
50% (busy hour)32 V (Vdd_Low1)——
≤30% (medium)25 V (Vdd_Low2)——
What you must re-tune when lowering Vdd
Lowering Vdd changes PA behaviour. You must re-tune: (1) CFR working point — pre-CFR gain register 0xb0290000: 0xD7 for occupancy > 50%, 0x128 for ≤ 50%. (2) Output power via DAC current. ACLR/EVM must stay within spec throughout the transition.
Transition order is critical: when load DROPS → lower Vdd AFTER occupancy has dropped (not before — you'd clip at the new Vdd). When load RISES → raise Vdd BEFORE occupancy increases (not after — the signal would clip at the old low Vdd).
Gate bias (Vgg) — second lever
The gate bias Vgg3_p (tested at −6.5 V datasheet, −5.5 V, −4.5 V) trades quiescent current for linearity. Adjusting Vgg adds further power savings especially when Vdd is already below nominal.
Safe PA bias sequencing (RENESAS)
GaN PA (RENESAS F8410/F84012) has drain rail (VDD) and gate rails (VGG1/2/3). Enabled by AND of TX_EN and MC_EN. Bias must follow the RENESAS sequence to avoid device damage. Even fully OFF: draws ~108 mA from VDD1 + ~1 mA leakage.
M12 Reading the RCT Config — tc_cadence, Group-IDs, Test-IDs, KPI limits Advanced click to expand▾
Tests are DATA, not code
In RuAuto you almost never write a new test in Python. A test is a generic method driven by JSON. To "write" or change a test you edit the config. Reading the config IS reading the test.
The 4-layer lookup chain
LayerFileContains
1. Entry INIsetup.ini / setup_conf.iniLists which JSON files to load for each section
2. tc_cadence.jsonTest-IDs + Group-IDs + Cadence-IDsPer-test parameters, scheduling, P0/P1/P2 selection
3. fdd/tdd_test_setup.jsonDUT configurationIPs, bands, antenna-to-RFIO mapping
4. FHGW_Box_kpi_thresholds.jsonPass/fail limitsKPI numbers with 3GPP references
Real ACLR Test-ID (from your tc_cadence.json)
"test_Tx_ACLR": { "tm": "1.1", // E-TM test model 1.1 (QPSK, all RBs) "test_type": "ACP", // → SCPI sa_set_ACP_mode "prb": "273", // full carrier loaded "trb": "1", // transceiver index "test_duration": "960000", // microseconds — long for ACLR dwell "sample_time": "3", // average 3 samples "KPIs": { "aclr_kpi": 54, "aclr_kpi_tolerance": 1 } }
Real Group-ID and Cadence-ID
"TS_DL_CI": { "IsDL": true, "band": "n78", "frequency": ["M"], "BW": ["40"], "SCS": "30", "tm": ["1.1"], "ext_trig_delay": "0.00998675", "Tests": ["test_Tx_BS_Output_Power", "test_Tx_modulation_analysis", "test_Tx_ACLR"] } "P0": ["TS_DL_CI", "TS_UL_CI"]
4G vs 5G structural difference
4G Test-IDs are THIN — just a filter (e.g. frequency: [fm], etm: [1.1]) and the KPI number lives in the threshold file.
5G Test-IDs are FAT — each carries test_type, prb, test_duration, AND an inline KPIs block. For 4G: read the threshold file for limits. For 5G: read tc_cadence.json.
M13 RU Features & Operations — uSleep, PA protection, RSSI accuracy, IQ playback Advanced click to expand▾
1. uSleep (Micro-Sleep)
What uSleep is: PA (biggest power consumer, 40–200W) switches OFF during empty OFDM symbols. At low traffic, 60–80% of symbols may be empty → proportional power saving. Finer-grained than Dynamic Vdd (per-symbol vs per-subframe).
Failure: EVM spikes on symbol 0 after sleep but OK on symbol 1+ → PA bias slow to ramp. Check RENESAS gate bias sequencing registers.
2. Reduced Carrier Output Power
How it works: Lower the DAC current register or V ATT in RFFE. PA backs off → naturally more linear → ACLR/EVM improve. But efficiency drops (PA wastes more power as heat per useful watt out). Always wait 60s after power change for DPD to re-adapt before measuring ACLR.
3. RU Capabilities
4. Tilt (Electrical Beam Tilt)
5. RSSI Accuracy
6. IQ Playback and Recording
7. Variable Load Tests (DPD)
8. Dynamic Range
9. PA Protection
10. PA Shutdown Process
Key rule: Startup and shutdown are mirror images. Startup: Vdd ON first → then Vgg ON. Shutdown: Vgg OFF first → then Vdd OFF. Always check get_faults after shutdown — should return empty for a clean sequence.
M14 RSSI & Receive Chain — dBFS vs dBm, ADC calibration, dynamic range results Advanced click to expand▾
The real RSSI calibration method
Inject a CW tone at band centre at 3 known power levels (e.g. −40.5, −60.5, −70.5 dBm). Read RSSI at each. Fit an approximate straight line. Compute the average offset. Write that offset per-ADC into /etc/configs/hardware.json (the ADC_ADJUST vector — one entry per ADC 0–7). Then automation sweeps the input over [−40 dBm : 1 dB : −120 dBm] and records corrected RSSI.
Band-to-ADC mapping (real hardware)
B1 uses ADCs 0, 1, 4, 5. B3 uses ADCs 2, 3, 6, 7. Each ADC is calibrated separately with its own ADC_ADJUST offset. This is why get_rssi returns 8 values — one per ADC, and which one matters depends on your band and flavor.
Real RSSI accuracy results
ADCBandADC RMS at sensitivity point (dBFS)2 dB error margin (dBm)
0B1−44.9−95.5
2B3−43.3−93.5
Per-antenna results ranged ~−76 to −90 dBm for the 2 dB error margin. The spread across ADCs/antennas is exactly why each ADC gets its own offset — a single global offset would be wrong for some.

M15 UL RCT Embedded & Dynamic Test — ul-rct-test, 4-stage pipeline, real results Expert click to expand▾
What UL RCT embedded is
Validates the entire uplink receive path — antenna to BLER — against 3GPP FRCs. "Embedded" means it runs entirely on the FHGW: no DU, no external test PC, one CLI command. A signal generator still injects the FRC waveform; everything else is on-RU. Catches receive-chain regressions at box level, fast, before DU integration.
The 4-stage pipeline
StageWhat it doesResource

M16 TDD LTE & PHY DU Impact — frame structure, special subframe, HARQ, PSS/SSS Advanced click to expand▾
TDD vs FDD — the key difference
FDD (B1/B3/B8/B28): separate paired UL/DL frequencies, transmit and receive simultaneously. TDD (B41): UL and DL share the same frequency, alternating in time slots. TDD works in unpaired spectrum. The price: more complex scheduling, more stringent timing requirements.
TDD frame structure — what you must know for B41
PW products use two combinations: (UL/DL config 2, SSF config 7) and (UL/DL config 3, SSF config 8). The special subframe splits into: DwPTS (downlink data) + Guard Period (propagation delay protection) + UpPTS (SRS/PRACH or extra guard).
ConfigDwPTS symbolsGP symbolsUpPTS symbols
SSF config 71022
SSF config 81112
PSS/SSS position changes in TDD
SignalFDD positionTDD position
PSSLast symbol of slots 0, 103rd symbol of special subframes (sf 1, 6)
SSS2nd-last symbol of slots 0, 10Last symbol of slot 1 (sf 0) and slot 11 (sf 5)
PDCCHUp to 3 OFDM symbols≤2 symbols in sf 1 and 6
TDD advantages and challenges
Advantage — Reciprocity: UL and DL share the same frequency, so SRS measurements from UEs directly drive DL beamforming weights. No CSI feedback needed. This is the massive MIMO advantage for B41.
Challenge — Timing: Cross-slot interference between neighbouring cells if their DL/UL configurations don't align. Requires stringent PTP timing (grandmaster Falcon, IEEE-1588v2, <1 µs accuracy).
FHGW TDD constraint: Only PRACH config index 4 supported, Frame Config 2 / SSF Config 6. This limits which cell sizes and PRACH formats can be used on B41.
REF RF & RCT Glossary — quick definitions of every term Reference click to expand▾
TermDefinition
ACLRAdjacent Channel Leakage Ratio — wanted / adjacent power in dBc. Test 6.6.2. Higher is better.
ADC / DACAnalog-to-Digital / Digital-to-Analog Converter. The boundary between digital IQ and analog RF.
AAUActive Antenna Unit — radio chains + antenna array integrated in one unit.
BLERBlock Error Rate — fraction of transport blocks with errors. Rx pass criterion: ≤ 5%.
Cable loss / de-embeddingCharacterising test-path loss and adding it back so power is reported at the connector.
CFRCrest Factor Reduction — clips OFDM peaks before DPD/PA to reduce PAPR.
dBcdB relative to the carrier. Used for ACLR, spurs, harmonics.
dBFSdB relative to full scale — digital headroom. 0 dBFS = clipping. NOT the same as dBm.
DPDDigital Pre-Distortion — pre-warps signal with PA inverse so cascade is linear.
DuplexerPasses TX and RX simultaneously on separate ports (FDD). In TDD replaced by a switch.
EARFCNE-UTRA Absolute Radio Frequency Channel Number — integer that maps to a carrier frequency.
EIRPEffective Isotropic Radiated Power = TX(dBm) + antenna gain(dBi) − losses. Best direction.
E-TME-UTRA Test Model — defined downlink signal for TX conformance tests.
EVMError Vector Magnitude — how far symbols miss ideal, as %. Test 6.5.2.
FRCFixed Reference Channel — defined uplink signal for Rx tests. Pass criterion: BLER ≤ 5%.
Friis formulaNF cascade equation — first stage dominates total NF.
FHGWFronthaul Gateway — the digital+RF radio platform (Xilinx ZU67 RFSoC).
LNALow-Noise Amplifier — first Rx stage. Sets the receiver noise figure. Most critical Rx component.
OBUE / SEMOperating Band Unwanted Emissions / Spectrum Emission Mask. Spectrum must fit under a stepped ceiling.
P1dB1 dB compression point — where PA gain drops 1 dB from linear. Maximum useful linear power.
PAPRPeak-to-Average Power Ratio — OFDM peaks ~10 dB above average. Forces PA back-off.
PRACHPhysical Random Access Channel — UE's first uplink contact. Uses Zadoff-Chu preambles.
RB / PRBResource Block — 12 subcarriers. The scheduling unit in LTE/NR.
RSSIReceived Signal Strength Indicator — total in-band power at the Rx input (dBm).
SensitivityMinimum input power meeting error-rate target. Test 7.2. Set by NF.
TRPTotal Radiated Power — EIRP integrated over the full sphere (OTA).
VSWRVoltage Standing Wave Ratio = (1+|Γ|)/(1−|Γ|). Near 1 = good match.
Zadoff-ChuConstant-amplitude sequence with sharp autocorrelation. The PRACH signature waveform.

The 3-layer architecture (golden rule)
TEST LAYER source/features/ test_*.py / *.robot ← assertions only ↓ STEPS LAYER source/steps/ CwsSteps, AttenuatorSteps ← workflows ↓ PRODUCT LAYER source/products/ VRU, CWS, NR, HNG, RRH ← SSH/CLI/XML to device
A test never talks to a radio directly. When a test fails: wrong number → Test layer (limit/assertion). Radio won't configure → Steps/Product layer. Missing instrument → config (env_setup.json).

python run_pytest.py --conf-file-path configuration/setup_configuration/RCT-5G-GR-FHGW-TRX4/tdd_test_setup.json --test-mode conformance --cadence P0 source/features/4g/tdd/Tx/conformance_nr_tdd_speed.py

PPT1 RSSI ADC Adjustment Results — actual calibration data from your hardware Intermediate click to expand▾
Firmware version tested
Build Label: gc1e2cb17-b0103 Git Branch: develop Git Commit: c1e2cb1780e82622a1811b95c1e046395bf58eed PL Build Date: 2025-05-27 19:48:52 XSA: vvdn_dbru_4cc_top.bit
Calibration procedure (verbatim from the deck)
The calculation of the required offset correction was done by setting a known power level at the signal generator, measuring the RSSI that is read, and repeating the process for 3 different power levels. Measurements were done using a CW tone at the center frequency of each band.
After 3 measurements, an approximated linear line is fitted and an average offset is determined. This offset is written to /etc/configs/hardware.json — the ADC_ADJUST vector, one entry per ADC (0–7). Then automation sweeps: [-40 dBm : 1 dB step : -120 dBm]
Summary results — ALL RFFEs summed, Antenna 0
ADC IndexBandANTADC RMS at sensitivity point (dBFS)2 dB Error Margin point (dBm)
0B10−44.9−95.5
2B30−43.3−93.5
Full per-antenna results (RFFE0, all antennas)
ADCBandADC_Adj (dBFS)3dB Sensitivity Point (dBFS)2dB Margin Point (dBm)
0B1−20.9−59.2−84.5
1B1−24.6−59.5−82.5
2B3−20.8−55.7−86.5
3B3−23.1−58.0−84.5
4B1−21.6−60.7−80.5
5B1−24.2−58.9−88.5
6B3−28.3−54.9−82.5
7B3−30.5−54.0−88.5
2 dB error margin = the power level at which the RSSI reading deviates from the linear fit by 2 dB. This is the practical sensitivity point of the RSSI measurement — below this, the readout is no longer reliable. The per-ADC spread (−80.5 to −88.5 dBm) is exactly why each ADC needs its own ADC_ADJUST offset in hardware.json.
3 dB point = the power level just above the ADC noise floor — the deepest the ADC can still "see" any signal at all. The 2 dB error margin is always higher (less negative) than the 3 dB point, since you need some margin above the noise floor before RSSI readings become meaningful.

Configuration variables
