Measurement procedure (B1B3 example)
Vdd_Nominal = 40 V: Measure ACLR/EVM/Tx Power at 100%, 50%, 30%, 0% occupancy — this is the reference.
Vdd_Low1 = 32 V, Occupancy = 50%: Compensate CFR and adjust Tx power via DAC Current to match 40 V reference. Measure 50%, 30%, 0% occupancy.
Vdd_Low2 = 25 V, Occupancy = 50%: Same — compensate CFR + DAC, measure all occupancies.
For each Vdd point: measure current from main PSU (−48 V), PSU #1–3, DC-DC converters (via CB-MCU). Calculate drain efficiency = RF power out / DC power in.
Also measure: temperature sensors (FHGW / RFFE / Common-Board). Verify ACLR/EVM stay within 3GPP spec throughout all Vdd transitions.
What the measurements prove
Beamforming gain verification: at coherent phases across all elements, verify ~+12 dB gain for B1/B3/B41 (12-element arrays) and ~+6 dB for B8/B28 (6-element arrays) relative to single PA TX power. This is the antenna array gain in action — phase alignment across all branches producing constructive interference in the beam direction.
PPT3 FHGW Embedded RCT — standalone UL test, CLI, memory management, real timing Advanced click to expand▾
Why it exists
Traditional UL RCT needs: DU + PHY Docker + FHSRV Docker + RU + signal generator + grandmaster + networking. The embedded RCT removes everything except the RU and signal generator. One CLI command. Catches RX-chain regressions at the box level, fast, before DU integration.
Prerequisites
FHGW with embedded RCT firmware image (includes ru-ulsim and ru-dvt-cli)
Signal generator with 3GPP FRC waveforms (A1-3, A3-x, A5-x at target bandwidth)
RF cabling from signal generator to target antenna port
NO DU required · NO external test PC required for execution · NO external test scripts
4-stage pipeline (with real timing data)
StageComponentWhat it does% of processing time
1IQ RecordCaptures raw IQ from FPGA channel-filter tap into tmpfs. ~2.5 MB/frame at 61.44 Msps.~25%
2Downsample (lte_downsample)Converts FHGW sample rate to PHY decoder input rate~24%
3PHY Decode (test_ulsim)O-RAN 7.2x low-PHY: FFT, channel estimation, demap, decode, CRC~49%
4ResultsBLER, SNR, RSSI to shell and per-run log files~2%
Total time per sensitivity step: ~33 seconds. PHY decode dominates at 49% — this is the bottleneck. Memory: 768 MB pre-reserved as 2 MB hugepages for PHY decoder, 1 GB tmpfs at boot for binaries + IQ. Auto-cleanup keeps only the 5 most recent runs.
CLI modes and examples
ul-rct-test 35 a13 10 0 100 --debug # Full run, all params, with debug output ul-rct-test -sc 4 2 # Shortcut mode, positional args ul-rct-test -l # List all supported scenarios (18 total) ul-rct-test 10 a34 0 # → Result: BLER 0.00% SNR 24.6 dB Modes: Normal: summary only (BLER, SNR, RSSI) — built for Python automation Debug: per-stage timing + full PHY logs + constellation output
Supported scenarios
18 scenarios total: A1-3 QPSK (sensitivity cases) and A3/A5 QPSK/64QAM (PUSCH performance cases), across B1/B3 at 5/10/15/20 MHz. A1 = Rx sensitivity. A3/A5 = PUSCH throughput performance. The framework is band-agnostic — extensible to NR FRCs.

EXP1 Expert RF topics — PLL/LO, mixers, filters deep dive, phase noise, IQ imbalance Expert click to expand▾
PLL (Phase-Locked Loop) — the LO source
Every mixer in your RU needs a Local Oscillator (LO) at exactly the carrier frequency. The LO is generated by a PLL: a feedback system that locks a Voltage-Controlled Oscillator (VCO) to a precise reference frequency (usually a 10 MHz TCXO or OCXO).
PLL structure: Reference → Phase Detector → Loop Filter → VCO → ÷N divider → Phase Detector (feedback) VCO output frequency = N × Reference frequency To get 1842.5 MHz with 10 MHz reference: N = 184.25 (fractional-N PLL) Phase noise performance: VCO noise + 20·log(N) dB + reference noise
The ÷N multiplication degrades phase noise by 20·log(N) dB. For N=184: 20·log(184) = +45 dB of phase noise degradation vs the reference. This is why crystal oscillator quality matters so much at GHz frequencies — noise is multiplied up.
Your EXA can measure LO phase noise: Mode → Phase Noise Application. Sweep offset from 100 Hz to 40 MHz. A result worse than −85 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset will cause measurable LTE EVM degradation.
Mixer theory — frequency translation
A mixer multiplies two signals: RF × LO. The output contains sum and difference frequencies: f_out = f_RF ± f_LO. For downconversion: f_IF = f_RF − f_LO. For direct conversion (zero-IF, used in your RU): f_LO = f_RF, so f_IF = 0 (baseband).
The image frequency problem: in a superhet (non-zero IF) architecture, there exists an image at f_RF_image = f_LO − f_IF that also mixes down to f_IF. An image-reject filter before the mixer must suppress this. In direct conversion (zero-IF), the image is the negative frequency component — handled by the IQ architecture (using I and Q channels to cancel the image mathematically).
Key mixer specs: Conversion gain (how much gain/loss at the IF output), IIP3 (linearity — two-tone IMD), LO-to-RF isolation (how much LO leaks to the RF port — causes DC offset in zero-IF), noise figure (typically 5–10 dB for passive mixers).
IQ imbalance — source of EVM floor
Zero-IF downconversion produces I and Q baseband signals. For perfect IQ demodulation, the I and Q paths must have exactly equal gain and exactly 90° phase difference. In practice there's always some mismatch:
Gain imbalance (ε): I and Q paths have different amplification Phase imbalance (φ): The 90° LO phase split is not exactly 90° Image rejection ratio (IRR) = 20·log₁₀(√((1+ε²+2ε·cosφ) / (1+ε²−2ε·cosφ))) 1° phase error + 0.1 dB gain error → IRR ≈ 40 dB → EVM floor ~1% 3° phase error + 0.5 dB gain error → IRR ≈ 30 dB → EVM floor ~3%
IQ imbalance shows up as EVM that is uniform across all RBs, temperature-dependent, and doesn't improve when you reduce TX power. The calibration firmware in your FHGW measures and corrects IQ imbalance during the calibration routine. If calibration has not run recently, IQ imbalance can be the hidden cause of marginal EVM.
Filter types — complete guide
Filter typePassbandRolloffPhaseWhere used in your RU
ButterworthMaximally flat (no ripple)Moderate (−20 dB/decade per pole)GoodIF filtering where flat passband matters
Chebyshev Type IEquiripple passbandSteeper than ButterworthModerateMost bandpass/duplexer filters — your E5071C S21 screen shows this
Elliptic (Cauer)Equiripple in pass AND stopSteepest possible for given orderPoorDuplexers needing extreme TX→RX isolation
SAW/BAWVery sharp, compactExcellentModerateB1/B3/B8 bandpass filters on your RFFE board (BFCN-xxxx parts)
BesselFlatGentleLinear (excellent)Pulse/wideband where group delay flatness matters
SFDR — Spurious-Free Dynamic Range
SFDR is the range between the signal level and the highest spurious/intermodulation product in the output. It determines how strong a signal can be while still being able to see weak signals in its presence.
SFDR = (2/3) × (IIP3 − Pnoise) For a 12-bit ADC: SFDR ≈ 6.02 × 12 − 1.76 = 70 dB (theoretical) Real ADCs: SFDR typically 3–10 dB below theoretical due to harmonics, clock jitter
SFDR matters most in receiver tests: ACS (adjacent channel selectivity) and blocking tests inject a strong interferer alongside a weak wanted signal. If the receiver's SFDR is insufficient, the interferer creates intermodulation products that land in the wanted channel and cause BLER degradation even though the wanted signal is at the correct level.
EXP2 SCPI Instrument Automation — control EXM/EXA via Python, real commands Expert click to expand▾
SCPI basics
SCPI (Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments) is a text-based protocol over LAN (TCP port 5025), USB, or GPIB. Every key on the EXM/EXA front panel has an equivalent SCPI command. RuAuto uses SCPI exclusively — every measurement in tc_cadence.json eventually calls an SCPI function.
Python setup and connection
pip install pyvisa pyvisa-py import pyvisa rm = pyvisa.ResourceManager() # Connect to EXM by IP: inst = rm.open_resource('TCPIP::192.168.1.100::5025::SOCKET') inst.write_termination = ' ' inst.read_termination = ' ' # Basic query: print(inst.query('*IDN?')) # → Keysight,E6640A,MY12345678,A.01.23
Real SCPI commands from RuAuto (your exact workflow)
# Reset and select LTE FDD personality inst.write('*RST') inst.query('*OPC?') inst.write('INST:SEL LTEAFDD') # Set center frequency (B3 mid): inst.write('CCARrier:REFerence 1842500000') # Hz # Set reference level: inst.write('DISP:WIND:TRAC:Y:RLEV -10') # dBm # Apply cable loss correction: inst.write(':CORR:BTS:GAIN -77') # negative = loss # Channel Power measurement: inst.write('CONF:CHPower') inst.write('INIT:CONT ON') inst.write('CHPower:AVERage:STATe ON') inst.write('CHPower:AVERage:COUNt 20') result = float(inst.query(':READ:CHPower:CHPower?')) print(f"Channel Power: {result:.2f} dBm") # ACLR measurement: inst.write('CONF:ACP') inst.write(':READ:ACP?') # returns: carrier_power, lower_aclr, upper_aclr # EVM measurement (modulation analysis): inst.write('CONF:EVM') inst.write('EVM:FREQ:CENT 1842500000') evm = float(inst.query(':READ:EVM:EVM?')) print(f"EVM: {evm:.2f} %") # TDD gating (for B41): inst.write('sa_set_gate_view_state ON') inst.write('sa_set_trigger_gate_length 0.001') # 1 ms gate
Automation pattern — sensitivity sweep
import numpy as np def rssi_sweep(sig_gen, fhgw_cli, band, start_dbm=-40, stop_dbm=-120, step=1): results = [] for power in np.arange(start_dbm, stop_dbm, -step): # Set signal generator power sig_gen.write(f':POW {power}dBm') time.sleep(0.5) # settle # Read CLI RSSI from FHGW cli_rssi = fhgw_cli.run('get_rssi') # Read DU RSSI via OAM du_rssi = oam_client.get_rssi_dbm(band) results.append({ 'input_dbm': power, 'cli_rssi_dbm': cli_rssi['dbm'], 'cli_rssi_dbfs': cli_rssi['dbfs'], 'du_rssi_dbm': du_rssi, 'gap_db': abs(cli_rssi['dbm'] - du_rssi) }) return results # → CSV → plot dynamic range curve

PPT1 RSSI ADC Adjustment Results — actual calibration data from your hardware Intermediate click to expand▾
Firmware version tested
Build Label: gc1e2cb17-b0103 Git Branch: develop Git Commit: c1e2cb1780e82622a1811b95c1e046395bf58eed PL Build Date: 2025-05-27 19:48:52 XSA: vvdn_dbru_4cc_top.bit
Calibration procedure (verbatim from the deck)
The calculation of the required offset correction was done by setting a known power level at the signal generator, measuring the RSSI that is read, and repeating the process for 3 different power levels. Measurements were done using a CW tone at the center frequency of each band.
After 3 measurements, an approximated linear line is fitted and an average offset is determined. This offset is written to /etc/configs/hardware.json — the ADC_ADJUST vector, one entry per ADC (0–7). Then automation sweeps: [-40 dBm : 1 dB step : -120 dBm]
Summary results — ALL RFFEs summed, Antenna 0
ADC IndexBandANTADC RMS at sensitivity point (dBFS)2 dB Error Margin point (dBm)
0B10−44.9−95.5
2B30−43.3−93.5
Full per-antenna results (RFFE0, all antennas)
ADCBandADC_Adj (dBFS)3dB Sensitivity Point (dBFS)2dB Margin Point (dBm)
0B1−20.9−59.2−84.5
1B1−24.6−59.5−82.5
2B3−20.8−55.7−86.5
3B3−23.1−58.0−84.5
4B1−21.6−60.7−80.5
5B1−24.2−58.9−88.5
6B3−28.3−54.9−82.5
7B3−30.5−54.0−88.5
2 dB error margin = the power level at which the RSSI reading deviates from the linear fit by 2 dB. This is the practical sensitivity point of the RSSI measurement — below this, the readout is no longer reliable. The per-ADC spread (−80.5 to −88.5 dBm) is exactly why each ADC needs its own ADC_ADJUST offset in hardware.json.
3 dB point = the power level just above the ADC noise floor — the deepest the ADC can still "see" any signal at all. The 2 dB error margin is always higher (less negative) than the 3 dB point, since you need some margin above the noise floor before RSSI readings become meaningful.

Configuration variables
Vgg3_p: −6.5 V (datasheet), −5.5 V, −4.5 V Occupancy: 100%, 50%, 30%, 0% (Traffic Static Load Types) Pre-CFR Gain register 0xb0290000: Occupancy > 50%: 0xD7 Occupancy ≤ 50%: 0x128
Measurement procedure (B1B3 example)
Vdd_Nominal = 40 V: Measure ACLR/EVM/Tx Power at 100%, 50%, 30%, 0% occupancy — this is the reference.
Vdd_Low1 = 32 V, Occupancy = 50%: Compensate CFR and adjust Tx power via DAC Current to match 40 V reference. Measure 50%, 30%, 0% occupancy.
Vdd_Low2 = 25 V, Occupancy = 50%: Same — compensate CFR + DAC, measure all occupancies.
For each Vdd point: measure current from main PSU (−48 V), PSU #1–3, DC-DC converters (via CB-MCU). Calculate drain efficiency = RF power out / DC power in.
Also measure: temperature sensors (FHGW / RFFE / Common-Board). Verify ACLR/EVM stay within 3GPP spec throughout all Vdd transitions.
What the measurements prove
Beamforming gain verification: at coherent phases across all elements, verify ~+12 dB gain for B1/B3/B41 (12-element arrays) and ~+6 dB for B8/B28 (6-element arrays) relative to single PA TX power. This is the antenna array gain in action — phase alignment across all branches producing constructive interference in the beam direction.
PPT3 FHGW Embedded RCT — standalone UL test, CLI, memory management, real timing Advanced click to expand▾
Why it exists
Traditional UL RCT needs: DU + PHY Docker + FHSRV Docker + RU + signal generator + grandmaster + networking. The embedded RCT removes everything except the RU and signal generator. One CLI command. Catches RX-chain regressions at the box level, fast, before DU integration.
Prerequisites
FHGW with embedded RCT firmware image (includes ru-ulsim and ru-dvt-cli)
Signal generator with 3GPP FRC waveforms (A1-3, A3-x, A5-x at target bandwidth)
RF cabling from signal generator to target antenna port
NO DU required · NO external test PC required for execution · NO external test scripts
4-stage pipeline (with real timing data)
StageComponentWhat it does% of processing time
1IQ RecordCaptures raw IQ from FPGA channel-filter tap into tmpfs. ~2.5 MB/frame at 61.44 Msps.~25%
2Downsample (lte_downsample)Converts FHGW sample rate to PHY decoder input rate~24%
3PHY Decode (test_ulsim)O-RAN 7.2x low-PHY: FFT, channel estimation, demap, decode, CRC~49%
4ResultsBLER, SNR, RSSI to shell and per-run log files~2%
Total time per sensitivity step: ~33 seconds. PHY decode dominates at 49% — this is the bottleneck. Memory: 768 MB pre-reserved as 2 MB hugepages for PHY decoder, 1 GB tmpfs at boot for binaries + IQ. Auto-cleanup keeps only the 5 most recent runs.
CLI modes and examples
ul-rct-test 35 a13 10 0 100 --debug # Full run, all params, with debug output ul-rct-test -sc 4 2 # Shortcut mode, positional args ul-rct-test -l # List all supported scenarios (18 total) ul-rct-test 10 a34 0 # → Result: BLER 0.00% SNR 24.6 dB Modes: Normal: summary only (BLER, SNR, RSSI) — built for Python automation Debug: per-stage timing + full PHY logs + constellation output
Supported scenarios
18 scenarios total: A1-3 QPSK (sensitivity cases) and A3/A5 QPSK/64QAM (PUSCH performance cases), across B1/B3 at 5/10/15/20 MHz. A1 = Rx sensitivity. A3/A5 = PUSCH throughput performance. The framework is band-agnostic — extensible to NR FRCs.

EXP1 Expert RF topics — PLL/LO, mixers, filters deep dive, phase noise, IQ imbalance Expert click to expand▾
PLL (Phase-Locked Loop) — the LO source
Every mixer in your RU needs a Local Oscillator (LO) at exactly the carrier frequency. The LO is generated by a PLL: a feedback system that locks a Voltage-Controlled Oscillator (VCO) to a precise reference frequency (usually a 10 MHz TCXO or OCXO).
PLL structure: Reference → Phase Detector → Loop Filter → VCO → ÷N divider → Phase Detector (feedback) VCO output frequency = N × Reference frequency To get 1842.5 MHz with 10 MHz reference: N = 184.25 (fractional-N PLL) Phase noise performance: VCO noise + 20·log(N) dB + reference noise
The ÷N multiplication degrades phase noise by 20·log(N) dB. For N=184: 20·log(184) = +45 dB of phase noise degradation vs the reference. This is why crystal oscillator quality matters so much at GHz frequencies — noise is multiplied up.
Your EXA can measure LO phase noise: Mode → Phase Noise Application. Sweep offset from 100 Hz to 40 MHz. A result worse than −85 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset will cause measurable LTE EVM degradation.
Mixer theory — frequency translation
A mixer multiplies two signals: RF × LO. The output contains sum and difference frequencies: f_out = f_RF ± f_LO. For downconversion: f_IF = f_RF − f_LO. For direct conversion (zero-IF, used in your RU): f_LO = f_RF, so f_IF = 0 (baseband).
The image frequency problem: in a superhet (non-zero IF) architecture, there exists an image at f_RF_image = f_LO − f_IF that also mixes down to f_IF. An image-reject filter before the mixer must suppress this. In direct conversion (zero-IF), the image is the negative frequency component — handled by the IQ architecture (using I and Q channels to cancel the image mathematically).
Key mixer specs: Conversion gain (how much gain/loss at the IF output), IIP3 (linearity — two-tone IMD), LO-to-RF isolation (how much LO leaks to the RF port — causes DC offset in zero-IF), noise figure (typically 5–10 dB for passive mixers).
IQ imbalance — source of EVM floor
Zero-IF downconversion produces I and Q baseband signals. For perfect IQ demodulation, the I and Q paths must have exactly equal gain and exactly 90° phase difference. In practice there's always some mismatch:
Gain imbalance (ε): I and Q paths have different amplification Phase imbalance (φ): The 90° LO phase split is not exactly 90° Image rejection ratio (IRR) = 20·log₁₀(√((1+ε²+2ε·cosφ) / (1+ε²−2ε·cosφ))) 1° phase error + 0.1 dB gain error → IRR ≈ 40 dB → EVM floor ~1% 3° phase error + 0.5 dB gain error → IRR ≈ 30 dB → EVM floor ~3%
IQ imbalance shows up as EVM that is uniform across all RBs, temperature-dependent, and doesn't improve when you reduce TX power. The calibration firmware in your FHGW measures and corrects IQ imbalance during the calibration routine. If calibration has not run recently, IQ imbalance can be the hidden cause of marginal EVM.
Filter types — complete guide
Filter typePassbandRolloffPhaseWhere used in your RU
ButterworthMaximally flat (no ripple)Moderate (−20 dB/decade per pole)GoodIF filtering where flat passband matters
Chebyshev Type IEquiripple passbandSteeper than ButterworthModerateMost bandpass/duplexer filters — your E5071C S21 screen shows this
Elliptic (Cauer)Equiripple in pass AND stopSteepest possible for given orderPoorDuplexers needing extreme TX→RX isolation
SAW/BAWVery sharp, compactExcellentModerateB1/B3/B8 bandpass filters on your RFFE board (BFCN-xxxx parts)
BesselFlatGentleLinear (excellent)Pulse/wideband where group delay flatness matters
SFDR — Spurious-Free Dynamic Range
SFDR is the range between the signal level and the highest spurious/intermodulation product in the output. It determines how strong a signal can be while still being able to see weak signals in its presence.
SFDR = (2/3) × (IIP3 − Pnoise) For a 12-bit ADC: SFDR ≈ 6.02 × 12 − 1.76 = 70 dB (theoretical) Real ADCs: SFDR typically 3–10 dB below theoretical due to harmonics, clock jitter
SFDR matters most in receiver tests: ACS (adjacent channel selectivity) and blocking tests inject a strong interferer alongside a weak wanted signal. If the receiver's SFDR is insufficient, the interferer creates intermodulation products that land in the wanted channel and cause BLER degradation even though the wanted signal is at the correct level.
EXP2 SCPI Instrument Automation — control EXM/EXA via Python, real commands Expert click to expand▾
SCPI basics
SCPI (Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments) is a text-based protocol over LAN (TCP port 5025), USB, or GPIB. Every key on the EXM/EXA front panel has an equivalent SCPI command. RuAuto uses SCPI exclusively — every measurement in tc_cadence.json eventually calls an SCPI function.
Python setup and connection
pip install pyvisa pyvisa-py import pyvisa rm = pyvisa.ResourceManager() # Connect to EXM by IP: inst = rm.open_resource('TCPIP::192.168.1.100::5025::SOCKET') inst.write_termination = ' ' inst.read_termination = ' ' # Basic query: print(inst.query('*IDN?')) # → Keysight,E6640A,MY12345678,A.01.23
Real SCPI commands from RuAuto (your exact workflow)
# Reset and select LTE FDD personality inst.write('*RST') inst.query('*OPC?') inst.write('INST:SEL LTEAFDD') # Set center frequency (B3 mid): inst.write('CCARrier:REFerence 1842500000') # Hz # Set reference level: inst.write('DISP:WIND:TRAC:Y:RLEV -10') # dBm # Apply cable loss correction: inst.write(':CORR:BTS:GAIN -77') # negative = loss # Channel Power measurement: inst.write('CONF:CHPower') inst.write('INIT:CONT ON') inst.write('CHPower:AVERage:STATe ON') inst.write('CHPower:AVERage:COUNt 20') result = float(inst.query(':READ:CHPower:CHPower?')) print(f"Channel Power: {result:.2f} dBm") # ACLR measurement: inst.write('CONF:ACP') inst.write(':READ:ACP?') # returns: carrier_power, lower_aclr, upper_aclr # EVM measurement (modulation analysis): inst.write('CONF:EVM') inst.write('EVM:FREQ:CENT 1842500000') evm = float(inst.query(':READ:EVM:EVM?')) print(f"EVM: {evm:.2f} %") # TDD gating (for B41): inst.write('sa_set_gate_view_state ON') inst.write('sa_set_trigger_gate_length 0.001') # 1 ms gate
Automation pattern — sensitivity sweep
import numpy as np def rssi_sweep(sig_gen, fhgw_cli, band, start_dbm=-40, stop_dbm=-120, step=1): results = [] for power in np.arange(start_dbm, stop_dbm, -step): # Set signal generator power sig_gen.write(f':POW {power}dBm') time.sleep(0.5) # settle # Read CLI RSSI from FHGW cli_rssi = fhgw_cli.run('get_rssi') # Read DU RSSI via OAM du_rssi = oam_client.get_rssi_dbm(band) results.append({ 'input_dbm': power, 'cli_rssi_dbm': cli_rssi['dbm'], 'cli_rssi_dbfs': cli_rssi['dbfs'], 'du_rssi_dbm': du_rssi, 'gap_db': abs(cli_rssi['dbm'] - du_rssi) }) return results # → CSV → plot dynamic range curve

VID1 Constellation Diagram Diagnosis — reading impairments from IQ plots (YouTube aQd_zBytid8) Intermediate click to expand▾
▶ Watch: Interpreting Constellation Diagrams (YouTube) — covers how to diagnose signal impairments from the IQ scatter plot. Here is everything the video teaches, applied to your EXM and RU work.
What a constellation diagram is
A constellation diagram plots received IQ samples as dots on a 2D plane. The ideal symbol positions are shown as reference points (circles or crosses). Every received sample should land exactly on an ideal point. The spread, shape, and position of the cloud around each ideal point tells you exactly what is wrong with the signal.
How to read it on your EXM
On the E6640A EXM: Meas → EVM → Display → Constellation. You see all received symbols as dots. Perfect signal: tight clusters at each constellation point. Impaired signal: clouds, rings, rotations, or asymmetric spreads.
Complete impairment diagnosis table
What you see on constellationRoot causeWhere to look in your RU
All dots rotated by a fixed angle (whole constellation spun)Carrier frequency offset — LO is not exactly on channel center. The constellation spins at a rate = frequency error × 2π.Check EARFCN config. Measure frequency error in EVM Meas Setup. LO PLL lock status.
Dots expand outward (concentric rings instead of tight clusters)Phase noise on LO — random phase jitter smears each point into an arc.Check EXA Phase Noise measurement on LO output. Clean up 10 MHz reference. Temperature of oscillator.
Uniform cloud (all points equally smeared in all directions)AWGN / thermal noise — signal level too low relative to noise floor. Too much NF in the chain, or signal too weak.Check received power level. Check LNA NF. Check cable loss and external attenuation.
Cross-shaped smear (points elongated along I or Q axis)IQ imbalance — gain mismatch between I and Q paths. One axis has more noise than the other.Run IQ calibration on FHGW. Check I/Q gain balance in baseband. ADC channel offset.
Points split — each ideal point becomes two ghost pointsPhase imbalance (quadrature error) — I and Q paths are not exactly 90° apart.Run IQ calibration. Check LO quadrature hybrid splitter.
Inner constellation points OK, outer points smearedAM-AM compression — PA or ADC compressing on the high-power symbols. High PAPR peaks hit P1dB.Reduce TX power. Check DPD convergence. Verify CFR threshold. Check ADC not clipping (dBFS near 0).
Points in a curved arc instead of a straight lineAM-PM distortion — phase shifts with amplitude. PA nonlinearity that DPD hasn't corrected.Check DPD model. Reduce TX power. DPD observation path may be saturated.
Entire constellation shifted off-centre (DC offset)DC offset in baseband — LO leakage in direct-conversion (zero-IF) mixer appears as DC component.Run DC offset calibration. Check zero-IF calibration registers in FHGW.
Every other point wrong — 2-point ambiguityPilot contamination or wrong cell ID (PCI) — EXM descrambling wrong reference signals.Set correct PCI in EXM Meas Setup. Verify RU PCI in YANG model.
Columns of points compressed horizontallyMemory effects in PA — the distortion depends on recent signal history, not just current amplitude. DPD doesn't fully correct.Memory DPD (longer filter taps). Check PA temperature — thermal effects cause memory.
Specific RBs have bad EVM, others OKFrequency-selective fading or filter notch — affects only certain subcarriers.Check cable connector quality. Check duplexer/filter response on VNA. Multipath in test setup.
EVM bad at start of each subframe, improves laterPA startup transient — PA not fully settled after TDD switch-on. Bias sequencing issue.Check uSleep wake timing. Check RENESAS bias sequence. Increase guard period.
EVM floor breakdown (what limits your minimum EVM)
Total EVM² = EVM_noise² + EVM_phase² + EVM_IQ² + EVM_BFP² + EVM_DPD² EVM_noise: from thermal noise and receiver NF EVM_phase: from LO phase noise (at subcarrier offsets within channel BW) EVM_IQ: from IQ imbalance (gain + phase mismatch) EVM_BFP: from BFP compression in eCPRI fronthaul (~0.1–0.3%) EVM_DPD: residual from imperfect DPD model Practical floor: a perfectly calibrated system still has ~0.3–0.5% EVM from noise + BFP alone. If you see EVM > 1% with everything calibrated → DPD or PA issue.
When EVM is exactly at the 3GPP limit (e.g. 8% for 64QAM) — reduce TX power by 3 dB. If EVM drops significantly → PA compression. If EVM stays the same → noise or IQ calibration issue.
VID2 Spectrum Analyzer ACLR Measurement Setup — complete step-by-step (YouTube 1xGncBvWv6U) Intermediate click to expand▾
▶ Watch: Understanding Spectrum Analyzers — ACLR (YouTube) — how ACLR is set up on a real analyzer. Everything from that video applied to your EXA/EXM.
What ACLR actually measures (the physics)
When a PA amplifies an OFDM signal, its nonlinearity creates intermodulation products. These fall at frequencies outside the original channel — in the adjacent channels. ACLR measures how much power leaked out: it is the ratio of the power in the adjacent channel to the power in the main channel, expressed in dBc (negative = adjacent is quieter). Higher dBc value = less leakage = better.
ACLR = 10×log₁₀(P_adjacent / P_carrier) [dBc, always negative] 3GPP limit for LTE Wide Area BS: E-UTRA offset (±1 carrier BW): ≥ 45 dBc UTRA offset (5/10 MHz offset): ≥ 50 dBc PW internal gate: typically 54–55 dBc (tighter than 3GPP)
Step-by-step setup on your EXA (for manual ACLR)
StepKeySettingWhy
1ModeLTE FDD (or TDD for B41)Loads LTE measurement personality
2FreqCenter = carrier freq (e.g. 1842.5 MHz for B3 fm)Centers the display on your carrier
3AMPTDRef Level = expected power + 10 dBSignal fits in screen without clipping
4AMPTD → Ext GainEnter your cable loss as negative (e.g. −77)De-embeds path loss — all readings now at RU port
5MeasACP (Adjacent Channel Power)Selects ACLR measurement mode
6Meas Setup → Radio StdLTE FDDSets LTE-specific channel definitions
7Meas Setup → BW10 or 20 MHz (match your RU)Defines the carrier and adjacent channel widths
8BW → RBW100 kHz (3GPP spec for E-UTRA ACLR)Wrong RBW = wrong result — 3GPP mandates this
9TrigFree Run (FDD) or Frame (B41 TDD)TDD: must sync to frame or you average UL+DL
10BW → Average20–50 sweepsReduces noise on the adjacent channel measurement
11Read resultLower ACLR and Upper ACLR values in dBcMust both be ≥ 45 dBc (E-UTRA) to pass
Why ACLR fails and how to debug it
ACLR failure patternMost likely causeFix
Both sides fail symmetrically (Lower and Upper same value)DPD not converged or PA compressionWait for DPD convergence (30–60 s). Reduce TX power 1 dB. Check DPD Input Power PreCheck.
One side worse than the otherMemory effects or mixer spurCheck for LO harmonics. Memory DPD issue. PA temperature.
ACLR fails only at B41TDD gating not set — averaging over UL slotsEnable Frame trigger. Set gate delay ~3.1 ms, gate length ~2.8 ms.
ACLR passes but EVM failsDifferent impairments — ACLR = spectral regrowth, EVM = in-channel qualityIQ calibration, frequency error, phase noise issue inside channel.
ACLR suddenly degrades 10+ dB from previous good resultDPD has diverged or PA protection tripped and recovered badlyReboot RU. Check DPD Gain Register PreCheck. Verify CFR register.
Automatic ACLR in RuAuto (what happens under the hood)
sa_set_ACP_mode() # Set EXA to ACP measurement mode sa_set_radio_standard('LTE_FDD') sa_set_channel_bw(10e6) # 10 MHz channel BW sa_set_averaging(20) # 20 sweeps cable_loss = extract_cable_loss(band, freq) sa_set_gain_correction(-cable_loss) # de-embed path result = sa_read_aclr() # returns [carrier_dBm, lower_dBc, upper_dBc] verdict = 'PASS' if min(abs(result[1]), abs(result[2])) >= aclr_kpi else 'FAIL'
VID3 Spectrum Analyzer Deep Dive — FFT, RBW, dynamic range, noise floor (YouTube rMVAQsUudSs) Intermediate click to expand▾
▶ Watch: Understanding Spectrum Analyzers (YouTube) — FFT, RBW, dynamic range. Here is the complete teaching from that video.
How a spectrum analyzer works internally
A modern spectrum analyzer (your EXA N9010B) is a swept heterodyne receiver combined with an FFT engine. The signal is downconverted to IF, filtered (RBW filter), detected (RMS power detector), and the result plotted as power vs frequency. Modern instruments also do FFT-based analysis for speed.
RBW — the most important setting to understand
RBW (Resolution Bandwidth) = bandwidth of the IF filter before detection Effect on noise floor: Noise floor (dBm) = DANL + 10×log₁₀(RBW_Hz) EXA DANL ≈ −163 dBm/Hz (with preamp ON) RBW = 1 MHz: Noise floor = −163 + 60 = −103 dBm RBW = 100 kHz: Noise floor = −163 + 50 = −113 dBm ← ACLR standard RBW = 1 kHz: Noise floor = −163 + 30 = −133 dBm ← spurious search RBW = 100 Hz: Noise floor = −163 + 20 = −143 dBm ← phase noise meas
Narrower RBW = lower noise floor = can see weaker signals AND spurs. But narrower RBW = slower sweep (sweep time ∝ span/RBW²). For ACLR: 3GPP mandates 100 kHz RBW to match the integration bandwidth correctly. Using wrong RBW changes ACLR reading by exactly 10×log₁₀(RBW_used/RBW_correct).
VBW — Video Bandwidth (trace smoothing)
VBW is a post-detection filter that smooths the displayed trace. It does NOT change the noise floor — it only averages the noise fluctuations visually. Rule: VBW ≥ RBW always. Setting VBW < RBW suppresses noise peaks that could actually be real spurs — dangerous for spurious emission tests.
Dynamic range of a spectrum analyzer
Dynamic range = displayed range you can measure simultaneously without errors Limited from below: DANL (noise floor) — sets the minimum detectable signal Limited from above: mixer compression — too strong input causes clipping, false spurs Practical dynamic range: EXA with 30 dB attenuator: ≈ 70–80 dB simultaneous range EXA with 0 dB attenuator + preamp: ≈ 80–90 dB range but compression at −30 dBm input For ACLR of 55 dBc: if carrier = −15 dBm at EXA input, adjacent = −70 dBm Need noise floor below −70 dBm → use RBW 100 kHz → floor ≈ −113 dBm ✓
Sweep time — the trade-off
Swept analyzer sweep time ≥ k × Span / RBW² k ≈ 2 for most analyzers Example: Span = 100 MHz, RBW = 100 kHz → min sweep time = 2 × 100e6 / (100e3)² = 0.02 s = 20 ms Example: Span = 100 MHz, RBW = 10 kHz → min sweep time = 2 s (100× slower!)
Zero Span mode — time domain at one frequency
Setting Span = 0 Hz converts the spectrum analyzer into a power-vs-time recorder at one fixed frequency. Used for: viewing TDD frame structure (DL on, UL off), measuring PA switch-on transient, seeing DPD convergence in real time. Critical for B41 TDD debugging.
Noise figure of the spectrum analyzer itself
EXA N9010B typical DANL: Without preamp: −135 dBm/Hz (NF ≈ 39 dB — too noisy for sensitivity testing) With preamp: −163 dBm/Hz (NF ≈ 15 dB — usable for Rx sensitivity) For REFSENS test (−69 dBm in 10 MHz): Signal at EXA ≈ −69 − cable_loss dBm Need noise floor well below signal → always use preamp for Rx tests
The −174 dBm/Hz figure: this is thermal noise at room temperature (290K) — kTB where k=1.38×10⁻²³ J/K, T=290K, B=1 Hz → kT = 4×10⁻²¹ W = −174 dBm. Every 3 dB increase in temperature adds 3 dB to this floor. Every 10× bandwidth increase adds 10 dB. This is the absolute physical minimum noise any receiver can ever achieve.
VID4 RF Engineering Topics — signal chain, IQ, mixers (YouTube swjgr4YBhRM) Intermediate click to expand▾
▶ Watch: RF Topics — signal chain overview (YouTube) — complete RF signal chain from antenna to ADC, covering all major components. Key concepts from this video:
The complete receiver signal chain — component by component
Antenna → Duplexer/Switch → BPF (image reject) → LNA → BPF (channel select) → VGA → Mixer+LO → BPF (IF/baseband) → ADC → DSP. Each stage has a specific job and adds specific impairments. Understanding this chain is the foundation of every RF test you run.
Why component ORDER in the chain matters so much
System NF dominated by FIRST stage (Friis): NF_sys ≈ NF_1 + (NF_2 − 1)/G_1 + ... Put a 3 dB attenuator BEFORE the LNA: NF_sys = 3 + (NF_LNA − 1)/0.5 ← the attenuator's loss is added directly If LNA NF = 2 dB, G = 20 dB: With attenuator: NF_sys ≈ 3 + (1.58−1)/0.5 = 3 + 1.16 = 4.16 dB Without attenuator: NF_sys ≈ 2 + tiny = 2.01 dB → The 3 dB attenuator before LNA costs 2.15 dB in system NF = significantly worse sensitivity
IQ architecture — how direct conversion works
In a direct-conversion (zero-IF) receiver, the LO runs exactly at the carrier frequency. Two mixers multiply the RF signal by the LO and by the LO shifted 90°, producing the I (in-phase) and Q (quadrature) baseband components. These are the two outputs of the ADC — both are needed to recover amplitude and phase information.
RF input: A·cos(2π·f_RF·t + φ) LO_I: cos(2π·f_RF·t) LO_Q: sin(2π·f_RF·t) ← 90° shifted I output = A·cos(φ) ← amplitude × cosine of phase Q output = A·sin(φ) ← amplitude × sine of phase From I and Q: amplitude = √(I²+Q²), phase = arctan(Q/I)
How IQ data relates to RSSI and dBFS
RSSI from IQ samples: P_IQ = (1/N) × Σ(I_n² + Q_n²) [linear, sum of squared amplitudes] RSSI_dBFS = 10×log₁₀(P_IQ / FS²) [relative to ADC full scale] Converting dBFS → dBm: RSSI_dBm = RSSI_dBFS + ADC_offset ADC_offset = known gain from antenna port to ADC input Example: RSSI_dBFS = −44.9 dBFS, ADC_offset = +50.6 dB (RF chain gain) RSSI_dBm = −44.9 + 50.6 = −(100 - 44.9 - 50.6) ... Actual calculation uses the ADC_ADJUST table in hardware.json ADC_ADJUST accounts for: RF gain, cable loss, analog filter, ADC scale factor This is why the calibration sets a fixed CW tone and measures the offset directly
EXP3 PA Classes A/B/AB/C/F — efficiency vs linearity trade-off in your GaN PA Advanced click to expand▾
Why PA class matters for your work
The PA in your Metro AAU RFFE is a GaN (Gallium Nitride) transistor biased and operated in a specific class that trades linearity against efficiency. Your PA efficiency test plan (Module 11 / PPT2) directly measures this. Understanding PA classes explains WHY DPD is necessary and WHY dynamic Vdd saves power.
PA classes — the complete picture
ClassConduction angleMax efficiencyLinearityUsed where
Class A360° (always on)50%Excellent — always in linear regionLow-power driver stages, test equipment
Class B180° (half cycle)78.5%Poor at zero-crossing — crossover distortionPush-pull audio, rarely in RF
Class AB180°–360° (adjustable bias)50–78%Good — biased slightly above cutoffMost base station PAs, your RENESAS F8410 operates here
Class C<180° (cutoff biased)>78.5%Very poor — only works for CW/FMTransmitters for constant-envelope signals only
Class F180° + harmonic tuning>90% theoreticalGood with DPDHigh-efficiency RF PAs, some 5G designs
DohertyTwo-amplifier combination60–70% at backed-off powerGood with DPDYour Metro AAU — the standard for LTE/5G base stations
Why Doherty is THE choice for LTE/5G base stations
A single Class AB PA has peak efficiency near saturation but very poor efficiency when backed off for PAPR headroom. At 10 dB back-off (typical for LTE OFDM): Class AB efficiency drops to ≈ 15%. A Doherty PA maintains ~60% efficiency at 6–8 dB back-off by using a carrier amplifier (always on, Class AB) and a peaking amplifier (only turns on at high power peaks, Class C). The two amplifiers combine through a quarter-wave transformer.
Doherty efficiency at output back-off (OBO): At OBO = 0 dB (saturation): η ≈ 78% (both amps at full power) At OBO = 6 dB (normal OFDM): η ≈ 60% (carrier amp efficient, peaking off) At OBO = 10 dB (deep backoff): η ≈ 45% (only carrier amp running) vs Class AB at OBO = 6 dB: η ≈ 25% (huge difference!)
How gate bias (Vgg) sets the operating class
In your GaN PA (RENESAS F8410), the gate voltage Vgg3_p sets the quiescent current which sets the conduction angle which sets the operating class. Your PA efficiency test plan tests Vgg3_p at −6.5 V (near cutoff = more Class C, lower quiescent current, more efficient), −5.5 V, and −4.5 V (more Class AB, more linear, more quiescent current). The test finds the optimal Vgg that satisfies both ACLR/EVM spec AND maximum efficiency.
Class A: why your EXA uses it (and your RU doesn't)
Test equipment uses Class A amplifiers for their excellent linearity. Your EXA internal amplifiers and your signal generator output stage are Class A — they must not add any distortion to the signal being measured. The 50% max efficiency is acceptable for instruments that run from wall power. The GaN PA in your RU runs at 40+ V drain, delivers 20 W RF, and must be as efficient as possible — that's why Doherty at Class AB is used, and why DPD linearizes the nonlinearity.
EXP4 Noise floor from first principles — thermal noise, kTB, −174 dBm/Hz derivation Advanced click to expand▾
Where −174 dBm/Hz comes from
Thermal noise is the random motion of electrons in any resistor at any temperature above absolute zero. It sets the absolute minimum noise floor of any receiver, regardless of how good the electronics are.
Thermal noise power in bandwidth B: P_noise = k × T × B k = Boltzmann constant = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K T = temperature in Kelvin (room temp = 290 K = 17°C) B = bandwidth in Hz At B = 1 Hz: P_noise = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4.0×10⁻²¹ W Converting to dBm: P_noise = 10×log₁₀(4.0×10⁻²¹ / 10⁻³) = 10×log₁₀(4.0×10⁻¹⁸) = −174 dBm So: thermal noise density = −174 dBm per Hz at room temperature (290 K) For any bandwidth: Noise floor (dBm) = −174 + 10×log₁₀(B_Hz) B = 10 MHz (LTE): −174 + 70 = −104 dBm B = 20 MHz (LTE): −174 + 73 = −101 dBm B = 100 MHz (5G): −174 + 80 = −94 dBm
Adding noise figure to get receiver noise floor
Receiver noise floor = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW) + NF Your RU Rx chain NF (estimated): LNA NF: ~2 dB Filter insertion loss before LNA: ~0.5 dB (adds to NF) Duplexer loss before LNA: ~0.5 dB (adds to NF) System NF ≈ 3 dB For B1 10 MHz: Noise floor = −174 + 70 + 3 = −101 dBm Required SNR for QPSK 1/3: ~−1 dB (can decode below noise floor with coding gain!) Sensitivity = −101 + (−1) = −102 dBm 3GPP REFSENS = −69 dBm → your RU easily beats this ✓
Why sensitivity tests have SUCH a wide margin from −69 dBm
The 3GPP Wide Area BS REFSENS of −69 dBm seems easy — your actual sensitivity is around −100 to −112 dBm. The 3GPP limit is set for the worst-case Wide Area BS with poor NF, high interference, and broad operating conditions. The limit is a floor — real base stations must be much better. In your RSSI calibration data: the 2 dB error margin (the practical RSSI sensitivity) is −93.5 to −95.5 dBm, showing your actual RU is ≈25 dB better than the 3GPP floor.
Noise at different temperatures (useful for temp testing)
TemperatureKelvinThermal noise densityChange from room temp
−40°C (cold outdoor)233 K−175.6 dBm/Hz−1.6 dB (quieter)
+17°C (room, 290K)290 K−174.0 dBm/Hzreference
+55°C (hot outdoor)328 K−173.0 dBm/Hz+1.0 dB (noisier)
+85°C (PA junction)358 K−172.5 dBm/Hz+1.5 dB (noisier)
This is why sensitivity specs are referenced to 290 K. When you run sensitivity tests with the unit hot (after long TX sessions), the noise floor rises slightly. Always let the RU reach thermal steady state before sensitivity tests.
EXP5 PRACH detector internals — noise estimator, peak multiplier, timing advance math Expert click to expand▾
The full PRACH detection pipeline
Stage 1 — Front end: Remove CP → apply FFT → extract PRACH subcarriers (839 bins at 1.25 kHz spacing) Stage 2 — Root correlation: For each root u being tested: Correlate received signal with conjugate of root ZC: Y = X × ZC_u* Apply IFFT → get power-delay profile (839 taps, one per possible cyclic shift) Stage 3 — Noise estimation: Take the correlation output after IFFT Form noise vector: all taps EXCEPT the K preamble positions (exclude K windows) Noise_est = mean(noise_vector_power) [average of all "empty" delay taps] Stage 4 — Peak detection: For each of the K preamble windows: Find peak power in that window: P_peak Detection threshold: P_peak / Noise_est > peak_multiplier If exceeded → preamble detected at that cyclic shift Timing advance = peak_position × (1/FFT_size) × symbol_duration
What the noise estimator actually does — intuition
The correlation output has 839 delay taps. For a given root u with ZCZ=12, there are K ≈ 6–7 preamble windows (occupied delay taps) and 839 − K×Ncs ≈ 700+ "empty" taps where no valid preamble should appear. The noise estimator averages power in these empty taps — that average IS the noise floor. The peak multiplier then sets: "if the peak is X times above this noise floor, call it a detection."
The detection threshold trade-off
Higher peak_multiplier: → Fewer false alarms (noise spikes mistaken for preambles) ✓ → More missed detections (real weak preambles not detected) ✗ → Better for dense urban where random UEs cause false alarms Lower peak_multiplier: → More detections of weak preambles ✓ → More false alarms ✗ → Better for large cells where UEs are far away and weak RuAuto test_Rx_PRACH sweeps power and finds the threshold where miss detection rate = 1% This measured threshold must be ≤ PRACH_KPI (e.g. −87 dBm + DSA offset per band)
Timing advance from PRACH — how it works
The delay tap position of the detected peak = propagation delay of UE Round-trip delay = 2 × distance / c For 1 km cell: delay = 2×1000 / 3×10⁸ = 6.67 μs One PRACH delay tap = Ncs × FFT_size / (839 × subcarrier_spacing) = Ncs × 0.001 ms / 839 (for 1.25 kHz format 0 PRACH) Timing Advance command sent to UE = detected delay taps × tap_duration UE then transmits that much earlier so signal arrives aligned at eNB
Connecting PRACH to your test results
In your test_Rx_PRACH output: "timing advance avg/std" shows the measured round-trip delay and its consistency. High std dev = the detector is struggling at the noise floor (inconsistent peak position). Low std dev = clean detection. The miss-detection rate curves you see in the results are exactly the probability of the peak/noise ratio exceeding the threshold at each input power level.
EXP6 dBFS ↔ dBm conversion — the complete guide with your real calibration numbers Intermediate click to expand▾
The fundamental difference
dBmdBFS
What it measuresAbsolute RF power at a physical portDigital amplitude relative to ADC max
Reference point1 mW into 50Ω at the connectorADC full-scale output (maximum code)
RangeAny value (positive or negative)Always ≤ 0 dBFS (0 = clipping)
Where measuredAt RF port, after all the hardwareIn the digital domain, after ADC
Used inLink budget, test results, 3GPP specspower_monitor, get_rssi raw output
Why you CANNOT simply subtract a fixed number
Many engineers think: "dBFS to dBm = just add 50 dB (or whatever the gain is)." This is only true if the gain chain from RF port to ADC is perfectly known AND constant. In reality it varies with: temperature, frequency, which ADC channel, which RFFE, calibration state, and firmware version. This is why hardware.json has a per-ADC ADC_ADJUST vector — each ADC needs its own offset.
The conversion formula using your real calibration data
RSSI_dBm = RSSI_dBFS + ADC_ADJUST + chain_gain_compensation Where ADC_ADJUST is the measured offset from your RSSI calibration: ADC 0 (B1): ADC_ADJUST = −20.9 dBFS ADC 2 (B3): ADC_ADJUST = −20.8 dBFS ADC 5 (B1): ADC_ADJUST = −24.2 dBFS (different because different RF path) Example: ADC 0 reads −44.9 dBFS at sensitivity point → RSSI_dBm ≈ −44.9 + ADC_ADJUST + RF_gain_total The 2dB-error-margin point = −95.5 dBm (from your RSSI Results deck) So total conversion offset = −95.5 − (−44.9) = −50.6 dB Meaning: 1 dBFS at ADC 0 input = (−50.6) dBm at RU antenna port
What the get_rssi command actually does
get_rssi output for ADC 0: rssi_dbfs: raw ADC measurement in dBFS (e.g. −44.9 dBFS) rssi_dbm: rssi_dbfs + ADC_ADJUST[0] (pre-compensated using hardware.json) The firmware reads ADC_ADJUST from /etc/configs/hardware.json Adds it to the raw dBFS reading Returns the compensated dBm value If hardware.json is wrong (offset not calibrated for your unit): → get_rssi dBm is wrong by however much the offset is off → This is what the RSSI calibration procedure (your PPT1) corrects
Practical rules for your daily work
ReadingdBFS valueWhat it meansAction
DL power_monitor−21 dBFSNormal load, good headroomOK — continue
DL power_monitor> −8 dBFSNear ADC clippingReduce DL power or check CFR
UL get_rssi−44.9 dBFSAt sensitivity test point for B1This is your REFSENS measurement point
UL get_rssi−68 dBFS or worseAt or below ADC noise floorSignal too weak — cannot measure reliably
UL get_rssi−5 dBFS or betterStrong signal, ADC nearly fullCheck for overload — reduce VGA gain

Phase & Angle Calibration using VNA E5071C — Complete Guide

SOLT calibration · Phase response · Group delay · Antenna element phase matching · Beamforming calibration · Cable phase characterisation · Step-by-step procedure for your lab

VNA1 Why phase calibration matters — beamforming, MIMO, cable characterisation Beginner click to expand▾
Phase in your AAU — the core reason
Your Metro AAU has 12 antenna elements (B1/B3/B41) steered by digital phase shifters (PE44820DS). Each element must transmit at a precise phase relative to the others. The beam points in the direction where the phases add constructively. A 5° phase error on one element degrades the beam pattern — the main lobe shifts, the gain drops, and side lobes increase. This is why TX_CAL (transmit calibration) exists and why the VNA is your primary tool for verifying it.
What the VNA measures that matters for phase
VNA measurementParameterUse in your work
S21 PhasePhase of forward transmission (deg)Phase difference between two cable/filter paths. Used to match cable electrical lengths before connecting to RU antenna ports.
S11 PhasePhase of reflection (deg)Characterises antenna port impedance phase. Combined with magnitude gives full impedance on Smith chart.
Group Delay−dφ/dω (ns)How much delay the path adds vs frequency. Constant group delay = linear phase = no pulse distortion. Ripple in group delay = multipath or resonance in connector/filter.
Electrical LengthPhase converted to metresCompares electrical lengths of two cables. For beamforming: cables to all antenna elements should have matched electrical length ±1°.
Phase ImbalanceΔPhase between Port1 and Port2Directly measures the phase mismatch between two TX paths — what OB_CAL corrects for in firmware.
The three types of phase calibration you need
TypeWhat you calibrateVNA technique
1. Cable electrical length matchingSF141 test cables from FHGW BOB to EXA/EXMS21 phase at each band centre frequency → match pairs to within ±2°
2. Antenna element phase responsePhase shift introduced by each TX path (RFFE)S21 phase sweep across band → compare all 8/12 paths → identify outliers
3. Filter / duplexer phase characterisationPhase vs frequency across the passband of BPF, duplexer, triplexerS21 phase + group delay sweep → verify linear phase in passband, check group delay ripple
VNA2 VNA calibration — SOLT/SOLR, why it matters, what errors it removes Intermediate click to expand▾
Why you MUST calibrate before any phase measurement
The VNA measures phase at its test ports. But everything between the VNA port and your DUT (cables, adaptors, connectors) adds phase. Without calibration, you are measuring the phase of your test setup, not the DUT. A 30 cm test cable at 2 GHz adds ~72° of phase. After SOLT calibration, the reference plane moves to the cal kit connector tips — the cable phase is mathematically removed.
SOLT calibration — Short, Open, Load, Thru
SOLT removes 12 systematic error terms: Port 1: Directivity, Source Match, Reflection Tracking Port 2: Directivity, Source Match, Reflection Tracking Transmission: Forward/Reverse Tracking, Forward/Reverse Isolation Procedure: SHORT → Γ = −1 (180° reflection) — known reflection standard OPEN → Γ = +1 (0° reflection) — known reflection standard LOAD → Γ = 0 (50Ω match) — sets the reference impedance THRU → direct connection P1→P2 — sets transmission reference
Step-by-step SOLT on your E5071C
StepAction on E5071CWhy
1Set frequency range: Start = lowest band freq − 10%, Stop = highest + 10%. For B1/B3/B41: Start 1700 MHz, Stop 2700 MHz.Cal must cover the full measurement range. Outside the cal range results are uncorrected.
2Set number of points: 401 minimum, 1601 for phase accuracy. More points = smoother phase trace.Phase resolution = frequency span / (points − 1). Coarse points = phase ripple artefacts.
3Set IF BW: 1 kHz for phase measurements (narrower = lower noise = better phase accuracy).Phase noise on VNA = random phase error. Narrow IF BW reduces noise. Tradeoff: slower sweep.
4Set power: −5 to −10 dBm (keep DUT in linear region).Measuring passive components (cables, filters) — low power avoids any nonlinearity.
5Press Cal → Cal Wizard → SOLT → 2-Port.2-port cal corrects all 12 error terms including transmission phase.
6Connect SHORT to Port 1 cable tip → press SHORT → wait for sweep.Characterises Port 1 reflection. Short must be from your calibration kit (85052D or similar).
7Connect OPEN to Port 1 → press OPEN → wait.The open standard has a known fringing capacitance model — E5071C corrects for this automatically.
8Connect LOAD to Port 1 → press LOAD → wait.50Ω reference. Load quality determines directivity — use a high-quality cal kit load (>40 dB return loss).
9Repeat SHORT, OPEN, LOAD on Port 2.Port 2 has its own error terms — must be characterised independently.
10Connect Port 1 cable directly to Port 2 cable (THRU) → press THRU.This sets the transmission reference plane. After this, S21 = 0 dB / 0° = calibrated baseline.
11Press Done/Apply → Cal status shows "Cor" (corrected).All 12 error terms are now stored. Measurement uncertainty drops from ±several degrees to ±0.1–0.5°.
12Verify cal: connect a known standard (e.g. THRU). S21 should show 0.00 dB ± 0.05 dB and 0.0° ± 0.5°.Always verify cal before trusting measurements. If verification fails → redo cal (dirty connector, wrong kit).
NEVER remove or flex the cal cables after completing SOLT. Any cable movement changes the electrical length and invalidates the calibration. If you need to reposition, redo the cal from Step 6. This is the most common source of phase measurement errors in the lab.
Cal kit selection: use the Keysight 85052D (3.5mm) or 85032F (N-type) for your SF141 cables. The cal kit model number must match what is selected in the E5071C — wrong cal kit = wrong correction model = phase errors even with "Cor" showing.
VNA3 Cable electrical length & phase matching — step-by-step for your SF141 cables Intermediate click to expand▾
Why cable phase matching matters
In your test setup, multiple cables connect the FHGW BOB SMA ports to the EXA/EXM. For multi-port measurements (e.g. comparing TX power across 4 antenna elements simultaneously using a switch matrix), each cable must have the same electrical length — otherwise you are adding cable-to-cable phase differences to your measurement. For beamforming calibration, cable phase differences directly appear as beam pointing errors.
Electrical length vs physical length
Electrical length (degrees) = 360 × f × L × √εr / c Where: f = frequency (Hz) L = physical length (metres) εr = relative permittivity of the cable dielectric c = 3×10⁸ m/s For SF141 semi-rigid cable (εr ≈ 2.1, velocity factor VF ≈ 0.695): At 2140 MHz, 1 metre of SF141: Phase = 360 × 2140e6 × 1 × √2.1 / 3e8 = 360 × 2140e6 × 1.449 / 3e8 = 360 × 10.33 = 3720° = 10.33 full wavelengths So 1 mm difference in SF141 cable length at 2140 MHz = 3.72° phase difference For beamforming: target match within ±2° = within ±0.54 mm physical length!
Procedure — measuring and matching cable electrical lengths
StepActionTarget
1Complete SOLT calibration as above (VNA2)Cal verified, S21 = 0 dB / 0°
2E5071C: Marker → Add Marker → set to band centre freq (e.g. 2140 MHz for B1)Marker 1 at exact test frequency
3Connect Cable A between Port 1 and Port 2. Read S21 phase at marker: e.g. −245.3°Record as φ_A
4Swap to Cable B. Read S21 phase: e.g. −248.7°Record as φ_B
5Phase difference = φ_B − φ_A = −3.4°Target: |ΔΦ| ≤ 2° for cable matching
6If |ΔΦ| > 2°: use E5071C Marker → Electrical Delay function. Enter the delay to null the phase difference. The display shows the equivalent physical length difference.Electrical delay shows how many mm one cable is longer
7Trim the longer cable (precision cable cutter) or select a different cable from stock.After trimming: re-measure, verify |ΔΦ| ≤ 2°
8Repeat at all band centre frequencies: 2140 (B1), 1842.5 (B3), 942.5 (B8), 780.5 (B28), 2545 (B41)Phase match verified at all operating frequencies
9Label matched cable pairs and store together. Never mix matched cables.Matched pair stored as "CAL PAIR B1/B3 - 2026-07"
Using Electrical Delay on E5071C to null cable phase
On E5071C: Scale → Electrical Delay → enter delay value in seconds This shifts the phase trace by: ΔΦ = 360 × f × delay To null a cable: measure phase at marker → compute delay = phase / (360 × f) Example: phase difference = 3.4° at 2140 MHz Required delay = 3.4 / (360 × 2140e6) = 4.41 ps Physical length = delay × c / √εr = 4.41e-12 × 3e8 / 1.449 = 0.91 mm So Cable B is 0.91 mm longer than Cable A. Trim 0.91 mm off Cable B to match.
E5071C display formats for phase work
FormatE5071C menuBest for
Phase (−180° to +180°)Format → PhaseSeeing phase vs frequency. Jumps at ±180° (phase wrapping) are normal — use "unwrap" if needed.
Unwrapped PhaseFormat → Expanded PhaseRemoves 360° jumps — shows true monotonic phase vs frequency. Essential for group delay measurement.
Group DelayFormat → Delay−dφ/df in nanoseconds. Flat = linear phase = good. Ripple = multipath or filter resonance.
Electrical LengthMarker → Electrical DelayConverts phase to metres at the marker frequency.
Smith ChartFormat → Smith ChartS11 impedance — phase of reflection vs frequency plotted on impedance plane. Use for antenna port matching.
PolarFormat → PolarS21 as magnitude + phase on polar plot. Useful for seeing phase variation with frequency.
VNA4 Antenna element phase calibration — measuring TX path phase across all 8/12 elements Advanced click to expand▾
What you are measuring
Each of the 8 or 12 TX paths in your AAU (from FHGW DAC output to RFFE antenna port) introduces a different phase shift. Sources of inter-element phase difference: slightly different trace lengths on PCB, component tolerance in phase shifters, connector variations, filter group delay differences. The OB_CAL (observation calibration) corrects these in firmware — but first you need to MEASURE them to know how much correction is needed.
Setup for multi-element phase measurement
Test setup: VNA Port 1 → SMA cable → FHGW BOB TX_A port (reference input) VNA Port 2 → SMA cable → Antenna element N output (DUT output) Measure: S21 = (signal at element N output) / (signal at FHGW BOB input) Parameter of interest: S21 Phase at band centre frequency Repeat for all N elements (N = 0 to 7 for 8-element array) Compare: φ_element_N vs φ_element_0 (reference element) Ideal: all elements have same S21 phase (ΔΦ = 0° between any two elements) Acceptable: |ΔΦ| ≤ 5° element-to-element before firmware correction After OB_CAL: residual ΔΦ ≤ 1° (firmware compensates the rest)
Step-by-step procedure
StepActionRecord
1Power on FHGW. Activate the band under test (e.g. B1). Ensure DL carrier is NOT transmitting — you need the DAC to be driven from the VNA, not from DU traffic. Set FHGW to passthrough/loopback mode or use BOB SMA as standalone input.Band, EARFCN, channel BW
2SOLT calibrate VNA from Port 1 cable tip to Port 2 cable tip (VNA2 procedure). Cal frequency range: cover full band + ±10%.Cal verified: S21 = 0 dB / 0.0° with THRU
3Set format: S21 Phase. Add Marker 1 at exact band centre (e.g. 2140.000 MHz for B1).Marker frequency confirmed
4Connect Port 1 → TX_A0 input, Port 2 → Antenna element 0 output. This is your reference element.φ_0 = e.g. −312.5°
5Keep Port 1 connected. Move Port 2 → Antenna element 1 output.φ_1 = e.g. −315.2°. ΔΦ_1 = φ_1 − φ_0 = −2.7°
6Repeat for elements 2–7 (or 2–11 for 12-element array).ΔΦ_N for each element
7Plot ΔΦ_N vs element number. Should be approximately flat (within ±5°). Any element with |ΔΦ| > 10° → suspect that element path for hardware fault.Phase spread table
8Enter the measured ΔΦ_N values as initial correction offsets in the FHGW firmware phase calibration table (per-element phase register). OB_CAL then fine-tunes further.Per-element phase offset written to FHGW
9After OB_CAL completes: repeat VNA measurement. Residual ΔΦ should now be ≤ 1° — the firmware has corrected the hardware phase errors.Residual phase spread after cal
Phase vs frequency sweep — checking linear phase across the band
For a TX path to be usable for wideband signals (e.g. 20 MHz LTE), the phase must be LINEAR across the band (constant group delay). Nonlinear phase = group delay variation = pulse distortion = EVM degradation.
Measure: S21 Expanded Phase across full band B1: 2110 to 2170 MHz (60 MHz sweep) Good result: straight line (linear phase) → group delay flat Phase slope = −Group delay × 360 × f → constant slope = constant delay = OK Bad result: ripple in phase → resonance in filter/connector → fix connector or replace filter Acceptable group delay variation: ≤ 10 ns across the band for LTE Check formula: EVM from group delay ripple ≈ 2π × f_subcarrier × ΔGD × 100% For 15 kHz subcarrier, 5 ns GD ripple: EVM ≈ 2π × 15e3 × 5e-9 = 0.047% (negligible) For 15 kHz subcarrier, 100 ns GD ripple: EVM ≈ 0.94% (significant)
On E5071C: after measuring S21 phase, switch to Format → Delay to see group delay directly in nanoseconds. A flat trace = good linear phase. Peaks/dips in group delay at specific frequencies = resonances from imperfect connector mating, damaged cable, or filter out of spec.
VNA5 Beamforming angle calibration — mapping phase shift to beam angle, verifying PE44820DS Advanced click to expand▾
From phase difference to beam angle
For a uniform linear array with element spacing d: Beam angle θ = arcsin(λ × ΔΦ / (2π × d)) Where: λ = wavelength = c/f ΔΦ = progressive phase shift between adjacent elements (radians) d = element spacing (typically λ/2 for maximum scan range) For λ/2 spacing: d = λ/2 → θ = arcsin(ΔΦ/π) ΔΦ = 0° → θ = 0° (broadside, beam perpendicular to array) ΔΦ = 30° → θ = arcsin(30/180) = 9.6° scan ΔΦ = 60° → θ = 19.5° scan ΔΦ = 90° → θ = 30° scan ΔΦ = 180° → θ = 90° (endfire — maximum scan, impractical) Your B1/B3 4-column array (12 elements): Scan range: typically ±60° in azimuth Each 1° phase step → ~0.3° beam shift (at broadside)
Verifying the phase shifter (PE44820DS) with VNA
The PE44820DS is a digitally-controlled phase shifter. It has 6 or 8 control bits, giving 64 or 256 discrete phase states. Each state should produce a predictable, repeatable phase shift. The VNA verifies: (1) each state produces the correct phase, (2) insertion loss is consistent across states, (3) there are no stuck bits.
StepActionPass criterion
1Connect VNA Port 1 → phase shifter input, Port 2 → phase shifter output. SOLT calibrate.S21 = 0 dB / 0° at state 0 (reference)
2Set phase shifter to state 0 (all bits = 0 = minimum phase shift). Record S21 phase at band centre.Reference phase φ_0
3Step through all phase states (0, 1, 2, ... 63 for 6-bit device). At each state record S21 phase and S21 magnitude.Phase: each step should increment by ~360/64 = 5.625° · Magnitude: should stay within ±0.5 dB across all states
4Plot measured phase vs state number. Should be monotonically increasing, approximately linear.Phase linearity: deviation from ideal ≤ ±2° per state
5Check magnitude variation: |S21| should not vary more than ±0.5 dB as phase state changes.Magnitude flatness across states ≤ ±0.5 dB
6Toggle bit 0 only (LSB). Phase should shift by 5.625°. Toggle bit 5 (MSB). Phase should shift by 180°.Each bit contributes correct phase weight: MSB=180°, next=90°, 45°, 22.5°, 11.25°, 5.625°
7Repeat at cold (−20°C) and hot (+55°C) if temperature chamber available. Phase shift should be within ±3° of room temperature value.Temperature coefficient ≤ 0.05°/°C typical for GaAs phase shifters
A stuck bit in the phase shifter (one bit permanently 0 or 1) causes the phase to jump by that bit weight when it should not. In your beam pattern this appears as a sidelobe spike at a fixed direction. If you see an unexplained sidelobe in OTA measurements, check the phase shifter with this procedure first.
Full TX chain phase calibration sequence (combining VNA steps)
Complete sequence for one antenna element: 1. VNA: Measure cable electrical length → confirm within ±2° of reference cable 2. VNA: Measure S21 phase of pre-PA path (FHGW BOB → phase shifter input): Set phase shifter to state 0. Record φ_prePA. 3. VNA: Measure S21 phase of full TX path (FHGW BOB → antenna port): φ_total = φ_prePA + φ_phaseShifter(state) + φ_PA + φ_filter + φ_combiner 4. FHGW CLI: Set per-element phase offset register to compensate φ_total Command: write_phase_cal_reg element_N offset_deg 5. Activate all elements simultaneously. Set all phase shifters to state 0. Measure OTA beam pattern in anechoic chamber (or near-field scanner). Verify main beam at θ = 0° (broadside) → confirms cal correct. 6. Command phase shifters to steer beam to θ = 15°, 30°, 45°. Verify beam follows at each angle within ±2°. 7. If beam angle error > 2°: re-run VNA measurement on outlier element, identify the phase error source, correct register.
VNA6 Practical VNA phase tips — common mistakes, connector care, temperature effects Intermediate click to expand▾
Top phase measurement mistakes and how to avoid them
MistakeEffect on phase measurementPrevention
Not torquing connectors to specLoose connector → air gap → changed dielectric → phase error of 5–20°. Also reproducibility is terrible.Always use a torque wrench: SMA = 0.45 Nm (4 in-lb), N-type = 1.36 Nm (12 in-lb), 3.5mm = 0.9 Nm (8 in-lb).
Moving cables after calAny bend changes electrical length. A 90° flex of a semi-rigid cable causes ≈0.5–2° phase shift.Tape cables in position after cal. Use cable clamps. If cables move → redo cal.
Temperature driftVNA synthesiser and cables change phase with temperature. 1°C drift → ~0.1–0.5° phase change in cables.Warm up VNA for 30 minutes before cal. Measure in temperature-stable environment. Re-cal if room temp changes >2°C.
Wrong cal kit selectedE5071C applies wrong correction coefficients → systematic phase error of 1–5°.Confirm: Cal → Cal Kit → verify kit model matches your physical kit (85052D, 85032F, etc.).
Measuring outside cal frequency rangeNo correction applied → results uncalibrated → wrong phase.Always set measurement freq range BEFORE calibrating. Cal covers exactly the set sweep range.
Phase wrapping confusionPhase displayed as −180° to +180°. Jumps at boundaries look like discontinuities but are normal.Use Format → Expanded Phase to unwrap. Or use Electrical Delay to shift the trace away from ±180°.
Dirty or damaged connectorsEven invisible contamination → extra capacitance → phase shift AND return loss degradation.Inspect with magnifier or microscope before every connection. Clean with IPA and lint-free swab. Replace any connector with visible centre pin damage.
Too few frequency pointsPhase ripple artefacts between measured points — looks like a real resonance but is just interpolation.Use ≥401 points for component measurements. Use 1601 points for precision phase work.
SCPI commands to automate VNA phase measurement
// E5071C SCPI for automated phase measurement: // Set up measurement :SENS1:FREQ:STAR 2110000000 // Start freq: 2110 MHz (B1 band edge) :SENS1:FREQ:STOP 2170000000 // Stop freq: 2170 MHz (B1 band edge) :SENS1:SWE:POIN 1601 // 1601 points :SENS1:BWID 1000 // IF BW = 1 kHz :SOUR1:POW -10 // Source power = -10 dBm :CALC1:PAR1:DEF S21 // Measure S21 :CALC1:FORM PHAS // Format: Phase :CALC1:MARK1:STAT ON // Marker 1 ON :CALC1:MARK1:X 2140000000 // Marker at 2140 MHz // Trigger and read :TRIG:SOUR BUS // Bus trigger :TRIG:SING // Single sweep *OPC? // Wait for completion :CALC1:MARK1:Y? // Read marker 1 phase (degrees) // → e.g. -312.456 (degrees at 2140 MHz) // Read group delay :CALC1:FORM GDEL // Switch to group delay format :CALC1:MARK1:Y? // Read group delay (seconds) // → e.g. 2.341E-9 (2.341 ns at 2140 MHz) // Read full trace data :CALC1:DATA:FDAT? // Returns all 1601 phase points as CSV
Quick phase check — 5 minute procedure for daily use
Full SOLT cal takes 10–15 minutes. For a quick daily check without full cal:
Use a previously saved cal state: Recall → Cal → select last saved cal file. Valid if frequency range and cables unchanged since last full cal.
Verify with THRU: connect THRU and check S21 = 0 dB ±0.2 dB and 0° ±1°. If within tolerance → use saved cal. If not → do full SOLT.
For cable phase comparison only (relative measurement, not absolute): connect Cable A as THRU → Save trace → connect Cable B → use Data/Memory → shows ΔΦ directly. No SOLT needed for relative measurements.
E5071C memory trace: Trace → Data → Memory Save. Then Data → Show Data/Memory → displays the difference between current and saved trace. Phase difference is shown directly.
VNA7 Worked example — full B1 TX path phase calibration from scratch Expert click to expand▾
Scenario
You have a Metro AAU unit (unit 509, RFFE2 recently reflashed via JTAG). After reflash you need to verify the B1 TX path phase response on all 4 B1 antenna elements and confirm OB_CAL brings them within ±1° of each other.

B1 uses ADCs 0,1,4,5 and B3 uses ADCs 2,3,6,7.

eCPRI + DownlinkeCPRI fronthaul carrying DL dataThe physical Ethernet connection between DU and AAU carrying: (1) IQ data (downlink carrier payload), (2) control plane timing (sync), (3) management plane config. In your lab: typically 10GbE SFP+ cable, IP-addressed, with PTP grandmaster for timing.
The 4-cable connection from AAU to EXM — exactly what those red lines are
Your diagram shows 4 red cables going from the AAU to the EXM. These connect the 4 antenna column TX outputs (A, B, C, D) on the RFFE to the EXM's 4 input ports (RF1, RF2, RF3, RF4 or via a switch matrix). Each cable carries the combined B1+B3 signal from that column — the diplexer/triplexer inside the RFFE has already combined B1 TX + B3 TX onto the single TX_A (or TX_B/C/D) port.
In practice, since the EXM has only 1–2 RF input ports, your setup uses an RF switch matrix (Mini-Circuits or similar) to route each column in turn to the EXM. RuAuto controls this switch matrix automatically — it measures column A, switches to column B, measures, switches to C, etc.

NF

Understanding Noise Figure — Complete Guide

From your PDF: Understanding Noise Figure by Iulian Rosu YO3DAC/VA3IUL · Thermal noise · NF derivation · Friis cascade · All 5 noise types · Applied to your LNA/RU/EXA

NF1 Thermal noise foundation — kTB, −174 dBm/Hz, Johnson-Nyquist, noise voltage Beginner click to expand▾
What thermal noise is
Thermal noise is a random fluctuation in voltage caused by the random motion of charge carriers in any conducting medium at a temperature above absolute zero. It cannot exist at absolute zero because charge carriers cannot move at absolute zero. Every resistor, every conductor, every component in your RF chain generates it — this is the irreducible noise floor of physics.
Thermal noise voltage — the RMS formula
Vn = √(4kTRB) k = Boltzmann constant = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K T = Temperature in Kelvin (K = 273 + °C, so room temp = 290 K) R = Resistance in ohms B = Bandwidth in Hz Example: 100 kΩ resistor at room temp, 1 MHz BW: Vn = √(4 × 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 100×10³ × 1×10⁶) = √(1.6×10⁻⁹) = 40.7 μV RMS Key rules: - Larger R → more noise voltage - Higher T → more noise voltage - Wider B → more noise voltage - LOW impedance = desirable for low noise circuits
Thermal noise POWER — the −174 dBm/Hz reference
Available noise power from a matched source: P = kTB At room temperature (T = 290 K), B = 1 Hz: P = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4.0×10⁻²¹ W = −174 dBm/Hz This is THE reference noise level. At room temperature, in 1 Hz bandwidth, no receiver can ever have a noise floor below −174 dBm — it is the physical limit. For any bandwidth: Noise floor (dBm) = −174 + 10×log₁₀(B_Hz) B = 200 kHz (GSM): −174 + 53 = −121 dBm B = 10 MHz (LTE): −174 + 70 = −104 dBm B = 20 MHz (LTE): −174 + 73 = −101 dBm B = 100 MHz (5G): −174 + 80 = −94 dBm
Key insight from the PDF: "Temperatures correspond to power levels. When the temperature of a resistor is doubled, the power output from it is doubled." And: "Powers from uncorrelated sources are additive, so noise temperatures are additive." This is why you cannot subtract noise — you can only add it. Every component in your receiver chain makes it worse, never better.
Noise bandwidth vs 3 dB bandwidth
Noise Bandwidth (B) is defined as the equivalent rectangular passband that passes the same amount of noise power as the actual filter. It is approximately equal to the 3 dB bandwidth for most practical filters. For best sensitivity, B should be no wider than required for the information content. This is why you set RBW = 100 kHz for ACLR (not 1 MHz) — narrower RBW = lower noise floor = can see weaker adjacent channel signals.
NF2 Noise Figure definition — SNR degradation, Noise Factor vs NF, receiver sensitivity formula Intermediate click to expand▾
What Noise Figure measures
Introduced by Harald T. Friis in 1944, Noise Figure characterises the degradation in Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) caused by a device. An ideal noiseless amplifier would amplify signal AND noise equally — it would not change the SNR. A real amplifier adds its own internal noise, reducing the SNR at the output vs the input. NF measures exactly how much worse the SNR got.
Noise Factor (F) and Noise Figure (NF)
Noise Factor (linear, not dB): F = SNR_input / SNR_output = (S_in/N_in) / (S_out/N_out) Since circuits always add noise: SNR_out < SNR_in → F > 1 always Noise Figure (dB): NF = 10 × log₁₀(F) = SNR_in(dB) − SNR_out(dB) Perfect noiseless device: F = 1, NF = 0 dB Real LNA: F ≈ 1.26 to 2.0, NF ≈ 1 to 3 dB Real mixer: F ≈ 3 to 10, NF ≈ 5 to 10 dB Attenuator (10 dB): F = 10, NF = 10 dB exactly
Critical insight — attenuator before LNA
A 10 dB attenuator placed at the INPUT of an amplifier will increase the total Noise Figure of the system with 10 dB. This is the most important practical rule from the PDF, and it directly affects your test setup.
If you place a 10 dB pad BEFORE your LNA (or before the EXA input): the signal drops 10 dB but the noise floor stays at −174 dBm/Hz (cannot go lower). SNR degrades by 10 dB. This is why your EXA has an internal attenuator that you must set correctly — setting it too high degrades the EXA noise figure and limits your sensitivity measurement accuracy. The Screenshot 2 ADC overrange happened because too little attenuation was used.
Receiver sensitivity from NF
Receiver_NF (dB) = 174 + Sensitivity(dBm) − 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) − Required_SNR(dB) Rearranged to find sensitivity: Sensitivity(dBm) = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) + NF + Required_SNR Your B1 example: BW = 10 MHz → 10×log₁₀(10×10⁶) = 70 dB NF_system ≈ 3 dB (LNA dominates) Required SNR for QPSK 1/3 FRC ≈ −1 dB (below noise with coding gain) Sensitivity = −174 + 70 + 3 + (−1) = −102 dBm 3GPP REFSENS = −69 dBm (Wide Area BS limit) Your actual = −102 dBm → 33 dB better than required ✓ Narrow BW and smaller required SNR relax the NF requirement.
The real-world amplifier model
Every real amplifier is modelled as: an ideal noiseless amplifier + an internal noise source at the input. The noise source adds noise BEFORE the ideal amplifier. The ideal amplifier then amplifies everything (signal + original noise + added noise) by its gain G.
Example: 10 dB gain amplifier, NF = 3 dB Input: signal at −40 dBm, noise floor at −174 dBm/Hz Internal noise source adds: NF − 0 = 3 dB worth of noise (doubles the noise power) After ideal amplifier gain of 10 dB: Signal output: −40 + 10 = −30 dBm Noise output: −174 + 10 + 3 = −161 dBm/Hz SNR input: −40 − (−174) = 134 dB SNR output: −30 − (−161) = 131 dB NF = 134 − 131 = 3 dB ✓ (matches the NF we said the amp has)
NF3 Friis cascade formula — why the LNA dominates, worked examples for your RU chain Advanced click to expand▾
Friis formula — total NF of a cascaded chain
F_total = F₁ + (F₂−1)/G₁ + (F₃−1)/(G₁×G₂) + (F₄−1)/(G₁×G₂×G₃) + ... Where: F = Noise Factor (LINEAR, not dB) of each stage G = Gain (LINEAR, not dB) of each stage Convert: F = 10^(NF_dB/10) G = 10^(Gain_dB/10) Convert back: NF_total = 10×log₁₀(F_total)
The golden rule — first stage dominates
The first amplifier in a chain has the most significant effect on the total noise figure. Every subsequent stage is divided by the cumulative gain of all preceding stages. With a good LNA (NF=2 dB, Gain=20 dB = linear gain 100), the second stage contribution is divided by 100 — essentially negligible.
Two amplifiers, both 10 dB gain (G=10 linear), both NF=3 dB (F=2.0): F_total = 2 + (2−1)/10 = 2 + 0.1 = 2.1 NF_total = 10×log₁₀(2.1) = 3.22 dB (Second amp only adds 0.22 dB to the 3 dB from first amp!) Now swap order — 3 dB NF amp first, then 6 dB NF amp: F1=2.0, G1=10, F2=4.0 F_total = 2.0 + (4.0−1)/10 = 2.0 + 0.3 = 2.3 → NF = 3.62 dB Swap — 6 dB NF amp first, then 3 dB NF amp: F1=4.0, G1=10, F2=2.0 F_total = 4.0 + (2.0−1)/10 = 4.0 + 0.1 = 4.1 → NF = 6.13 dB Difference: 3.62 vs 6.13 dB — same two amplifiers, different order = 2.5 dB system NF difference!
The cascaded amplifier worked example from the PDF
Both amps: 10 dB gain, NF = 3 dB Signal enters at −40 dBm, noise at −174 dBm/Hz After Amp 1: Signal = −40 + 10 = −30 dBm Noise = −174 + 10 + 3 = −161 dBm/Hz = 20 × kTB (20 times above noise floor) Entering Amp 2: Noise floor at Amp 2 input = −161 dBm/Hz = 20 × kTB Amp 2 internal noise source adds 1 × kTB (NF = 3 dB) Total noise at Amp 2 input = 20 + 1 = 21 × kTB Increase in noise from Amp 2 = (21/20) = 1.05 → 10×log₁₀(1.05) = 0.21 dB Amp 2 only degrades SNR by 0.21 dB, NOT 3 dB! Why? Because the noise entering Amp 2 (−161 dBm/Hz) is already 13 dB above kTB. The Amp 2 internal noise is tiny compared to the already-amplified noise from Amp 1. This proves: the FIRST amplifier dominates — always minimise NF of the first stage.

Rule from the PDF: "If two amplifiers have the same NF but different gains, the higher gain amplifier should precede the lower gain amplifier." And: "The lower noise figure amplifier should usually go first." Both rules point to the same thing — put your best (lowest NF, highest gain) amplifier absolutely first in the chain, immediately after the antenna.
NF4 NF of passive devices — attenuators, mixers, filters, cables, your test setup Intermediate click to expand▾
Golden rule for passive lossy devices
The Noise Figure of an attenuator (or any purely resistive lossy passive device) equals its attenuation in dB. A 10 dB attenuator has exactly 10 dB NF. This is a fundamental result — the device attenuates the signal but cannot attenuate the thermal noise floor below kTB.
Attenuator (L dB loss): NF = L dB F = 10^(L/10) (linear) Example: 30 dB attenuator pad: NF = 30 dB, F = 1000 (linear) Signal drops 30 dB. Noise floor stays at −174 dBm/Hz. SNR degrades by 30 dB. BUT: if noise at attenuator input is ABOVE kTB (e.g. −144 dBm/Hz = 30 dB above kTB) Then SNR degradation < 30 dB (noise dominates before attenuator) The attenuator still attenuates both signal and noise by 30 dB But noise cannot go below kTB, so the noise floor "hits bottom" after the attenuator
