The PDF states: "An attenuator placed at the input of a system will increase the total Noise Figure with the same amount of its attenuation." This is why for SENSITIVITY tests you remove or minimise all external pads between the RU antenna port and the EXM input. For TX tests it doesn't matter — the signal is 50+ dBm above the noise floor.
Antenna note — NOT a noise source
From the PDF: "The radiation resistance of the antenna does not convert power to heat, and so is not a source of thermal noise." The antenna's 50Ω radiation resistance is not a thermal resistor — it represents power radiated into (or received from) space. This is why a well-matched antenna pointing at cold sky can effectively have a very low noise temperature (a few kelvin for radio astronomy antennas). Your base station antenna does see the thermal environment (ground, buildings, interference) but the antenna itself does not add thermal Johnson noise.
NF5 All 5 noise types — Thermal, Shot, Flicker/1f, White, Burst — with RF context Advanced click to expand▾
Noise typeAlso calledSourceFrequency behaviourRF context
ThermalJohnson-Nyquist noiseThermal agitation of electrons in any conductor above 0KWhite (flat across all frequencies). Power ∝ temperature and bandwidth.Fundamental limit of all receivers. Sets the −174 dBm/Hz noise floor. Gaussian amplitude distribution. Dominates in wideband RF systems.
Shot noiseSchottky noiseDiscrete nature of charge (electrons crossing a potential barrier — PN junction, transistor)White (flat). Power ∝ DC bias current.Present in every active device: LNA transistors, mixer diodes. Combined with thermal noise in a junction diode. Proportional to bias current — higher bias → more shot noise (but also more gain).
Flicker / 1/fPink noise, excess noiseCrystal surface defects in semiconductors, oxide coating on vacuum tube cathodesIncreases at low frequencies (∝ 1/f). Decreases with frequency. Not white noise.Most important at low frequencies. In GaAs FETs: corner frequency (where 1/f = white noise) can be 100 MHz — directly within LTE/5G bands. Your GaN PA has 1/f noise that can appear as LO phase noise or close-in spurious. Metal film resistors better than carbon for low 1/f noise.
White noise—Any source with flat spectrumFlat (constant) across frequencyCategory name: Thermal noise and Shot noise are both white noise. "White" = like white light, contains all frequencies equally. Your spectrum analyzer noise floor is white noise.
Burst / PopcornBurst noiseHeavy metal ion contamination in semiconductor junctionsRandom discrete level shifts (bursts). Power ∝ 1/f². Very device-specific.Sounds like popcorn if audio-amplified. Appears as random sudden shifts in bias current. Can manifest as intermittent spurious emissions or random ACLR degradation in a PA with contaminated junctions. Very rare in modern clean-room processes.
1/f noise corner frequency — especially important for GaAs/GaN
The corner frequency fc = point where 1/f noise power = white noise power Process type → typical fc: Precision bipolar: fc = 1 Hz to 10 Hz (very good) High-freq bipolar: fc = 1 Hz to 10 kHz MOSFETs: fc = 100 kHz to 1 MHz (channel length⁻¹) GaAs FET / InGaP HBT: fc = 100 MHz (your RFFE technology!) For your GaN PA (RENESAS F8410 — GaN on SiC): 1/f corner can be at 10–100 MHz This means 1/f noise from the PA is present WITHIN the LTE channel Mechanism: 1/f noise modulates the gate → phase modulation of the carrier → phase noise This is why GaN PAs contribute to close-in phase noise even with clean LO signals
Noise reduction strategies (from the PDF)
Keep source resistance and amplifier input resistance LOW — high resistance = more thermal noise voltage (Vn = √(4kTRB))
Reduce circuit bandwidth to minimum required — narrower BW = less noise power integrated
Use LNA as the FIRST stage — lowest NF, highest gain, before anything else
Use metal film resistors not carbon composition — much lower 1/f noise for low-frequency, low-noise stages
Proper grounding, shielding, filtering — prevents external interference adding to noise floor
Lowest DC supply that still meets spec — less bias current = less shot noise
Negative feedback at transistor level — unbypassed emitter resistor (10–30 Ω) reduces noise by sensing and feeding back current fluctuations. Up to 20 dB PM/AM noise reduction demonstrated.
At high frequencies: BJTs perform better for low source impedance; MOSFETs better for high source impedance — choose the right transistor technology for the application

Screenshot 2 ADC overrange — explained via NF theory
In your Screenshot 2 (TRX1 Modulation Analysis), EXM showed "ADC over range" with Channel Power = 48.333 dBm and Ext Gain = −56 dB. The NF analysis explains what happened:
Signal at EXM port = 48.333 dBm − 56 dB external path = −7.667 dBm EXM internal attenuator = 10 dB (as set) Signal at EXM mixer input = −7.667 − 10 = −17.667 dBm EXM mixer maximum safe input ≈ −20 to −30 dBm → Signal at −17.667 dBm is ABOVE the safe mixer input range → Mixer compression → ADC overrange → measurement invalid Fix: increase external attenuator to 30 dB → mixer input = −37.667 dBm ✓ OR: increase EXM internal atten to 30 dB via AMPTD menu OR: set RF Range to 60 dBm (tells EXM to expect stronger signal) NF implication: adding more attenuation raises the EXM effective NF for that measurement but for a TX power/EVM test where signal is at 48 dBm, this doesn't matter — the signal is 80+ dB above kTB, so EXM NF is irrelevant.
RSSI sensitivity point — connecting NF theory to your measurement
Your RSSI calibration procedure measures sensitivity by sweeping input power. The sensitivity point is where the RU can just detect the signal above its own noise floor. From Friis, your RU system NF ≈ 3 dB (LNA 2 dB + duplexer 0.5 dB + margin 0.5 dB) For B1 10 MHz: Noise floor = −174 + 70 + 3 = −101 dBm Required SNR for BLER ≤ 5% with QPSK 1/3 FRC ≈ −1 dB Sensitivity = −101 + (−1) = −102 dBm Your measured 2 dB error margin points from RSSI Results deck: ADC 0 (B1): −95.5 dBm ADC 2 (B3): −93.5 dBm These are 6–8 dB above the theoretical −102 dBm — consistent with: - Real LNA NF slightly higher than ideal - Duplexer loss adds to system NF - ADC quantisation noise contribution - Calibration conservatism (2 dB error margin is not the 0 dB point)
Why the PDF PDF reference (Friis 1944) matters
The PDF cites: Friis, H.T., "Noise Figures of Radio Receivers," Proc. of the IRE, July 1944. Harald Friis invented this framework in 1944 — and it is still the exact same formula used in your RuAuto sensitivity tests, your EXM noise floor calculations, and your RSSI calibration. 80 years later, kTB = −174 dBm/Hz and the Friis cascade formula still determine whether your AAU passes its 3GPP conformance tests.
PDF download available in your GitHub repo: docs/Understanding Noise Figure.pdf
DSA

Sensitivity & DSA — How they connect, what DSA really means

From your Understanding Noise Figure PDF + your lab procedure · What sensitivity is physically · How DSA is derived from sensitivity · Why modulation matters · Your exact numbers

DSA1 What sensitivity really is — from physics to your lab measurement Intermediate click to expand▾
Your current understanding — correct but surface level
You currently measure sensitivity as: minimum power injected from EXM, minus cable loss, at which the RU still decodes the signal. That is the measured sensitivity — the engineering test. But the PDF explains why that number is what it is, from first principles.
Sensitivity from first principles — the complete formula
Sensitivity (dBm) = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) + NF + Required_SNR Breaking down each term: −174 = kTB thermal noise floor at room temp, 1 Hz BW (physics absolute limit) +10×log(BW) = noise grows with bandwidth (unavoidable — wider BW = more noise) +NF = your hardware adds noise above the physics floor (set by LNA mostly) +Required_SNR = minimum SNR your modem needs to decode the modulation Your B1 10 MHz numbers: −174 + 70 (10 MHz) + 3 (system NF) + (−1) (QPSK 1/3 FRC SNR req) = −102 dBm 3GPP REFSENS limit = −69 dBm → your RU beats it by 33 dB ✓
Why cable loss directly degrades sensitivity
From the PDF: "An attenuator placed at the input of a system will increase the total Noise Figure with the same amount of its attenuation." Your test cable sits BEFORE the LNA — it is electrically a lossy passive device in the receive chain. A 2 dB cable loss = 2 dB higher system NF = 2 dB worse sensitivity. This is why you subtract cable loss when calculating the true RU sensitivity — you are not just correcting a power reading, you are removing the noise penalty your cable added to the measurement.
True RU sensitivity = EXM output power − cable_loss − connector_loss = what the RU actually sees at its antenna port Example: EXM outputs −97 dBm, cable loss = 2.5 dB True RU input = −97 − 2.5 = −99.5 dBm If RU decodes at this level → sensitivity = −99.5 dBm ✓
DSA2 Modulation and required SNR — why sensitivity changes with modulation order Intermediate click to expand▾
Why modulation changes the sensitivity number
The "Required SNR" term in the sensitivity formula is entirely determined by the modulation scheme and coding rate. Higher modulation order = symbols closer together on the constellation = need cleaner signal (higher SNR) to distinguish them = worse sensitivity.
ModulationBits/symbolRequired SNR (approx)Sensitivity impact vs QPSK
QPSK 1/3 (FRC A1)2−1 dBReference — best sensitivity
QPSK 1/22+1 dB2 dB worse than A1
16QAM 1/2 (FRC A3)4+5 dB6 dB worse sensitivity
64QAM 3/4 (FRC A5)6+16 dB17 dB worse sensitivity
256QAM 5/68+25 dB26 dB worse sensitivity
This is why 3GPP defines different FRC (Fixed Reference Channels) for sensitivity tests — A1 (QPSK 1/3) gives the best sensitivity number, A5 (64QAM) gives the worst. In your ul-rct-test results you can see different sensitivity numbers for each FRC: A1-3 achieves ~−112 dBm while A5 achieves only ~−85 to −93 dBm — a 20+ dB difference, entirely explained by the modulation SNR requirement.
DSA3 DSA — what it is, how it is calculated from sensitivity, your real values Advanced click to expand▾
What DSA stands for and means
DSA = Dynamic Signal Attenuation (or sometimes Downlink Signal Attenuation / Digital Step Attenuator depending on context). In your RCT framework and PRACH test configuration, DSA is the per-band offset applied to the base sensitivity threshold. It accounts for the fact that different bands have different RF path characteristics — different LNA NF, different duplexer loss, different filter insertion loss — so the sensitivity is different per band even with the same modulation.
How DSA is derived from sensitivity measurements
In RuAuto PRACH test configuration: PRACH detection threshold = base_dbm + DSA_per_band Where: base_dbm = baseline sensitivity threshold (e.g. −87 dBm) — measured reference DSA = per-band offset (positive or negative dB) relative to base_dbm DSA for each band is derived by: 1. Measure actual sensitivity per band (sweep EXM power until PRACH detects) 2. Compare to base_dbm reference 3. DSA = (actual_sensitivity_per_band) − base_dbm Example: base_dbm = −87 dBm (reference) B1 measured sensitivity = −89 dBm → DSA_B1 = −89 − (−87) = −2 dB (B1 is 2 dB MORE sensitive) B3 measured sensitivity = −86 dBm → DSA_B3 = −86 − (−87) = +1 dB (B3 is 1 dB LESS sensitive) B8 measured sensitivity = −91 dBm → DSA_B8 = −91 − (−87) = −4 dB (B8 is 4 dB MORE sensitive)
Why each band has a different sensitivity (and therefore different DSA)
BandFrequencyWhy sensitivity differs
B11950 MHz ULLNA NF typically ~1.5–2 dB at 2 GHz. Duplexer loss ~0.5 dB. Good sensitivity baseline.
B31747.5 MHz ULSlightly lower frequency → slightly better LNA NF. Similar to B1.
B8897.5 MHz ULLower frequency → better LNA NF (~1 dB at 900 MHz). Better sensitivity than B1. Also less free-space path loss at lower frequency.
B28728 MHz ULEven lower frequency → best LNA NF. Best raw sensitivity. But duplexer at 700 MHz is harder to design → may have more filter loss.
B412545 MHz TDDHighest frequency → highest LNA NF (~2.5–3 dB at 2.5 GHz). Worst sensitivity. Also TDD switch adds insertion loss before LNA.
The full sensitivity → DSA derivation chain
Step 1: Physics sets the floor Noise floor = −174 + 10×log(BW) dBm [kTB — fixed by temperature and bandwidth] Step 2: Your hardware adds NF System NF = NF_duplexer + NF_LNA + tiny contributions from rest (Friis) Noise floor with hardware = −174 + 10×log(BW) + NF_system Step 3: Modulation sets the required SNR Sensitivity = noise_floor + Required_SNR (per FRC/modulation) Step 4: Measurement gives you the real number Inject signal from EXM → sweep power down → find BLER ≤ 5% threshold Correct for cable loss → this is your measured sensitivity per band Step 5: DSA = difference from reference DSA_band = Sensitivity_band − base_reference_dBm Step 6: RuAuto uses DSA in test threshold PRACH_pass_threshold = base_dbm + DSA_band Test passes if: PRACH detects at input power ≤ pass_threshold
DSA in your tc_cadence.json — what it looks like
// In PRACH_KPI section of tc_cadence.json: "PRACH_KPI": { "base_dbm": -87, "DSA": { "B1": -2.0, // B1 is 2 dB more sensitive than base "B3": -1.5, // B3 is 1.5 dB more sensitive "B8": -4.0, // B8 is 4 dB more sensitive (lower freq = lower NF) "B28": -5.0, // B28 best sensitivity (700 MHz) "B41": +1.5 // B41 worst (2545 MHz + TDD switch loss) } } // Pass criterion for each band: // Power at RU port ≤ (base_dbm + DSA_band) while PRACH detects // B1: ≤ −87 + (−2) = −89 dBm // B41: ≤ −87 + 1.5 = −85.5 dBm
This is exactly why DSA is measured per band separately during lab bring-up and stored in the config — the physics of NF means every band will have a slightly different sensitivity, and the PRACH detector threshold must match the real hardware capability. If DSA is wrong (e.g. set to 0 when the real offset is −3 dB), PRACH tests either always pass trivially (DSA too low) or always fail (DSA too high, threshold stricter than the hardware can achieve).

Key takeaway — what you should remember
Sensitivity = minimum power (at RU port, cable-loss corrected) for successful decode. Set by physics (kTB) + your hardware (NF) + your modulation (required SNR).
NF dominates = LNA is first in chain → Friis formula → LNA NF is system NF. Every other stage is negligible.
Cable loss = NF penalty = your 2 dB test cable before the LNA makes the system 2 dB worse. This is why you always subtract cable loss when reporting sensitivity — you are removing the noise penalty your test setup added.
DSA = the measured per-band sensitivity offset from a common reference. Derived experimentally. Stored in config. Used so the PRACH test threshold matches real hardware capability per band.
Modulation changes sensitivity by 17+ dB = QPSK 1/3 (A1, −102 dBm) vs 64QAM 3/4 (A5, −85 dBm). Same radio, same hardware, completely different sensitivity number. This is why your ul-rct-test results show different sensitivity per FRC scenario.
KTB K × T × B explained — what each constant is, why room temp is the reference Beginner click to expand▾
kTB = the three ingredients of thermal noise
k
Boltzmann Constant
1.38 × 10⁻²³ Joules/Kelvin
Fixed constant of nature — like the speed of light. Converts temperature into energy at the atomic level. You NEVER change this. It tells you how much kinetic energy each electron has at a given temperature. Every electron in every conductor is moving randomly — k quantifies that motion.
📌 Think of it as: the energy-per-degree converter
T
Temperature (Kelvin)
290 K = 17°C = room temperature
Kelvin = Celsius + 273. The IEEE standard uses 290 K as reference — not 300 K. Hotter = faster electrons = more random noise energy. At absolute zero (0 K = −273°C) electrons stop — no thermal noise. But nothing in your lab is at 0 K, so thermal noise always exists.
Temperature → noise power scale:
4 K (cryogenic LNA) → −198 dBm/Hz
290 K (room temp) → −174 dBm/Hz ← YOUR REFERENCE
600 K (hot PA) → −171 dBm/Hz
B
Bandwidth (Hz)
The measurement window width
The wider the frequency window you open, the more noise power you collect — linearly. Double the bandwidth = double the noise power = +3 dB noise floor. This is unavoidable — wider BW always means worse sensitivity. This is why narrow-band IoT can achieve better sensitivity than 20 MHz LTE using identical hardware.
Bandwidth → noise floor (at 290 K, NF=0):
1 Hz BW → −174 dBm
200 kHz (GSM) → −121 dBm
1.4 MHz (LTE) → −112 dBm
10 MHz (LTE) → −104 dBm ← your tests
20 MHz (LTE) → −101 dBm
100 MHz (5G NR) → −94 dBm
k × T × B at room temperature (290 K) in 1 Hz bandwidth:
1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4.0×10⁻²¹ W = −174 dBm/Hz
This is the ABSOLUTE MINIMUM noise floor at room temperature. No receiver can ever do better than this — it is a law of physics, not a design target.
Yes — −174 dBm/Hz is the minimum noise at room temperature
You said it exactly right. kTB = −174 dBm/Hz is the minimum possible noise at room temperature. It is not something you can engineer away. As long as your receiver is at 290 K (room temperature), every 1 Hz of bandwidth will contain at least −174 dBm of thermal noise power. The only way to go below this is to physically cool the receiver (cryogenic LNAs used in radio telescopes operate at 4–20 K and achieve noise floors approaching −190 dBm/Hz).
Why 290 K and not 300 K (25°C)?
IEEE defined 290 K as the standard noise temperature reference because it makes kT a round number: kT = 4.0×10⁻²¹ W/Hz exactly. At 300 K it would be 4.14×10⁻²¹ — messier. The difference is only 0.15 dB, negligible for engineering purposes. All 3GPP specs, all Keysight instruments, and all noise figure calculations use 290 K as the reference.

Why each stage matters differently — the Friis insight visualised

The single most important rule from all of this
Everything before the LNA costs you sensitivity. Everything after the LNA is free.
→ Your test cable before the LNA: every dB of loss = 1 dB worse sensitivity
→ Your duplexer before the LNA: every dB of insertion loss = 1 dB worse sensitivity
→ Your connector quality before the LNA: loose connector = worse sensitivity
→ Your LNA itself: its NF determines the system. 1 dB better LNA = 1 dB better sensitivity
→ Your mixer NF: irrelevant — divided by LNA gain (×100)
→ Your ADC: irrelevant for sensitivity — quantisation noise is far below thermal noise
→ Your DU / software: irrelevant for NF — only affects required SNR (which depends on modulation)
CAREER

Your RF Mastery Roadmap — From Good to Exceptional

Concrete things to do, learn, and build — ordered by impact.

Skills that separate a great RF test engineer from a good one
RIGHT NOW
Master the link budget — daily habit
Before every test session, calculate on paper: what power should arrive at the DUT? What should the measurement instrument see? If the numbers don't match, find out why before you take a single measurement.
Engineers who do this catch setup errors in 5 minutes. Engineers who don't waste hours chasing ghost failures.
RIGHT NOW
Learn the VNA deeply — calibration is power
90% of engineers use the VNA but only 30% truly understand calibration. Being the person who can do a perfect 2-port SOLT, run time-domain analysis, and interpret Smith charts makes you the go-to for any hardware debug session.
1–3 MONTHS
Read TS 38.141-2 Chapters 6 and 7 completely
Not summaries — the actual spec. Every test you run has a 3GPP definition. When you can quote the spec when a result is questioned, you are the authority in the room. Download from 3gpp.org, free.
1–3 MONTHS
Build a personal test result database
For every test session, log: unit serial, firmware version, band, BW, channel model, result, temperature. After 3 months you'll see patterns no one else sees — which firmware changes affected which metrics, which bands have tighter margins.
3–6 MONTHS
Understand SCPI and automate one test
All your instruments (EXA, EXM, VNA) are SCPI-controllable over LAN/GPIB. Write a Python script to auto-configure the EXA for B3 ACLR, trigger a measurement, and save the result to a CSV. This skill multiplies your productivity 10×.
Start with: pip install pyvisa. Connect to EXA at its IP. Send ":FREQ:CENT 1842.5 MHz". Read ":MEAS:ACP?" back.
3–6 MONTHS
Learn noise figure measurement
NF is the single most important RX parameter but most test engineers have never measured it directly. Learn the Y-factor method and cold-source method. Use the EXA's noise figure application (N9069A option). When REFSENS fails, NF measurement tells you if it's the LNA or something else.
6–12 MONTHS
Master 3GPP spec navigation
Know which spec defines what: TS 38.101 (UE RF), TS 38.104 (gNB requirements), TS 38.141-1/2 (gNB conformance), TS 38.211 (physical channels), TS 38.214 (scheduling). When someone reports a failure, you can go directly to the normative definition.
6–12 MONTHS
Understand O-RAN fronthaul deeply
Read O-RAN.WG4.CUS (Control, User, Sync plane spec). Understand Category A vs Category B O-RU. Know what M-plane, C-plane, U-plane, S-plane carry. This knowledge is rare and makes you essential in open RAN deployments.
LONG TERM
Build a reputation as the person who writes the test
The highest-value RF test engineers don't just run tests — they define test methodology, write the test plan, challenge the spec limits when they don't make sense, and propose new tests when gaps appear. Your Midboard V1.5 RCA is exactly this kind of work.
LONG TERM
Contribute to internal knowledge base
Write up every root cause you find — the B28 power issue, the RFFE JTAG re-flash procedure, the B1A fault investigation. In 3 years, this becomes the institutional memory that makes you irreplaceable. Other engineers will cite your findings for years after.
